stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to assist a 28-year-old G1P0 at 39+5 weeks who has been pushing for 2 hours with epidural analgesia. The fetal head is at +2 station and OA position, mostly visible without parting the labia. CTG shows recurrent late decelerations over the past 20 minutes. The midwife reports good descent with last 3 contractions but slow progress.

The mother is exhausted and finding it difficult to push effectively. Bladder is empty. Fetal weight estimated 3500 g. No previous instrumental delivery or shoulder dystocia.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 124/76, HR 102; FHR 110-130 with recurrent late decelerations, variability reduced
data_table.Examination: Cervix fully dilated, head at +2 station OA, caput +, no moulding, vertex visible without parting labia, intact pelvic floor
data_table.Investigations: CTG abnormal with recurrent late decelerations; bladder empty; consent obtained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue maternal pushing with coached effort for 30 more minutes and reassess if delivery does not occur
Vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery using a Kiwi OmniCup with maximum 3 cup detachments and 20 minutes total
Category 1 caesarean section via emergency theatre transfer with delivery within 30 minutes of decision
Wrigley outlet forceps delivery with episiotomy without trial of vacuum or maternal pushing effort change
Augment labour with oxytocin infusion at 1 mU/min and reassess descent after another 30 minutes of pushing

stem: You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 34-year-old G3P2 at day 14 postpartum after an emergency caesarean for placental abruption with intraoperative blood loss of 2800 mL requiring 4 units of red cells and 2 units of FFP. She has been unable to establish breastfeeding despite repeated attempts and has had no menstrual return. Over the past week she reports profound fatigue, cold intolerance, weight loss despite poor appetite, persistent dizziness on standing, and one episode of confusion with measured BSL of 2.4 yesterday morning. She had no postpartum hypertension or eclampsia.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 supine, 78/52 standing, HR 76, T 36.1, RR 16
data_table.Examination: Pale, mildly dehydrated, no goitre, no hyperpigmentation, no axillary or pubic hair loss yet, breasts non-engorged with poor expressible colostrum
data_table.Investigations: Na 128, K 4.4, glucose 3.1 (random), Hb 92, TSH 0.4 (low), free T4 7 (low), free T3 3 (low), prolactin 1.8 (very low for postpartum), cortisol 8 am 110 (low), LH and FSH inappropriately low, IGF-1 low

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Initiate oral levothyroxine 100 mcg daily and review thyroid function in 6 weeks at clinic
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg now, then 50 mg 6 hourly, with oral hydrocortisone replacement after admission
Oral fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily and electrolyte replacement with normal saline 1 litre over 4 hours
Subcutaneous recombinant growth hormone 0.2 mg daily and bone mineral density assessment as outpatient
MRI pituitary with gadolinium contrast as outpatient in 4 weeks then commence hormone replacement

stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar reviewing a 38-year-old G3P3 at day 6 postpartum after an uncomplicated normal vaginal delivery at term. She presents to ED with progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea (sleeping on 3 pillows), bilateral ankle oedema, and persistent dry cough over the past 4 days. She is breastfeeding. She has no previous cardiac history and had normal ECGs at booking.

She has no chest pain. CXR shows pulmonary congestion with bilateral pleural effusions. ECG shows sinus tachycardia 118 and non-specific T-wave inversion in lateral leads. Echocardiogram by cardiology shows global LV dysfunction with LVEF 28%, mild MR, no thrombus, dilated LV cavity.

data_table.Examination: Raised JVP 7 cm, bilateral basal crepitations to mid-zones, bilateral pitting ankle oedema, no murmur, S3 gallop present
data_table.Investigations: CXR: bilateral pulmonary congestion and pleural effusions; ECG: sinus tachycardia, non-specific lateral T inversion; troponin 0.05 (mildly raised); BNP 1840; echo: LVEF 28% with global hypokinesis, mild MR, dilated LV, no thrombus, no pericardial effusion
data_table.Medications: Iron + folate; paracetamol for perineal soreness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV ramipril 2.5 mg daily plus IV furosemide 40 mg with continued breastfeeding under cardiology review
Oral spironolactone 25 mg daily and oral digoxin 125 mcg daily as first-line for postpartum heart failure
IV furosemide 40 mg, oral metoprolol 25 mg twice daily, and avoid all anticoagulation due to recent delivery
Urgent percutaneous mechanical circulatory support with VA-ECMO at tertiary cardiac centre referral
IV furosemide, oral bisoprolol, oral enalapril, anticoagulation with enoxaparin, and bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily

subtopic_detail: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder - SSRI luteal-phase dosing
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of severe irritability, mood lability, anxiety, and breast tenderness occurring exclusively in the 10 days before her menses and resolving within 2 days of menstrual onset. She has been prospectively charting symptoms for 3 cycles, confirming the pattern. Symptoms significantly impair her work performance and relationships. She has no psychiatric history outside these cyclical episodes.

data_table.Investigations: TSH 2.1 mIU/L (ref 0.5-4.0), Hb 132 g/L, prospective daily symptom diary confirms luteal-phase symptoms across 3 consecutive cycles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill with extended continuous cycling
Continuous oral progesterone 200 mg daily throughout the cycle
Calcium carbonate 1200 mg daily with vitamin B6 supplementation
Sertraline 50 mg daily during the luteal phase of each cycle
GnRH agonist with add-back oestrogen and progesterone therapy

subtopic_detail: Adenomyosis - imaging diagnosis and medical management
stem: A 38-year-old woman, para 3, presents with progressively worsening heavy menstrual bleeding and severe dysmenorrhoea over the past 2 years. She describes passing large clots and needing to change pads hourly on the heaviest days. She does not desire future fertility. Pelvic examination reveals a uniformly enlarged, globular, and tender uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a diffusely enlarged uterus with heterogeneous myometrium, myometrial cysts, and a poorly defined endometrial-myometrial junction.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L, ferritin 12 microg/L, TSH 2.4 mIU/L, transvaginal ultrasound as described, endometrial biopsy shows no hyperplasia or malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system insertion with iron replacement
Tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses with NSAIDs
Combined oral contraceptive pill with continuous cycling regimen
GnRH agonist with add-back therapy for 6 months then reassess
Hysterectomy as definitive treatment given completed family

subtopic_detail: Premature ovarian insufficiency - workup and HRT indication
stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhoea for 8 months. She previously had regular cycles from menarche at age 13. She has no children and desires future fertility. She reports worsening hot flushes, vaginal dryness, and difficulty sleeping. She has no history of chemotherapy, pelvic radiation, or pelvic surgery. Her BMI is 23.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 68 IU/L (repeated at 4 weeks: 72 IU/L), LH 45 IU/L, oestradiol 52 pmol/L (<200 consistent with oestrogen deficiency), TSH 2.8 mIU/L, prolactin 180 mIU/L (ref <500), AMH undetectable, karyotype 46,XX

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Clomifene citrate for ovulation induction with cycle monitoring
Hormone replacement therapy with oestradiol and cyclical progesterone
Combined oral contraceptive pill for symptom management
Immediate IVF referral with donor oocytes as primary strategy
Bone densitometry and calcium supplementation without hormone therapy

subtopic_detail: Vulvodynia - diagnosis of exclusion and initial management
stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with a 12-month history of burning vulvar pain, particularly provoked by tampon insertion, intercourse, and prolonged sitting. She has been treated empirically with multiple courses of antifungals without improvement. Examination reveals no erythema, ulceration, or skin changes. A cotton-swab test elicits sharp pain localised to the vestibule bilaterally. Vaginal pH is 4.2, wet mount microscopy is normal, and swabs for candida and bacterial vaginosis are negative.

data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab: no candida, no clue cells, no trichomonads. Vulvar biopsy (if performed): non-specific chronic inflammation only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Extended course of oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 6 months
Topical betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% ointment twice daily
Topical lidocaine 5% ointment with pelvic floor physiotherapy referral
Oral amitriptyline 10 mg nightly titrated up to 75 mg as tolerated
Vestibulectomy with vaginal advancement flap surgical referral

subtopic_detail: Fetal growth restriction - umbilical artery Doppler surveillance
stem: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman at 32 weeks gestation is referred after a growth ultrasound shows estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile with a head circumference to abdominal circumference ratio of 1.2. Amniotic fluid volume is at the lower limit of normal. She has no history of pre-eclampsia symptoms, her blood pressure is 125/78 mmHg, and urinalysis shows no proteinuria. She had a normal anatomy scan at 20 weeks.

data_table.Investigations: Estimated fetal weight <3rd centile, HC:AC ratio 1.2, amniotic fluid index 8 cm (lower limit of normal), umbilical artery Doppler pulsatility index elevated (>95th centile) with forward end-diastolic flow present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Immediate delivery by emergency caesarean section at 32 weeks gestation
Repeat growth ultrasound in 4 weeks with routine antenatal care
Low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily with increased fetal movement counting
Antenatal corticosteroids with twice-weekly Doppler and delivery planning
Maternal bed rest with weekly biophysical profile scoring only

subtopic_detail: Chronic hypertension in pregnancy - antihypertensive choice and aspirin
stem: A 35-year-old woman, para 1, presents at 10 weeks gestation for her first antenatal visit. She has a 3-year history of essential hypertension currently managed with ramipril 5 mg daily. Her blood pressure today is 148/92 mmHg. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated. Her BMI is 31. Renal function and urinalysis are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg (confirmed on repeat), HR 78, BMI 31
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 62 micromol/L, urine protein:creatinine ratio 12 mg/mmol (normal <30), FBC normal, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication change?

options.text: Continue ramipril and add low-dose aspirin 150 mg at bedtime
Cease ramipril and substitute atenolol 50 mg daily with aspirin
Cease ramipril and commence amlodipine 5 mg daily without aspirin
Cease ramipril and observe without antihypertensive unless BP exceeds 160/110
Cease ramipril and start labetalol 100 mg twice daily with aspirin 150 mg

subtopic_detail: Gestational subclinical hypothyroidism - levothyroxine treatment threshold
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 9 weeks gestation has routine antenatal bloods showing an elevated TSH. She is asymptomatic with no goitre, no personal history of thyroid disease, and no family history of autoimmune conditions. She takes no medications other than pregnancy multivitamins. Her first-trimester screening is otherwise unremarkable.

data_table.Investigations: TSH 4.8 mIU/L (first trimester reference <4.0), free T4 13 pmol/L (ref 10-22), TPO antibodies positive at 185 IU/mL (ref <35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat TSH in 4 weeks and treat only if TSH exceeds 10 mIU/L
Commence carbimazole 5 mg daily for borderline thyrotoxicosis
Reassure and monitor, as TSH is only marginally above the reference range
Increase dietary iodine intake and recheck TSH at 20 weeks
Commence levothyroxine 50 microg daily with TSH monitoring every 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Dichorionic twin pregnancy - surveillance schedule and complications
stem: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, is found to have a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy on her first-trimester ultrasound. The twins are concordant in size and both have normal nuchal translucency measurements. She is otherwise well with no medical comorbidities. She asks about the monitoring plan for her pregnancy.

data_table.Investigations: First-trimester ultrasound: DCDA twins confirmed by thick membrane and lambda sign, CRL concordance within 5%, both NTs normal, combined first-trimester screen low risk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surveillance schedule?

options.text: Monthly growth ultrasounds from 24 weeks with delivery at 40 weeks
Fortnightly growth scans from 16 weeks with delivery at 36 weeks
Routine singleton schedule with additional scan only if clinically indicated
Weekly Doppler surveillance from 26 weeks with delivery at 34 weeks
Growth ultrasounds every 4 weeks from 20 weeks with delivery planned at 37 weeks

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with absent periods for 6 months. She previously had regular cycles. She denies pregnancy. Her BMI is 32 and she has noticed increasing facial hair and acne over the past year. She exercises moderately and reports no significant stress, weight loss, or dietary restriction. She is not taking any medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 72, BMI 32
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, TSH 2.5 mIU/L, prolactin 220 mIU/L (ref <500), FSH 5.2 IU/L, LH 14.8 IU/L, oestradiol 280 pmol/L

lead_in: Which additional investigation is most important to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: MRI pituitary to exclude prolactinoma or pituitary adenoma
Karyotype analysis to exclude Turner syndrome mosaicism
24-hour urinary free cortisol to exclude Cushing syndrome
Serum anti-Mullerian hormone to assess ovarian reserve
Total testosterone and pelvic ultrasound for ovarian morphology

subtopic_detail: Uterine fibroids - medical management with GnRH antagonist
stem: A 42-year-old woman, para 2, presents with heavy menstrual bleeding causing iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 95 g/L, ferritin 8 microg/L). She has a 6 cm intramural fibroid and a 3 cm submucosal fibroid identified on transvaginal ultrasound. She has trialled a levonorgestrel IUS which was expelled twice due to the submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity. She does not desire future fertility but wishes to avoid surgery if possible.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 95 g/L, ferritin 8 microg/L, pelvic ultrasound: 6 cm intramural fibroid in the posterior wall, 3 cm submucosal fibroid (type 2) distorting the endometrial cavity, uterine volume 280 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral relugolix combination therapy with add-back oestrogen and norethindrone
GnRH agonist depot injection for 6 months as definitive treatment
Tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses with IV iron infusion
Uterine artery embolisation as the preferred fibroid treatment
Myomectomy via hysteroscopic approach for both fibroids simultaneously

subtopic_detail: Acute uterine inversion - recognition and manual replacement
stem: A 29-year-old woman has just delivered a 4.2 kg baby vaginally. Controlled cord traction was applied during the third stage and the placenta delivered with difficulty. Immediately after, she becomes pale, hypotensive, and complains of severe lower abdominal pain. On examination there is a large, dark red mass visible at the introitus and the uterine fundus is not palpable abdominally. Estimated blood loss is 800 mL and rising.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 125, BP 85/50 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 96% on room air

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV oxytocin bolus and bimanual uterine compression for atonic PPH
IV fluid resuscitation with immediate manual replacement of the uterus
Emergency hysterectomy as definitive treatment for the inversion
Terbutaline 250 microg subcutaneously to relax the uterus then replace
Attempt manual removal of retained placental fragments first then reassess

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhoea for 5 months following surgical management of a missed miscarriage. She had two D&C procedures within 3 weeks due to retained products after the first. She reports cyclical lower abdominal pain each month but no menstrual bleeding. A progesterone withdrawal test with medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg for 10 days fails to produce a withdrawal bleed. Pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, FSH 6.5 IU/L, LH 8.2 IU/L, oestradiol 320 pmol/L, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, prolactin 180 mIU/L (ref <500)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Pelvic MRI to assess endometrial thickness and uterine anatomy
Saline infusion sonohysterography to outline the uterine cavity
Office hysteroscopy to visualise and potentially divide intrauterine adhesions
Hysterosalpingogram to assess tubal patency and cavity contour
Endometrial biopsy to assess endometrial response to oestrogen

subtopic_detail: Rh alloimmunisation - MCA Doppler monitoring and intrauterine transfusion
stem: A 34-year-old Rh-negative woman, gravida 3 para 2, is at 26 weeks gestation. Her first pregnancy was uneventful but she did not receive anti-D prophylaxis postpartum. Anti-D antibodies were detected at booking with a titre of 1:32. Serial titres have risen to 1:128 over the past 4 weeks. The fetus has been confirmed Rh-positive on cell-free fetal DNA testing. Current ultrasound shows normal amniotic fluid and fetal growth.

data_table.Investigations: Anti-D titre 1:128 (critical titre 1:16), cell-free fetal DNA confirms Rh-positive fetus, ultrasound: normal growth, AFI 14 cm, middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity 1.6 MoM (threshold for moderate-severe anaemia >1.5 MoM)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat MCA Doppler in 2 weeks and continue expectant management
Immediate delivery by caesarean section for ex-utero transfusion
Maternal plasmapheresis to reduce circulating anti-D antibody levels
Referral for cordocentesis and intrauterine transfusion at a fetal medicine centre
Commence maternal IV immunoglobulin infusion to suppress haemolysis

subtopic_detail: Maternal SLE in pregnancy - lupus nephritis versus pre-eclampsia discrimination
stem: A 30-year-old woman with known SLE presents at 28 weeks gestation with worsening oedema, hypertension, and proteinuria. She was in clinical remission on hydroxychloroquine for 12 months before conception. Over the past week her blood pressure has risen to 155/98 mmHg, and she has developed significant proteinuria. She has no headache or visual symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, platelets 165 x10^9/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L (baseline 55), urine PCR 280 mg/mmol, C3 0.52 g/L (low, ref 0.9-1.8), C4 0.08 g/L (low, ref 0.1-0.4), anti-dsDNA 85 IU/mL (elevated, ref <30), urate 0.38 mmol/L (normal), LDH 195 U/L (normal), ALT 28 U/L

lead_in: Which feature most strongly supports a diagnosis of lupus nephritis flare rather than pre-eclampsia?

options.text: Rising creatinine from baseline with new-onset significant proteinuria
Hypertension developing after 20 weeks gestation in a primigravida
Platelet count remaining above 150 with normal liver transaminases
Significant peripheral oedema with rapid weight gain over one week
Falling complement C3 and C4 levels with rising anti-dsDNA antibodies

subtopic_detail: Fetal macrosomia in gestational diabetes - delivery timing and mode
stem: A 36-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, with gestational diabetes on insulin therapy is at 38 weeks gestation. Her previous delivery was an uncomplicated vaginal birth of a 3.5 kg baby. Growth ultrasound today estimates fetal weight at 4.8 kg (>97th centile) with an abdominal circumference above the 99th centile. Glycaemic control has been suboptimal despite insulin dose adjustments, with recent postprandial readings consistently 8-10 mmol/L.

data_table.Investigations: EFW 4.8 kg (>97th centile), AC >99th centile, amniotic fluid index 24 cm (upper limit of normal), HbA1c 6.2% (44 mmol/mol), cervix 2 cm dilated, Bishop score 7

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Offer induction of labour at 38-39 weeks with early recourse to caesarean
Elective caesarean section at 39 weeks without trial of labour
Continue expectant management until spontaneous labour at term
Increase insulin doses aggressively and delay delivery until 40 weeks
Urgent caesarean section today for macrosomia and polyhydramnios

subtopic_detail: Uterine rupture - recognition during trial of labour after caesarean
stem:
A 32-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, is undergoing a trial of labour after one previous lower-segment caesarean section. She is at 39 weeks with a singleton cephalic presentation and was progressing well in active labour. At 7 cm dilatation, the CTG suddenly shows a prolonged fetal bradycardia to 70 bpm. She reports sudden, severe abdominal pain that persists between contractions.

On examination the previously regular contractions have ceased and there is tenderness over the lower uterine segment. Vaginal examination shows the presenting part is now at a higher station than 30 minutes ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 118, BP 95/60 mmHg, fetal heart rate 70 bpm sustained for 4 minutes
data_table.Examination: Uterine tenderness over lower segment, loss of contractions, presenting part recession from station -1 to -3

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Placental abruption with emergency category 1 caesarean preparation
Uterine rupture with immediate category 1 caesarean and laparotomy
Cord prolapse with immediate vaginal examination and fetal elevation
Scar dehiscence with IV tocolysis and continued close monitoring
Uterine hyperstimulation with IV terbutaline and position change

subtopic_detail: Cervical cancer in pregnancy - management by stage and gestation
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation has a cervical screening test performed at her first antenatal visit that returns oncogenic HPV 16 positive with high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion on cytology. Colposcopy shows a 1.5 cm visible lesion on the anterior cervical lip. Colposcopically directed biopsy confirms invasive squamous cell carcinoma. MRI of the pelvis shows a tumour confined to the cervix with no parametrial extension, no lymph node involvement, and tumour depth of invasion 6 mm (FIGO stage IB1).

data_table.Investigations: HPV 16 positive, cytology: HSIL, biopsy: invasive SCC, MRI: stage IB1 (tumour confined to cervix, 1.5 cm, depth 6 mm, no parametrial involvement, no lymph nodes)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Immediate radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection
Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy commencing at 14 weeks gestation
Defer definitive treatment with serial colposcopic and MRI surveillance
Large loop excision of the transformation zone to remove the lesion
Concurrent chemoradiation as per non-pregnant treatment protocol

subtopic_detail: Retained placenta - management approach and timing
stem: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, has just delivered a healthy 3.4 kg baby vaginally. Active management of the third stage was performed with IM oxytocin 10 IU at delivery of the anterior shoulder. Controlled cord traction was attempted but the placenta has not delivered after 45 minutes. The cord is intact and there is steady vaginal bleeding estimated at 500 mL. The uterus is firm and well-contracted. The bladder has been emptied with a catheter.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/72 mmHg, estimated blood loss 500 mL, well-contracted uterus palpable at the umbilicus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat IV oxytocin infusion and continue controlled cord traction
Umbilical vein injection of saline and oxytocin to aid separation
Arrange pelvic ultrasound to confirm placental location before intervening
Manual removal of placenta in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia
Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate spray to relax the cervix and uterus

subtopic_detail: Peripartum thrombotic microangiopathy - TTP versus HELLP versus aHUS
stem: A 28-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks gestation presents with headache, confusion, and petechiae. She was previously well with normal antenatal screening. Blood pressure is 145/90 mmHg. Blood film shows schistocytes and polychromasia. Her platelets have dropped from 220 to 18 x10^9/L over 3 days. Liver transaminases are normal and there is no proteinuria. Her creatinine is 62 micromol/L (baseline 50). LDH is markedly elevated at 2800 U/L.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 82 g/L, platelets 18 x10^9/L, reticulocyte count 8.2% (elevated), blood film: schistocytes, polychromasia, LDH 2800 U/L, haptoglobin <0.1 g/L, ALT 32 U/L, AST 38 U/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, urine PCR 10 mg/mmol (normal), fibrinogen 3.8 g/L (normal), INR 1.0

lead_in: Which investigation is most critical to guide immediate management?

options.text: Complement C3, C4, and factor H levels to assess for aHUS
Liver ultrasound with Doppler to assess for hepatic infarction
DIC screen with D-dimer, fibrinogen, and fibrin degradation products
Renal biopsy to distinguish between TTP and HUS histologically
ADAMTS13 activity level with inhibitor screen before plasma exchange

subtopic_detail: Advice about a future pregnancy after a tubal ectopic
stem: A 29-year-old woman had surgery for a ruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy six weeks ago. The right tube and both ovaries looked normal at operation. She is well and plans to conceive again next year. She asks what should be done differently.

data_table.Operation: Laparoscopic left salpingectomy; no adhesions seen
data_table.Postoperative: Haemoglobin 118 g/L; uncomplicated recovery; hCG now undetectable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Arrange a transvaginal ultrasound at about six weeks next time
She will need in vitro fertilisation to conceive from now onwards
Hysterosalpingography should be arranged before she tries again
Her risk of another ectopic pregnancy is no higher than average
She should wait two years before attempting another pregnancy

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 9 weeks gestation presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and cramping lower abdominal pain for 4 hours. On speculum examination, the cervical os is open with tissue visible at the os. She has soaked through four pads in 2 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102 bpm, BP 105/68 mmHg, RR 18, Temp 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L (booking Hb 132 g/L), blood group A Rh-negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral mifepristone 200 mg now followed by vaginal misoprostol 800 mcg in 48 hours
Remove visible tissue from the cervical os with sponge forceps and arrange surgical evacuation
Establish IV access with fluid resuscitation and arrange urgent transvaginal ultrasound first
Administer IV oxytocin 10 units and observe for spontaneous expulsion over the next 4 hours
Administer intramuscular tranexamic acid 1 g and vaginal misoprostol 400 mcg sublingually

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with 8 months of amenorrhoea, frequent hot flushes disrupting sleep, and vaginal dryness affecting her quality of life. She has an intact uterus. Her mother had breast cancer diagnosed at age 74. She has no personal history of VTE, cardiovascular disease, or hormone-sensitive malignancy. BMI is 26 kg/m2.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 68 IU/L, oestradiol 42 pmol/L, mammogram (6 months ago) BI-RADS 1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial hormonal treatment?

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patches alone titrated to symptom control over 3 months
Oral conjugated equine oestrogens with continuous medroxyprogesterone acetate daily
Transdermal oestradiol patches combined with cyclical oral micronised progesterone
Oral tibolone 2.5 mg daily as a single-agent combined hormonal preparation
Vaginal oestrogen pessary alone for both vasomotor and urogenital symptoms

stem: A 28-year-old woman attends for routine cervical screening. She has no symptoms and no history of abnormal cervical pathology. She received the full course of HPV vaccination at age 13. Her last cervical screening test was a negative HPV test 5 years ago. She asks about the recommended screening interval and method.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her cervical screening?

options.text: She is overdue and should have a clinician-collected HPV test today with repeat screening in 3 years
She is not yet due for screening and should return at age 30 for her next scheduled HPV test
She should have conventional cytology given her vaccinated status and repeat screening in 3 years
She is due now and can choose either self-collected vaginal or clinician-collected cervical HPV test
She can safely extend her screening interval to 10 years given HPV vaccination and a prior negative result

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with irregular menstrual cycles occurring every 45-90 days for the past 3 years, moderate acne, and a BMI of 31 kg/m2. She has no hirsutism. She does not desire pregnancy. Pelvic ultrasound shows bilateral ovaries with 14 and 16 antral follicles respectively and normal ovarian volume.

data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 2.8 nmol/L (ref 0.5-1.8), SHBG 22 nmol/L (ref 20-130), free androgen index 12.7 (ref < 5), DHEAS 8.2 micromol/L (ref 2.7-9.2), TSH 2.1 mIU/L, prolactin 180 mIU/L (ref < 500), 17-OH progesterone 4.2 nmol/L (ref < 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Metformin 500 mg twice daily with dose titration over 4 weeks to a target of 2000 mg daily
Spironolactone 50 mg twice daily with monthly monitoring of serum potassium and renal function
Clomifene citrate 50 mg daily on days 2 to 6 with concurrent ultrasound follicle tracking
Cyproterone acetate 100 mg daily for 21 days each cycle as monotherapy for acne and hirsutism
Combined oral contraceptive pill with ethinylestradiol and cyproterone acetate plus lifestyle modification

stem: A 33-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation is diagnosed with gestational diabetes following a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. She has no prior history of diabetes. Her BMI at booking was 29 kg/m2. She has been performing self-monitoring of blood glucose levels for 2 weeks following dietary and exercise counselling.

data_table.Investigations: OGTT results - fasting 5.6 mmol/L (ref < 5.1), 1-hour 10.8 mmol/L (ref < 10.0), 2-hour 9.2 mmol/L (ref < 8.5). Home BSL diary (past week) - fasting 5.4-6.1 mmol/L, 1-hour postprandial 7.8-9.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg with dinner and titrate to achieve fasting BSL below 5.0 mmol/L
Continue dietary modification for an additional 2 weeks before reassessing glycaemic control
Commence insulin glargine at bedtime starting at 4 units with self-titration protocols
Commence glibenclamide 2.5 mg with breakfast as a first-line oral hypoglycaemic agent
Refer directly for elective caesarean section at 38 weeks given the elevated glucose levels

stem: A 30-year-old Rh-negative woman at 18 weeks gestation presents after a minor motor vehicle accident. She was wearing a seatbelt and reports mild abdominal discomfort but no vaginal bleeding. Fetal movements are present. Her antibody screen at booking was negative. The fetal Rh status is unknown.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg, RR 14, Temp 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus palpable at the umbilicus, non-tender, no uterine contractions on palpation, no vaginal bleeding on speculum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding Rh prophylaxis?

options.text: No anti-D required as there is no vaginal bleeding and the clinical examination is fully reassuring in this case
Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscularly and perform Kleihauer-Betke test for large fetomaternal haemorrhage
Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly and arrange follow-up ultrasound in 48 hours for reassessment
Defer anti-D until the routine 28-week prophylaxis dose as there is no evidence of active vaginal bleeding currently
Perform Kleihauer-Betke test first and administer anti-D only if the result confirms significant fetomaternal haemorrhage

stem: A 34-year-old woman at 33 weeks gestation presents with intense generalised pruritus for 5 days that is worse on her palms and soles at night. She has no rash, no abdominal pain, and no jaundice. She has had an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy.

data_table.Investigations: Total bile acids 48 micromol/L (ref < 6), ALT 72 U/L (ref < 35), AST 58 U/L (ref < 35), GGT 28 U/L (ref < 35), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (ref < 20), INR 1.0, hepatitis B and C serology negative, liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassurance that pruritus in pregnancy is common and prescribe emollients with chlorphenamine at night
Commence prednisolone 30 mg daily for presumed polymorphic eruption of pregnancy and review in 1 week
Commence ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily, weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring, and plan delivery at 37 weeks
Commence colestyramine 4 g four times daily and plan delivery at 39 weeks if symptoms persist on treatment
Commence ursodeoxycholic acid 250 mg twice daily, fortnightly bile acid monitoring, and plan delivery at 38 weeks

stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks gestation presents with persistent nausea and vomiting for 3 weeks. She has been unable to tolerate any oral intake for the past 48 hours and has lost 4 kg since her booking visit 3 weeks ago. She reports dark concentrated urine and dizziness on standing. She has tried oral ginger and small frequent meals without improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104 bpm, BP 95/62 mmHg (supine), BP 80/54 mmHg (standing), Temp 37.0 degrees C, weight 58 kg (booking 62 kg)
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, chloride 92 mmol/L, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, urea 8.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, TSH 0.08 mIU/L, free T4 24 pmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral ondansetron 4 mg wafer and trial of oral fluids before considering admission to hospital
Commence dexamethasone 8 mg IV twice daily as rescue antiemetic therapy for refractory symptoms
Commence IV thiamine 100 mg, initiate outpatient IV fluid infusions 3 times weekly, and prescribe metoclopramide
Admit for IV normal saline with potassium replacement, IV thiamine 100 mg, and IV ondansetron 4 mg 8-hourly
Start carbimazole 10 mg daily for thyrotoxicosis causing the vomiting and arrange thyroid recheck in 2 weeks

stem: A 38-year-old woman underwent suction curettage 2 weeks ago for a complete hydatidiform mole confirmed on histopathology. Her pre-evacuation beta-hCG was 285,000 IU/L. She is clinically well with no vaginal bleeding. She asks about follow-up requirements and when she can try to conceive again.

data_table.Investigations: Current beta-hCG 18,400 IU/L, chest X-ray normal, FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding post-molar follow-up?

options.text: Serial weekly beta-hCG until normal, then 6 monthly levels for 1 year before any conception attempt is allowed
No further monitoring needed as beta-hCG is declining appropriately and she can conceive at any time now
Register with the Australian GTD registry, commence chemotherapy now given the high initial beta-hCG level
Commence combined oral contraceptive pill immediately and repeat curettage to ensure complete uterine evacuation
Register with the GTD registry, serial weekly beta-hCG until normal, then monthly levels for 6 months with reliable contraception

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of vague pelvic fullness. Transvaginal ultrasound identifies a 7 cm left ovarian cyst that is unilocular with thin smooth walls, no solid components, no septae, and no internal vascularity on Doppler. The right ovary appears normal. She is premenopausal with regular cycles.

data_table.Investigations: CA-125 18 U/mL (ref < 35), beta-hCG negative, FBC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 8-12 weeks to assess for spontaneous resolution of the cyst
Urgent referral to gynaecological oncology for suspected ovarian malignancy based on size
Laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy to obtain histological diagnosis and prevent ovarian torsion
Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill to promote cyst resolution over the next 6 weeks
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast to better characterise the cyst before further management

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents at 7 weeks gestation with right-sided pelvic pain and light vaginal bleeding. She had a right salpingectomy 2 years ago for a tubal ectopic pregnancy. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a gestational sac with a yolk sac located eccentrically in the right cornual region of the uterus, surrounded by less than 5 mm of myometrium. The interstitial line sign is positive. Beta-hCG is 12,800 IU/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 122/74 mmHg, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mild right adnexal tenderness, no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 as for standard tubal ectopic protocol
Laparoscopic cornuostomy or cornual wedge resection by a surgeon experienced in this procedure
Expectant management with 48-hourly beta-hCG levels as the patient is currently haemodynamically stable
Emergency laparotomy with ipsilateral cornual resection and possible hysterectomy for definitive management
Ultrasound-guided local injection of methotrexate directly into the gestational sac under procedural sedation

stem: You are the registrar called to a delivery where the midwife reports the fetal head has delivered but the anterior shoulder has not followed despite gentle downward traction. The turtle sign is present with the fetal head retracting tightly against the perineum. McRoberts positioning with suprapubic pressure has been applied for 30 seconds without success. The estimated fetal weight was 4.2 kg on recent ultrasound.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 92 bpm, BP 130/82 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered in OA position, anterior shoulder impacted behind symphysis, turtle sign present, McRoberts with suprapubic pressure unsuccessful

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply fundal pressure to help push the anterior shoulder past the symphysis pubis and deliver the baby distally
Apply strong downward traction on the fetal head to deliver the impacted anterior shoulder beyond the symphysis
Perform an episiotomy to create more space for the anterior shoulder to pass through the soft tissue outlet
Perform internal rotational manoeuvres by applying pressure to the posterior shoulder to rotate into an oblique diameter
Move the patient onto all fours (Gaskin manoeuvre) as the immediate next intervention before any internal manoeuvres

stem: A 35-year-old woman is 10 minutes post-delivery of a term infant via normal vaginal birth after induction of labour with oxytocin. She suddenly becomes acutely dyspnoeic, agitated, and cyanotic. She rapidly loses consciousness and develops generalised tonic-clonic convulsions. The midwife notices profuse vaginal bleeding that does not respond to fundal massage and oxytocin.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, BP 70/40 mmHg, SpO2 78% on 15 L non-rebreather mask, RR 32, Temp 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care blood gas - pH 7.18, lactate 8.2 mmol/L, fibrinogen 0.6 g/L (ref 2.0-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate initial management priority?

options.text: Amniotic fluid embolism - activate massive transfusion protocol, commence aggressive resuscitation with high-flow oxygen, and prioritise early fibrinogen replacement
Massive pulmonary embolism - commence therapeutic heparin infusion and arrange CT pulmonary angiography while stabilising with vasopressors
Eclamptic seizure with uterine atony - administer magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose with bimanual uterine compression and uterotonics
Uterine atony with air embolism - position in left lateral with head down, commence IV oxytocin infusion, and aspirate air via central venous catheter
Septic shock from chorioamnionitis - commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics with aggressive fluid resuscitation and vasopressor support

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a 5-year history of worsening dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and cyclical dyschezia with rectal bleeding during menstruation. She has been trying to conceive for 18 months without success. Previous transvaginal ultrasound showed a 4 cm left ovarian endometrioma. She has tried combined oral contraceptive pill and oral progestogens, which provided partial symptom relief but she ceased them to attempt pregnancy. On examination, there is a fixed retroverted uterus with tender nodularity in the uterosacral ligaments and rectovaginal septum.

data_table.Investigations: AMH 18 pmol/L (age-appropriate), CA-125 82 U/mL (ref < 35), day 3 FSH 7.2 IU/L, partner semen analysis normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Resume combined oral contraceptive pill continuously for 6 months to suppress disease before natural conception attempts
Referral to a multidisciplinary endometriosis centre for laparoscopic excision with concurrent fertility planning
Commence GnRH agonist (leuprorelin) with add-back HRT for 6 months followed by IVF with no surgical intervention
Proceed directly to IVF without surgical treatment to minimise further delay in achieving fertility this year
Trial of dienogest 2 mg daily for 3 months as targeted endometriosis treatment while continuing to attempt conception

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation following IVF presents with sudden onset right iliac fossa pain radiating to the right flank, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. She describes the pain as intermittent and colicky, having started 4 hours ago. She has a known 8 cm right ovarian cyst that was identified at her IVF egg collection and has been monitored. On examination, there is tenderness in the right iliac fossa with guarding.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98 bpm, BP 115/72 mmHg, Temp 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 12.8 x10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L, urinalysis negative, fetal heart rate on Doppler 158 bpm. Ultrasound: enlarged right ovary 9 cm with peripherally displaced follicles and absent intraovarian venous flow on Doppler, free fluid in pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Conservative management with analgesia and antiemetics, observation for 24 hours, and repeat ultrasound tomorrow
Arrange urgent appendicectomy as the most likely diagnosis is acute appendicitis given the right iliac fossa pain
Urgent laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation, performed by a surgeon experienced in laparoscopy during pregnancy
Urgent laparotomy with right oophorectomy given the absent Doppler flow indicating likely complete ovarian necrosis
MRI pelvis to confirm the diagnosis before proceeding to surgery, with analgesia and antiemetics in the interim

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 29 weeks gestation presents with a gush of clear fluid from the vagina 2 hours ago. Sterile speculum examination reveals pooling of clear fluid in the posterior fornix. AmniSure test is positive. She has no contractions, no vaginal bleeding, and no fever. Fetal heart rate on CTG is 145 bpm with normal variability and no decelerations. Group B Streptococcus status is unknown.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 80 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: WCC 10.2 x10^9/L, CRP 4 mg/L, urine MCS pending, low vaginal swab taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Immediate delivery by caesarean section given the risk of ascending infection at 29 weeks gestational age with ruptured membranes
Administer oral erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly alone and plan delivery at 34 weeks if no complications arise in the interim
Commence IV amoxicillin and erythromycin for 48 hours then switch to oral, and administer corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation
Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now and repeat in 24 hours, commence erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days, and manage expectantly
Administer magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose for fetal neuroprotection, betamethasone for lungs, and plan delivery within 48 hours

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is seen at 20 weeks gestation for a routine ultrasound. Twin 1 has a deepest vertical pocket of amniotic fluid of 1.8 cm with a collapsed-appearing bladder. Twin 2 has a deepest vertical pocket of 12 cm with a distended bladder. Both twins have concordant estimated fetal weights. Umbilical artery Dopplers are normal in both twins.

data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound - Twin 1: DVP 1.8 cm (oligohydramnios), bladder not visualised, EFW 320 g (50th centile). Twin 2: DVP 12 cm (polyhydramnios), distended bladder, EFW 330 g (50th centile). Placenta anterior, single shared mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 2 weeks as the discordance may be transient and the Dopplers are currently reassuring
Amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac to reduce the deepest vertical pocket below 8 cm and relieve symptoms
Selective fetal reduction of the donor twin to protect the recipient from the complications of TTTS
Immediate delivery by caesarean section at 20 weeks as the condition is not compatible with continued pregnancy
Urgent referral to a fetal medicine centre for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental vascular anastomoses

subtopic_detail: Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia and vulval cancer
stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of a persistent, firm, raised vulval lesion on the left labium majus that has slowly enlarged. She reports intermittent pruritus and occasional bleeding when the lesion is irritated by clothing. She has a history of lichen sclerosus treated with topical clobetasol for 10 years. On examination, there is a 2.5 cm exophytic lesion on the left labium majus with irregular borders and contact bleeding. There are background white atrophic changes consistent with lichen sclerosus.

data_table.Examination: 2.5 cm firm exophytic lesion on left labium majus, irregular borders, contact bleeding, no palpable inguinofemoral lymphadenopathy, background lichen sclerosus changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Punch biopsy of the lesion under local anaesthesia with referral to gynaecological oncology for results and management
Increase clobetasol to daily application for 3 months as the lesion is likely a hypertrophic lichen sclerosus plaque
Wide local excision of the lesion with 1 cm margins as both diagnostic and therapeutic procedure at this visit
Apply topical imiquimod 5% cream three times weekly for 16 weeks for presumed HPV-related vulval intraepithelial neoplasia
Arrange MRI of the pelvis and inguinal regions to stage the lesion before proceeding with any local intervention

stem: A 34-year-old woman at 7 weeks gestation following IVF with double embryo transfer presents with acute right iliac fossa pain and light vaginal spotting over the past 6 hours. She has no significant past medical history. Transvaginal ultrasound confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy with fetal heart activity and a crown-rump length consistent with dates. A 28 mm right adnexal mass with a hyperechoic ring sign is identified, with moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104 bpm, BP 106/68 mmHg, T 36.9 C, RR 18, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Right adnexal tenderness, guarding in right iliac fossa, cervix closed.
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 48,000 IU/L, Hb 108 g/L, platelets 245 x10^9/L, group and save held.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG levels every 48 hours
Urgent laparoscopic right salpingectomy preserving intrauterine pregnancy
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate at 50 mg per square metre
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 48 hours to confirm the diagnosis
Laparotomy with bilateral salpingectomy and pregnancy termination

subtopic_detail: Interpreting the day 4 to day 7 hCG change after methotrexate
stem: A 30-year-old woman was given intramuscular methotrexate seven days ago for a tubal ectopic pregnancy. She has mild intermittent left iliac fossa discomfort, no dizziness and no shoulder tip pain. Her abdomen is soft.

data_table.Serum hCG: Day 0: 2,600 IU/L; day 4: 2,900 IU/L; day 7: 2,700 IU/L
data_table.Investigations: Hb 126 g/L; creatinine 64 micromol/L; ALT 24 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a second dose of intramuscular methotrexate today
Repeat the hCG in one week without any further treatment
Arrange laparoscopic salpingectomy on the emergency list
Admit for intravenous methotrexate over the next 24 hours
Begin a course of oral mifepristone and then misoprostol

stem:
A 36-year-old G3P2 woman at 37 weeks gestation presents with 4 days of progressive dyspnoea, now orthopnoeic with a dry cough. She was seen 48 hours ago by her GP who attributed the symptoms to the late third trimester. She has no history of hypertension or cardiac disease. Her two prior pregnancies were uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. On arrival she is sitting upright, visibly distressed, and unable to complete sentences.

Auscultation reveals bilateral basal crackles to the mid-zones and a third heart sound. There is no peripheral oedema beyond mild ankle swelling. Her blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and urinalysis shows no proteinuria. Bedside echocardiography demonstrates a left ventricular ejection fraction of 28% with global hypokinesis and no valvular pathology.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 88% on room air, T 36.6 C.
data_table.Investigations: NT-proBNP 8,400 pg/mL, troponin I 0.08 ng/mL (ULN 0.04), Hb 122 g/L, platelets 234 x10^9/L, ALT 32 U/L, creatinine 72 micromol/L, urine PCR < 10 mg/mmol. CTG: reassuring with no decelerations.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Commence IV magnesium sulfate infusion and plan urgent caesarean delivery
Administer IV labetalol 20 mg for blood pressure control and monitor closely
Commence high-flow oxygen and arrange urgent induction of labour with oxytocin
Commence IV furosemide and oxygen with urgent cardiology and obstetric review
Urgent CT pulmonary angiogram to exclude massive pulmonary embolism first

subtopic_detail: Antiphospholipid syndrome in recurrent pregnancy loss
stem: A 31-year-old woman attends the recurrent miscarriage clinic after three consecutive first-trimester losses, all between 8 and 10 weeks gestation. She has no living children. Investigations reveal persistently positive lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 14 weeks apart and anticardiolipin IgG at 62 GPL units (positive > 40). Her partner's karyotype and her own are normal. Thyroid function, glucose tolerance, and uterine cavity assessment by saline infusion sonography are all normal. She is now 6 weeks pregnant again, confirmed by ultrasound showing an intrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sac.

data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant: positive (confirmed on two occasions 14 weeks apart). Anticardiolipin IgG: 62 GPL (positive > 40). Anti-beta2 glycoprotein I IgG: negative. FBC, UEC, LFTs, TFTs: normal. OGTT: normal. Parental karyotypes: normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for this pregnancy?

options.text: Low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily alone without any anticoagulation therapy
Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1.5 mg per kg daily without additional aspirin
Low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily plus prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily
Warfarin at a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 throughout the entire pregnancy
Prednisolone 20 mg daily plus low-dose aspirin throughout the pregnancy

stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 woman at 9 weeks gestation presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and cramping lower abdominal pain for 6 hours. She has soaked through four pads in the last 2 hours. She is Rh-negative. On examination, the cervical os is open with products of conception visible at the os. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac containing a fetal pole with no cardiac activity and a crown-rump length of 18 mm. She is haemodynamically stable and wishes active management to resolve the miscarriage quickly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 94 bpm, BP 112/72 mmHg, T 36.8 C.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 116 g/L, blood group A Rh-negative, no irregular antibodies detected.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral mifepristone 200 mg followed by misoprostol 800 mcg in 24 to 48 hours
Surgical evacuation of retained products plus anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU
Expectant management with review in one week and serial beta-hCG levels
Vaginal misoprostol 800 mcg alone without prior mifepristone as a single dose
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV plus oxytocin infusion to reduce bleeding and observe

subtopic_detail: Menopausal hormone therapy route and VTE risk
stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with severe vasomotor symptoms including 12 to 15 hot flushes daily and significant sleep disturbance for the past 8 months since her last menstrual period. Her FSH is 68 IU/L confirming menopause. She has a BMI of 36 kg per square metre, a personal history of provoked deep vein thrombosis following knee arthroscopy 3 years ago (completed 3 months of rivaroxaban, now off anticoagulation), and well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine. She has an intact uterus. Lifestyle measures have been insufficient. She is requesting hormonal treatment for her symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 68 IU/L, oestradiol < 100 pmol/L, TSH 2.4 mIU/L, FBC normal, LFTs normal, lipid profile: total cholesterol 5.8 mmol/L, LDL 3.4 mmol/L, HDL 1.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate hormonal treatment approach?

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg daily plus oral medroxyprogesterone
Oral tibolone 2.5 mg daily as a combined oestrogenic and progestogenic agent
Venlafaxine 75 mg daily as a non-hormonal alternative for vasomotor symptoms
Oral oestradiol valerate 2 mg daily plus micronised progesterone 100 mg daily
Transdermal oestradiol 50 mcg patch plus oral micronised progesterone nightly

subtopic_detail: Management of cervical screening abnormality during pregnancy
stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 woman at 14 weeks gestation has her routine cervical screening test result return as HPV 16 positive with a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion on liquid-based cytology. She had a normal cervical screening test 3 years ago. She is well with no vaginal bleeding or discharge. She has no history of abnormal cervical screening and is a non-smoker.

data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening: HPV 16 detected. LBC: low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Colposcopy during pregnancy without biopsy unless high-grade disease suspected
Defer all investigation until 6 weeks postpartum for repeat cervical screen
Immediate large loop excision of the transformation zone under local anaesthesia
Repeat cervical screening in 12 months as HPV 16 with LSIL is low risk
Cervical biopsy under ultrasound guidance to obtain histological confirmation

stem: A 54-year-old woman who underwent total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy 6 months ago for heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids is experiencing significant vasomotor symptoms with 10 hot flushes daily, severe night sweats, and insomnia. She has well-controlled hypertension on perindopril and no personal or family history of breast cancer or VTE. Her BMI is 27 kg per square metre. She is requesting hormone therapy for symptom relief. Her baseline mammogram performed 4 months ago was normal.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 82 IU/L, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, lipid profile normal, mammogram (4 months ago): BI-RADS 1.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate hormone therapy regimen?

options.text: Combined continuous oestradiol and micronised progesterone daily long-term
Cyclical combined oestradiol for 25 days with progesterone for the last 14
Tibolone 2.5 mg daily as it combines oestrogenic and progestogenic activity
Oestradiol-only therapy either as transdermal patch or oral tablet daily
Vaginal oestrogen pessary alone for both vasomotor and urogenital symptoms

stem:
A 28-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome diagnosed at age 22 presents for review. She has oligomenorrhoea with 4 to 5 cycles per year and moderate hirsutism. She is not currently trying to conceive and uses condoms for contraception. Her BMI is 34 kg per square metre, having gained 12 kg over the past 3 years. She has acanthosis nigricans at the neck and axillae.

An oral glucose tolerance test shows a fasting glucose of 5.8 mmol/L and a 2-hour glucose of 9.4 mmol/L. Her HbA1c is 42 mmol per mol. Fasting lipids show total cholesterol 5.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L, and LDL 3.6 mmol/L. She asks which intervention is most important for her long-term health.

data_table.Investigations: OGTT: fasting 5.8 mmol/L, 2-hour 9.4 mmol/L. HbA1c 42 mmol/mol. Lipids: TC 5.9, TG 2.8, HDL 0.9, LDL 3.6 mmol/L. Testosterone 3.2 nmol/L (ULN 1.8). SHBG 18 nmol/L (low). LH 14 IU/L, FSH 5 IU/L.

lead_in: What is the single most important initial management priority?

options.text: Structured lifestyle intervention targeting 5-10% weight loss over 6 months
Combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle regulation and androgen suppression
Metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1 g twice daily for insulin resistance
Spironolactone 50 mg twice daily for hyperandrogenism and hirsutism control
Atorvastatin 20 mg daily for dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk reduction

stem: A 24-year-old nulliparous woman presents with a 3-year history of worsening dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain. Pain is worst in the 2 days before and during menstruation. She rates her pain as 8 out of 10 during menses despite regular paracetamol and ibuprofen. She is not currently planning pregnancy. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 25 mm left ovarian endometrioma but is otherwise unremarkable. She has not tried hormonal therapy previously.

data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 25 mm left ovarian endometrioma with ground-glass appearance. Uterus normal. Right ovary normal. No evidence of deep infiltrating endometriosis on ultrasound.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial medical treatment?

options.text: GnRH agonist depot injection monthly with add-back oestrogen therapy
Laparoscopic excision of the endometrioma and ablation of peritoneal disease
Oral danazol 200 mg twice daily for suppression of endometrial implants
Medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM every 12 weeks as depot injection
Combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to suppress menstruation

stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 31 weeks and 4 days gestation is admitted with epigastric pain, nausea, and malaise over 24 hours. Her blood pressure is 158/102 mmHg on two readings 15 minutes apart. She has brisk reflexes without clonus. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 48 mg/mmol. Blood results show evidence of haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets consistent with HELLP syndrome. The CTG is reassuring. Estimated fetal weight on recent growth scan is on the 32nd centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/102 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 37.0 C, RR 18.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L (was 118 at 28 weeks), platelets 68 x10^9/L, blood film: schistocytes and helmet cells, LDH 620 U/L, haptoglobin < 0.1 g/L, ALT 248 U/L, AST 312 U/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, urate 0.44 mmol/L, urine PCR 48 mg/mmol, fibrinogen 2.8 g/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section without corticosteroids given the HELLP diagnosis
Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now with planned delivery within 24 to 48 hours
Expectant management with IV dexamethasone to reverse the HELLP process
Urgent platelet transfusion to above 100 x10^9 per L then vaginal induction
Transfer to tertiary centre for plasma exchange as first-line HELLP treatment

stem:
A 35-year-old G2P1 woman with gestational diabetes diagnosed at 26 weeks is reviewed at 38 weeks gestation. She has been well controlled on metformin 1 g twice daily and insulin glargine 14 units at bedtime, with fasting glucose consistently 4.5-5.2 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial levels below 6.7 mmol/L. Her most recent growth scan at 36 weeks shows an estimated fetal weight on the 72nd centile with normal amniotic fluid index and umbilical artery Doppler.

She had a previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery at term. Her cervix is 2 cm dilated, soft, and 50% effaced with the presenting part at station minus 2.

data_table.Investigations: BSL diary: fasting 4.5-5.2 mmol/L, 2-hour postprandial < 6.7 mmol/L. Growth scan 36 weeks: EFW 72nd centile, AFI 14 cm, UA Doppler normal. HbA1c at 36 weeks: 38 mmol/mol.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery recommendation?

options.text: Elective caesarean section at 39 weeks given the insulin requirement
Expectant management until spontaneous labour onset up to 41 weeks gestation
Induction of labour between 38 and 39 weeks given her favourable cervix
Immediate induction today at 38 weeks due to the risk of late stillbirth
Continue current management and plan delivery at 40 weeks if still undelivered

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 woman has a low-lying placenta identified at her 20-week morphology scan. At repeat transvaginal ultrasound at 32 weeks, the placenta has migrated and the lower edge is now 4 cm from the internal os. However, colour Doppler reveals fetal vessels traversing the membranes over the internal cervical os, consistent with a velamentous cord insertion with vasa praevia.

She is asymptomatic with no bleeding and CTG is reassuring. The fetus is in cephalic presentation with an estimated fetal weight on the 45th centile.

data_table.Investigations: TVUS 32 weeks: placental edge 4 cm from internal os, velamentous cord insertion confirmed, colour Doppler shows fetal vessels crossing internal os. EFW 45th centile. AFI 16 cm.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Induction of labour at 37 weeks with continuous CTG and amniotomy avoidance
Expectant management at home with weekly CTG until spontaneous labour at term
Emergency caesarean section today due to the high risk of fetal haemorrhage
Inpatient monitoring with corticosteroids and planned caesarean at 35-36 weeks
Cervical cerclage at 32 weeks to prevent preterm labour and vessel rupture

subtopic_detail: Acute antihypertensive choice in severe pre-eclampsia
stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman at 34 weeks gestation is admitted with severe pre-eclampsia. Her blood pressure is 172/114 mmHg on two readings 5 minutes apart. She has a frontal headache but no visual disturbance and no epigastric pain. She has brisk reflexes without clonus. Magnesium sulfate infusion has been commenced for seizure prophylaxis. Urgent blood results show platelets 142 x10^9/L, ALT 38 U/L, and creatinine 74 micromol/L. CTG is reassuring. The obstetric team is planning delivery after corticosteroids but needs to control her blood pressure acutely.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 172/114 mmHg (confirmed), HR 88 bpm, T 36.9 C, SpO2 98%.
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 142 x10^9/L, ALT 38 U/L, creatinine 74 micromol/L, urine PCR 62 mg/mmol.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive for acute blood pressure control?

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg bolus repeated every 10 minutes as needed to a maximum
Oral nifedipine modified-release 30 mg as the sole acute intervention today
IV hydralazine 5 mg bolus repeated every 20 minutes to a maximum of 20 mg
IV enalaprilat 1.25 mg for rapid ACE inhibition and blood pressure reduction
IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated to achieve target blood pressure

stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 woman at 34 weeks gestation presents with intense generalised pruritus for 10 days, worst on her palms and soles and worse at night. There is no rash, no jaundice, and no abdominal pain. She has had two previous uncomplicated pregnancies. She is of South Asian background. She has been using emollients and antihistamines without relief. Her LFTs are mildly elevated and serum bile acids are significantly raised. Hepatitis B and C serology, liver ultrasound, and autoimmune liver screen are negative.

data_table.Investigations: Total bile acids 58 micromol/L (normal < 10), ALT 72 U/L (ULN 35), AST 64 U/L (ULN 35), GGT 32 U/L (normal), bilirubin 18 micromol/L (normal), ALP 180 U/L (elevated - normal in pregnancy). Hep B sAg: negative. Hep C Ab: negative. Platelets 224 x10^9/L. Coagulation screen: normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid 250 mg three times daily with delivery at 40 weeks
Colestyramine 4 g four times daily as the first-line treatment for pruritus
Reassurance that pruritus in pregnancy is common and self-limiting at delivery
Weekly CTG monitoring alone with plan for delivery at 38 to 39 weeks gestation
Ursodeoxycholic acid with weekly bile acid monitoring and delivery at 36-37 weeks

stem: A 36-year-old G3P2 woman (two prior caesarean sections) has major placenta praevia confirmed on transvaginal ultrasound at 32 weeks, with the placenta completely covering the internal cervical os. She has had no bleeding episodes during this pregnancy. She is Rh-positive. Fetal growth is on the 50th centile with normal Doppler studies. She is currently asymptomatic and lives 15 minutes from the hospital.

data_table.Investigations: TVUS 32 weeks: placenta completely covering internal os (major praevia). No evidence of placenta accreta on grey-scale or colour Doppler. EFW 50th centile. Hb 124 g/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Vaginal delivery via induction at 37 weeks with placental localisation on scan
Planned caesarean section at 36 to 37 weeks with senior obstetric team and blood
Immediate hospital admission at 32 weeks with delivery at 34 weeks by caesarean
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound at 36 weeks as the praevia will likely resolve
Expectant management until 39 weeks with emergency caesarean only if bleeding

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition and management
stem: A 38-year-old G4P3 woman is undergoing induction of labour at 40 weeks for post-dates pregnancy. She is 6 cm dilated following artificial rupture of membranes 30 minutes ago. She suddenly develops acute dyspnoea, becomes cyanotic, and loses consciousness. Her blood pressure drops to 62/38 mmHg and SpO2 falls to 78% on room air. Within minutes she develops profuse vaginal bleeding with dark non-clotting blood. The CTG shows prolonged fetal bradycardia at 70 bpm. The team initiates basic resuscitation with high-flow oxygen and IV fluid bolus.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 62/38 mmHg, HR 130 bpm, SpO2 78% on 15 L non-rebreather, GCS 3.
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care VBG: pH 7.14, lactate 8.2 mmol/L. Bedside coagulation: non-clotting sample. ECG: sinus tachycardia with right heart strain pattern.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the immediate management priority after initiating resuscitation?

options.text: Massive pulmonary embolism requiring IV thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg
Placental abruption with haemorrhagic shock requiring emergency blood transfusion
Amniotic fluid embolism requiring emergency perimortem caesarean within 5 minutes
Septic shock from chorioamnionitis requiring IV broad-spectrum antibiotics stat
Anaphylaxis to oxytocin infusion requiring IM adrenaline 500 mcg immediately

stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 woman at 10 weeks gestation presents with persistent vomiting for 3 weeks. She is unable to tolerate oral fluids and has lost 5 kg (7% of pre-pregnancy weight). She has been taking oral metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily without improvement. She denies abdominal pain, diarrhoea, or urinary symptoms. Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones. Her thyroid function shows a mildly suppressed TSH with normal free T4, consistent with hCG-mediated thyrotoxicosis of pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108 bpm, BP 96/62 mmHg, T 36.8 C, dry mucous membranes.
data_table.Investigations: Ketones 3+ on urinalysis. Na 134 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L (baseline 62), urea 8.2 mmol/L. TSH 0.08 mIU/L, free T4 18 pmol/L. Hb 148 g/L (haemoconcentrated). Beta-hCG 185,000 IU/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence carbimazole 10 mg daily for the biochemical thyrotoxicosis result
Switch oral metoclopramide to oral ondansetron 4 mg three times daily instead
Oral rehydration solution with small frequent sips and dietary ginger supplements
Admit for IV dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily as first-line inpatient treatment
Admit for IV fluid rehydration with potassium replacement and IV antiemetics

stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman at 39 weeks gestation with a cephalic presentation is in the first stage of labour with membranes intact. She has been progressing normally at 5 cm dilatation. The CTG has been reassuring. After spontaneous rupture of membranes with a rush of clear liquor, the midwife performs a vaginal examination and palpates pulsating loops of umbilical cord in the vagina below the presenting part. The CTG immediately shows variable decelerations with the fetal heart rate dropping to 80 bpm. The obstetric registrar is called urgently.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 92 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: variable decelerations, FHR nadir 80 bpm with slow recovery. Cervix 5 cm dilated.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Manually push the cord back above the presenting part and apply fundal pressure
Commence emergency oxytocin augmentation to expedite full cervical dilatation
Tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneously to stop uterine contractions
Digitally elevate the presenting part and call for emergency category 1 caesarean
Apply ventouse to the fetal head at 5 cm and attempt immediate vaginal delivery

subtopic_detail: Group B Streptococcus intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 38 weeks gestation presents in spontaneous labour with regular contractions. Her membranes ruptured 2 hours ago with clear liquor. Her vaginal-rectal swab taken at 36 weeks grew Group B Streptococcus. She has a documented penicillin allergy causing a widespread maculopapular rash (non-anaphylactic reaction). Her previous child was born at term without complications. She is 4 cm dilated and progressing well. She is afebrile and the CTG is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 C, HR 84 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg.
data_table.Investigations: 36-week GBS swab: positive. Documented penicillin allergy: non-anaphylactic rash. GBS susceptibility: sensitive to clindamycin (D-test negative).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery
IV cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours until delivery occurs
IV cefazolin 2 g initially then 1 g every 8 hours as the allergy is low-risk
IV vancomycin 1 g every 12 hours until delivery for penicillin-allergic patients
Oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours as an outpatient until delivery takes place

stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman underwent suction evacuation 2 weeks ago for a complete hydatidiform mole diagnosed at 11 weeks gestation on ultrasound (snowstorm appearance, no fetal parts). Histopathology confirmed complete hydatidiform mole with no evidence of invasion. Her pre-evacuation beta-hCG was 320,000 IU/L. Two weeks post-evacuation, her beta-hCG has fallen to 18,000 IU/L. She is currently asymptomatic with no vaginal bleeding. Chest X-ray is normal. She asks about the follow-up protocol and when she can try to conceive again.

data_table.Investigations: Pre-evacuation beta-hCG: 320,000 IU/L. 2-week post-evacuation beta-hCG: 18,000 IU/L. Histology: complete hydatidiform mole, p57 negative (confirming complete mole). CXR: normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up and contraception advice?

options.text: Monthly beta-hCG until normal then 6 months of surveillance with any contraception
Weekly beta-hCG until normal then monthly for 12 months with reliable contraception
Prophylactic single-agent methotrexate now to prevent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
Single beta-hCG at 6 weeks post-evacuation and if normal no further follow-up
Conception permitted once beta-hCG normalises without any surveillance period after

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to a general practice 72 hours after unprotected sexual intercourse requesting emergency contraception. Her last menstrual period was 14 days ago and her cycles are regular at 28 days. She weighs 58 kg and has no significant medical history. She is not taking any regular medications. She has never used an intrauterine device previously and is interested in the most effective option available. She is not currently planning pregnancy in the next 2 years.
lead_in: What is the most effective emergency contraception option for this patient?

options.text: Oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg as a single dose taken immediately at this visit
Oral ulipristal acetate 30 mg as a single dose taken immediately at this visit
Combined oral contraceptive (Yuzpe method) with two doses 12 hours apart now
Copper intrauterine device inserted today as the most effective available option
Oral mifepristone 200 mg as a single dose for emergency contraceptive purposes

stem: A 28-year-old woman undergoing IVF presents 5 days after oocyte retrieval with abdominal distension, nausea, and reduced urine output over 24 hours. She had 22 oocytes retrieved and received a trigger injection of hCG 10,000 IU. Fresh embryo transfer was performed 3 days ago. On examination she has tense ascites and bilateral pleural effusions. Her weight has increased by 4 kg since retrieval. Bloods show haemoconcentration and elevated creatinine.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104 bpm, BP 98/62 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 94% on room air, T 37.2 C.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 162 g/L (baseline 132), haematocrit 0.49, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 64), Na 128 mmol/L, K 5.4 mmol/L, albumin 22 g/L, urine output last 12 hours: 180 mL. US: bilateral enlarged ovaries (right 12 cm, left 10 cm), moderate ascites, bilateral pleural effusions.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IV crystalloid resuscitation with albumin infusion and VTE thromboprophylaxis
Aggressive IV diuresis with furosemide 40 mg to treat the fluid overload state
Urgent surgical drainage of bilateral ovarian cysts under general anaesthesia
Fluid restriction to 1 litre daily to prevent worsening ascites and effusions
Commence cabergoline 0.5 mg daily to reduce VEGF-mediated capillary permeability

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P3 woman has just delivered a 4,200 g baby vaginally after an 18-hour labour augmented with oxytocin. Active management of the third stage was performed. Ten minutes after placental delivery, she develops heavy vaginal bleeding estimated at 800 mL and ongoing. Uterine examination reveals a boggy, poorly contracted uterus. The placenta has been examined and appears complete. Bimanual uterine massage has been commenced.

An IV oxytocin infusion of 40 IU in 1 L normal saline is running. Her blood pressure is currently 108/66 mmHg with a heart rate of 112 bpm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg, SpO2 98%.
data_table.Investigations: EBL 800 mL and ongoing. Placenta complete on inspection. No genital tract laceration on examination.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step for this atonic uterus?

options.text: Increase the oxytocin infusion rate to 80 IU in 1 L and continue massage
Sublingual misoprostol 200 mcg as a single dose for uterotonic effect here
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV as the next pharmacological step in PPH management
IV cefazolin 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg for suspected endometritis component
IM ergometrine 250 mcg combined with ongoing bimanual massage and oxytocin

subtopic_detail: Rescue cerclage for cervical insufficiency with membrane prolapse
stem:
A 26-year-old G3P0 woman at 20 weeks and 3 days gestation presents with a sensation of vaginal pressure but no contractions. She has a history of two mid-trimester losses: one at 19 weeks and one at 21 weeks, both presenting with painless cervical dilatation. No cerclage was placed in this pregnancy due to late booking. On speculum examination, the cervix is 3 cm dilated with bulging amniotic membranes visible at the external os.

There is no vaginal bleeding, no evidence of membrane rupture, and no signs of chorioamnionitis. The membranes appear intact. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a cervical length of 0 mm with funnelling to the external os. CTG shows no uterine activity. Vaginal swabs for infection are sent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 C, HR 88 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, WCC 9.8 x10^9/L, CRP 4 mg/L.
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: cervical length 0 mm, funnelling to external os, membranes bulging through os. Fetal biometry consistent with 20 weeks. AFI 14 cm. No uterine activity on tocography.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management after counselling about risks and benefits?

options.text: Expectant management with bed rest and serial cervical length measurements only
Termination of pregnancy counselling as rescue cerclage has unacceptable risks
Emergency rescue cerclage after amniocentesis to exclude infection and tocolysis
Cervical pessary insertion as a less invasive alternative to surgical cerclage
Intramuscular progesterone 250 mg weekly alone as cervical insufficiency treatment

subtopic_detail: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy versus HELLP syndrome
