stem: A 30-year-old G1P0 woman at 36 weeks gestation presents with 5 days of nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, and progressive malaise. She has no history of hypertension or liver disease. On examination she appears mildly jaundiced. Her blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. There is no peripheral oedema. Blood results show markedly elevated transaminases, hypoglycaemia, hypofibrinogenaemia, and elevated bilirubin. Platelets are mildly reduced. Urine PCR is 12 mg/mmol. Her blood film shows no schistocytes or haemolysis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg, HR 98 bpm, T 37.4 C.
data_table.Investigations: ALT 412 U/L, AST 388 U/L, bilirubin 82 micromol/L (conjugated 68), ALP 320 U/L, albumin 24 g/L, glucose 2.8 mmol/L, ammonia 68 micromol/L (elevated), platelets 98 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (low), PT 18 s (elevated), APTT 42 s (elevated), LDH 310 U/L, haptoglobin 0.8 g/L (normal), blood film: no schistocytes. Urine PCR 12 mg/mmol. Uric acid 0.48 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: HELLP syndrome based on the liver enzyme elevation and low platelet count
Viral hepatitis based on the jaundice and markedly elevated liver transaminases
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy with unusually severe liver involvement
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy given the coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia and jaundice
Pre-eclampsia with severe features given the liver and coagulation abnormalities

stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 woman with gestational diabetes (insulin-requiring) is delivering vaginally at 39 weeks. After delivery of the fetal head, the head retracts tightly against the perineum (turtle sign) and the anterior shoulder does not deliver with the next contraction despite gentle downward traction. Shoulder dystocia is declared. The midwife calls for help. The time is noted. The mother is positioned with her buttocks at the edge of the bed. One minute has elapsed since delivery of the head.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre after calling for help?

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with simultaneous suprapubic pressure applied correctly
Immediate delivery of the posterior arm by sweeping it across the fetal chest
Fundal pressure to push the fetus through the pelvis with maternal effort
Zavanelli manoeuvre to replace the fetal head and deliver by emergency caesarean
Episiotomy as the first intervention to create space for shoulder delivery

stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 Rh-negative woman at 16 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident in which she was a restrained front-seat passenger. She reports minor abdominal discomfort but no vaginal bleeding. She has no abdominal tenderness, and the uterus is non-tender and appropriate for dates. Fetal heart tones are heard on Doppler. Ultrasound confirms a viable intrauterine pregnancy with no retroplacental haematoma.

Her blood group is O Rh-negative with no irregular antibodies on her most recent screen at 12 weeks. She has not yet received routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, T 36.7 C.
data_table.Investigations: Fetal Doppler: FHR 156 bpm. US: viable IUP, no retroplacental collection. Blood group: O Rh-negative. Antibody screen: negative. Kleihauer-Betke test: pending.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding Rh isoimmunisation prevention?

options.text: No anti-D required as there is no vaginal bleeding and the ultrasound is normal
Anti-D 625 IU IM within 72 hours and Kleihauer to check for large fetomaternal bleed
Anti-D 250 IU IM as the standard dose regardless of gestational age at any event
Defer anti-D until the routine 28-week antenatal prophylaxis dose is administered
Cross-match and transfuse Rh-negative packed red cells as a precautionary measure

stem:
A 30-year-old G1P0 woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is referred at 20 weeks gestation after her routine ultrasound shows significant growth discordance and amniotic fluid discrepancy between the twins. Detailed ultrasound confirms one twin (donor) has a deepest vertical pool of 1.2 cm with a stuck appearance against the uterine wall, while the other (recipient) has polyhydramnios with a deepest vertical pool of 12 cm.

The donor twin has an absent bladder on repeated imaging. Doppler studies show abnormal umbilical artery waveforms in the donor but normal in the recipient. Both twins have cardiac activity.

data_table.Investigations: Donor twin: DVP 1.2 cm (oligohydramnios), bladder not visualised, UA Doppler: absent end-diastolic flow. EFW 10th centile. Recipient twin: DVP 12 cm (polyhydramnios), distended bladder, UA Doppler: normal. EFW 50th centile. Quintero Stage III TTTS.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for this stage of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome?

options.text: Serial amnioreduction every 2 to 3 days to decompress the polyhydramnios sac
Expectant management with fortnightly ultrasound surveillance and growth scans
Selective fetal reduction of the donor twin by cord occlusion to save the recipient
Elective preterm delivery at 26 weeks after a course of antenatal corticosteroids
Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses at a referral centre

subtopic_detail: Pelvic inflammatory disease outpatient antibiotic regimen
stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to her GP with 5 days of lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, and a new malodorous vaginal discharge. She has a new sexual partner of 6 weeks and inconsistent condom use. She is not pregnant. On examination she has bilateral adnexal tenderness and cervical motion tenderness. Her temperature is 37.6 degrees C. Endocervical swabs have been collected for Chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, and a high vaginal swab for microscopy and culture. She is able to tolerate oral medications, is not vomiting, and is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 C, HR 82 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg.
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test: negative. Pelvic US: no tubo-ovarian abscess, minimal free fluid in pouch of Douglas. Swab results pending.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric outpatient antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral azithromycin 1 g single dose alone covering the most likely STI pathogen
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg twice daily for 14 days as sole treatment
IM ceftriaxone 500 mg stat plus oral doxycycline 100 mg BD and metronidazole BD
Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose plus oral azithromycin 1 g single dose
Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days alone without ceftriaxone cover

subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception selection by weight and timing
stem: A 30-year-old woman with a BMI of 32 kg per square metre presents to a sexual health clinic 96 hours after unprotected sexual intercourse during what she estimates was her fertile window. She had a positive ovulation predictor kit 2 days before the unprotected intercourse. She is otherwise healthy with regular 28-day cycles. She does not want an intrauterine device due to prior difficult insertion and a planned MRI in 2 weeks. She asks about oral emergency contraception options given the time elapsed and her weight.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate oral emergency contraception recommendation?

options.text: Oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg as it remains equally effective at any time up to 5 days
Double-dose levonorgestrel 3 mg to overcome the reduced efficacy at higher BMI
Oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg now plus a second dose of 1.5 mg in 12 hours apart
Oral ulipristal acetate 30 mg as it maintains efficacy to 120 hours and at higher BMI
No oral EC is effective at 96 hours so advise waiting and performing a pregnancy test

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends her 6-week postnatal check. She was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks gestation, managed with metformin and diet. Her baby was born at 39 weeks weighing 3.8 kg with no neonatal complications. She is breastfeeding well and has stopped metformin since delivery. Her fasting BSL this morning was 5.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76 mmHg, HR 74 bpm
data_table.Investigations: Fasting BSL 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding her glucose metabolism?

options.text: Reassure and advise annual fasting BSL
Restart metformin and monitor BSL diary
Arrange a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test
Check HbA1c and review in three months
Defer glucose testing until 12 months postpartum

stem: A 38-year-old primigravida presents at 11 weeks gestation for her first antenatal visit. Her BMI is 34 kg/m2. She has chronic hypertension managed with labetalol 200 mg twice daily. Her blood pressure today is 128/82 mmHg. She has no proteinuria. Her mother had pre-eclampsia in her first pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/82 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, BMI 34
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: protein negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic intervention at this visit?

options.text: Commence aspirin 150 mg nightly from now
Commence aspirin 100 mg daily from 16 weeks
Commence calcium 1.5 g daily supplementation
Increase labetalol to achieve BP below 120/80
Monitor with serial uterine artery Dopplers

stem: A 34-year-old woman at 36 weeks gestation presents for her scheduled ultrasound review. She had a low-lying placenta identified at her 20-week morphology scan. Today's transvaginal ultrasound shows the placental edge is 18 mm from the internal cervical os. She has had no vaginal bleeding during the pregnancy. Her previous two births were uncomplicated vaginal deliveries.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 70 bpm
data_table.Investigations: TVS: placental edge 18 mm from internal os, cephalic presentation, EFW 2850 g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Elective caesarean section at 37 weeks gestation
Elective caesarean section at 39 weeks gestation
Repeat ultrasound at 38 weeks before deciding
Plan a trial of vaginal delivery with monitoring
Perform amniocentesis for fetal lung maturity

subtopic_detail: IOL prostaglandin choice in scarred uterus
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 41+3 weeks gestation is being planned for induction of labour. She had one previous lower segment caesarean section for breech presentation. She desires a vaginal birth after caesarean. Her cervix is 1 cm dilated, 50% effaced, firm, posterior, with the presenting part at station -2. The fetal cardiotocograph is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 120/74 mmHg, HR 72 bpm
data_table.Investigations: CTG: reassuring, Bishop score 4, cephalic presentation, EFW 3.6 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate method for cervical ripening?

options.text: Vaginal prostaglandin E2 dinoprostone gel insertion
Transcervical Foley catheter balloon for ripening
Oral misoprostol 25 mcg administered two-hourly
Dinoprostone controlled-release vaginal pessary
Commence oxytocin infusion without prior ripening

stem: A 29-year-old woman has a normal vaginal delivery at 39 weeks. During the third stage of labour, she receives oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly for active management. Twenty minutes after placental delivery, estimated blood loss reaches 700 mL with ongoing bleeding. The uterus feels boggy on palpation. Bimanual uterine compression is commenced, and 40 IU oxytocin in 1 L normal saline is running as an infusion. She has a history of well-controlled asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 110 bpm, SpO2 98%
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy, placenta complete on inspection, no vaginal lacerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Administer sublingual misoprostol 800 mcg
Give intramuscular carboprost 250 mcg
Administer tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min
Administer IV oxytocin 5 IU slow bolus only
Give intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 9 weeks gestation presents with vaginal spotting. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a gestational sac measuring 28 mm with no fetal pole, consistent with an anembryonic pregnancy. She is haemodynamically stable with minimal bleeding. She has no allergies and no significant medical history. She expresses a preference to avoid surgery if possible.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/70 mmHg, HR 72 bpm
data_table.Investigations: TVS: 28 mm gestational sac, no fetal pole, no yolk sac, Hb 128 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Offer misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally with review
Recommend expectant management for two weeks
Arrange immediate surgical evacuation of uterus
Administer mifepristone 200 mg orally and review
Repeat ultrasound in one week to confirm diagnosis

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-year history of worsening dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia. Her pain is cyclical, beginning 2 days before menses and lasting 5 days. She has tried paracetamol and ibuprofen with limited relief. She is not planning pregnancy. Clinical examination reveals tenderness in the posterior fornix with nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 25 mm left ovarian endometrioma.

data_table.Examination: Posterior fornix tenderness, uterosacral nodularity bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic USS: 25 mm left ovarian endometrioma, normal right ovary, anteverted uterus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Commence naproxen 500 mg twice daily perimenstrually
Refer for diagnostic and therapeutic laparoscopy
Commence combined oral contraceptive pill continuously
Start depot leuprorelin 3.75 mg monthly injection
Commence oral medroxyprogesterone acetate 30 mg daily

stem: A 26-year-old woman with a BMI of 32 presents with oligomenorrhoea, acne, and hirsutism. She has been diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome based on Rotterdam criteria. She is not planning pregnancy currently. Her fasting glucose is 5.4 mmol/L and her 75 g OGTT 2-hour result is 8.8 mmol/L. Total cholesterol is 5.6 mmol/L with LDL 3.4 mmol/L. She has tried lifestyle modification for 6 months with a 2 kg weight loss.

data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 2-hour OGTT 8.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 38 mmol/mol, Total cholesterol 5.6 mmol/L, LDL 3.4 mmol/L, HDL 1.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional pharmacological intervention for her metabolic risk?

options.text: Commence atorvastatin 20 mg nightly for lipids
Add pioglitazone 15 mg daily as insulin sensitiser
Add spironolactone 50 mg daily for hyperandrogenism
Prescribe orlistat 120 mg with meals for weight loss
Commence metformin 500 mg and titrate to 1500 mg

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening in pregnancy with oncogenic HPV
stem: A 29-year-old primigravida attends her first antenatal visit at 10 weeks gestation. She reports her last cervical screening test 18 months ago was HPV positive (not HPV 16/18) with a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) on liquid-based cytology. The recommendation was a repeat test at 12 months, which she has not yet attended. She is otherwise well with no history of abnormal bleeding.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding her cervical screening?

options.text: Defer all cervical screening until 6 weeks postpartum
Perform cervical screening test now at this visit
Refer directly for colposcopy without retesting
Perform the screening test at second trimester visit
Arrange urgent colposcopy within two weeks

stem: A 33-year-old woman who delivered vaginally 3 days ago wishes to discuss long-acting reversible contraception before discharge. She had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 38 weeks with a second-degree perineal tear repaired primarily. She is breastfeeding. She is interested in a copper intrauterine device as she prefers non-hormonal contraception. She has no history of postpartum haemorrhage or endometritis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 74 bpm, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted, lochia normal, perineal repair intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding copper IUD insertion timing?

options.text: Insert the IUD before discharge from hospital
Plan insertion at the 6-week postnatal visit
Defer insertion until 12 weeks postpartum minimum
Insert the IUD at 2 weeks postpartum instead
Recommend an IUD is unsuitable postpartum

subtopic_detail: Menopause local vs systemic HRT for GSM
stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and recurrent urinary tract infections. She reached menopause naturally at age 52. She has no vasomotor symptoms. She tried vaginal moisturisers for 6 months with minimal improvement. She has a history of treated localised breast cancer 4 years ago, currently on tamoxifen with no evidence of recurrence. She is otherwise well.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Commence systemic combined oestrogen-progestogen HRT
Commence systemic oestradiol patches at 50 mcg dose
Switch tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor instead
Prescribe low-dose vaginal oestrogen cream topically
Prescribe oral ospemifene 60 mg daily for symptoms

stem: A 25-year-old woman at 9 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with a 3-week history of persistent nausea and vomiting. She is unable to tolerate any oral intake. She has lost 5 kg since her booking visit. She has had two previous presentations where she received IV fluids and was discharged. Urinalysis shows 3+ ketonuria. She appears dehydrated with dry mucous membranes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 98/60 mmHg, HR 106 bpm, Temp 36.5, weight loss 5 kg (8% body weight)
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+, Na 134 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L, Urea 8.2 mmol/L, Cr 82 micromol/L

lead_in: In addition to IV fluid resuscitation and antiemetics, what is the most important supplementation to commence?

options.text: Intravenous thiamine 100 mg before any dextrose
Oral folic acid 5 mg daily supplementation
Intravenous potassium chloride 40 mmol infusion
Oral pyridoxine 25 mg three times daily
Intramuscular vitamin B12 1000 mcg injection

stem: A 28-year-old Rh D-negative woman at 14 weeks gestation presents after a fall resulting in direct abdominal trauma. She has no vaginal bleeding and the fetus appears well on ultrasound. Her indirect Coombs test from booking bloods at 10 weeks was negative. She has not received any anti-D immunoglobulin during this pregnancy. The father of the baby is Rh D-positive.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 120/76 mmHg, HR 76 bpm
data_table.Investigations: USS: viable intrauterine pregnancy, no retroplacental haematoma, CTG not applicable at this gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding Rh D isoimmunisation?

options.text: No anti-D needed as there is no vaginal bleeding
Administer anti-D 250 IU IM within 72 hours only
Check Kleihauer-Betke test then give anti-D if positive
Repeat indirect Coombs test and defer anti-D if negative
Administer anti-D 250 IU IM as soon as possible

subtopic_detail: Obstetric cholestasis bile acid threshold and delivery
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 35 weeks gestation presents with a 1-week history of generalised pruritus that is worse at night, particularly affecting her palms and soles. She has no rash. Liver function tests show mildly elevated transaminases. Her total serum bile acids return at 42 micromol/L. The fetal cardiotocograph is reassuring. She has had no complications during the pregnancy to date.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 72 bpm
data_table.Investigations: ALT 68 U/L, AST 54 U/L, GGT 32 U/L, Bilirubin 14 micromol/L, Bile acids 42 micromol/L, Platelets 228 x10^9/L, CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence UDCA and plan delivery at 39 weeks
Reassure and repeat bile acids in one week
Commence UDCA and plan delivery at 37 weeks
Immediate delivery via induction of labour now
Commence colestyramine and monitor bile acids

subtopic_detail: Thyroid in pregnancy - levothyroxine TSH target
stem: A 30-year-old woman with pre-existing hypothyroidism attends at 8 weeks gestation. She takes levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, which has been stable for 2 years. She feels well with no symptoms of hypothyroidism. Her pre-pregnancy TSH was 1.8 mIU/L. Today's bloods show a TSH of 4.8 mIU/L with a free T4 of 12.2 pmol/L (reference 12-22).

data_table.Investigations: TSH 4.8 mIU/L, Free T4 12.2 pmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adjustment to her levothyroxine dose?

options.text: Increase levothyroxine to 125 mcg daily promptly
Maintain current dose and recheck TSH in 4 weeks
Increase levothyroxine to 200 mcg daily immediately
Add liothyronine 10 mcg daily to current dose
Switch to desiccated thyroid extract preparation

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation is found to have a haemoglobin of 88 g/L at routine blood testing. She reports fatigue and breathlessness on exertion. Her ferritin is 6 microg/L. She has been taking oral iron (ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily) for 4 weeks prescribed at her 28-week visit when her Hb was 102 g/L, but reports significant nausea and constipation limiting adherence. She has no bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 92 bpm
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 74 fL, Ferritin 6 microg/L, CRP 4 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to oral iron polymaltose every second day
Increase oral iron to twice daily with vitamin C
Arrange packed red blood cell transfusion now
Recheck iron studies in 2 weeks before deciding
Commence IV iron infusion (ferric carboxymaltose)

subtopic_detail: VTE prophylaxis risk assessment in pregnancy
stem: A 35-year-old woman presents at 10 weeks gestation for her booking visit. She had a provoked deep vein thrombosis 3 years ago following a long-haul flight, treated with rivaroxaban for 3 months. She has no family history of VTE. Thrombophilia screening performed after the DVT was negative. Her BMI is 28. She is otherwise well with no other risk factors.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis plan for this pregnancy?

options.text: No pharmacological prophylaxis is required in this pregnancy
Prophylactic LMWH from 28 weeks until 6 weeks postpartum
Continue rivaroxaban at current dose throughout pregnancy
Prophylactic LMWH from now until 6 weeks after delivery
Prophylactic LMWH for the 6 weeks postpartum period only

stem: You are the registrar attending a vaginal delivery. After delivery of the head, the chin retracts tightly against the perineum - the turtle sign. Gentle downward traction on the head does not deliver the anterior shoulder. The time is noted and the emergency buzzer is pressed. The mother is in lithotomy position. An assistant has arrived.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate manoeuvre?

options.text: Apply fundal pressure from above the uterus
Perform Zavanelli manoeuvre to replace the head
Perform an episiotomy to create more space
Apply McRoberts positioning with suprapubic pressure
Attempt rotational delivery of the posterior arm

stem: You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to the birth suite. A 26-year-old woman at 37 weeks gestation had spontaneous rupture of membranes 5 minutes ago. The midwife felt the umbilical cord prolapsing through the cervix during a vaginal examination. The cervix is 5 cm dilated. The fetal heart rate on CTG shows a prolonged deceleration to 80 bpm. The operating theatre is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal: BP 120/72, HR 88
data_table.Investigations: CTG: fetal bradycardia 80 bpm, cervix 5 cm dilated, cord palpable below presenting part

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action while preparing for delivery?

options.text: Clamp the cord and prepare for vaginal delivery
Commence oxytocin to expedite vaginal delivery
Elevate the presenting part digitally per vaginam
Administer terbutaline 250 mcg SC for tocolysis
Attempt to manually replace the cord above the cervix

stem: A 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation was diagnosed with GDM at 26 weeks. She has been on dietary modification and walking 30 minutes daily for 4 weeks. Her BSL diary over the past week shows consistent fasting readings of 5.3-5.6 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial readings of 6.8-7.2 mmol/L. She has gained 1.5 kg in 4 weeks. The fetal growth scan shows an estimated fetal weight on the 72nd centile with a normal amniotic fluid index.

data_table.Investigations: BSL diary: fasting 5.3-5.6 mmol/L, 2h postprandial 6.8-7.2 mmol/L, EFW 72nd centile, AFI normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her glycaemic management?

options.text: Continue dietary management and review in 2 weeks
Add metformin 500 mg with dinner and titrate
Refer to endocrinology before starting any medication
Commence glibenclamide 2.5 mg with breakfast
Commence evening intermediate-acting insulin (NPH)

subtopic_detail: HELLP syndrome vs severe pre-eclampsia differentiation
stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation presents with epigastric pain and nausea for 12 hours. Her blood pressure is 156/102 mmHg. She reports visual disturbances. Her bloods show platelets 68 x10^9/L, ALT 342 U/L, AST 298 U/L, LDH 840 U/L, and a blood film showing schistocytes. Her Hb is 98 g/L (was 124 at 28 weeks). Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 85 mg/mmol. She received a loading dose of magnesium sulfate and IV labetalol.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 156/102 mmHg, HR 96 bpm
data_table.Investigations: Plt 68 x10^9/L, ALT 342, AST 298, LDH 840, Hb 98, blood film: schistocytes, uPCR 85 mg/mmol, Cr 78 micromol/L, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management plan?

options.text: Administer betamethasone and deliver at 34 weeks
Commence plasma exchange for microangiopathic haemolysis
Give betamethasone now and deliver within 24-48 hours
Manage expectantly with daily bloods until 37 weeks
Administer dexamethasone 10 mg to treat HELLP directly

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 29 weeks gestation presents with sudden-onset constant abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding of approximately 200 mL. She has no history of trauma. She smokes 10 cigarettes per day. On examination, the uterus is tender and tonically contracted. The fetal heart rate on CTG shows reduced variability with recurrent late decelerations. Ultrasound confirms a retroplacental clot of approximately 5 cm. Her blood pressure is 142/92 mmHg with proteinuria on dipstick.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/92 mmHg, HR 108 bpm
data_table.Investigations: CTG: reduced variability with late decelerations, USS: 5 cm retroplacental clot, Hb 104 g/L, Plt 186, Fibrinogen 2.1 g/L, APTT 38s

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for observation with serial Hb and CTG
Proceed with emergency caesarean section now
Give betamethasone and plan delivery at 48 hours
Commence tocolysis to buy time for corticosteroids
Induce labour with amniotomy for vaginal delivery

stem: A 39-year-old primigravida at 41+2 weeks is undergoing induction of labour for post-dates pregnancy. She received two doses of vaginal dinoprostone gel (1 mg each, 6 hours apart) followed by a transcervical Foley catheter overnight. The balloon was expelled at 6 am with a cervix 3 cm dilated. An oxytocin infusion was commenced at 8 am. After 8 hours of oxytocin at maximum dose with adequate contractions (3 in 10 minutes), her cervix remains 3 cm dilated. The fetal CTG has been reassuring throughout. Membranes were ruptured artificially at 10 am with clear liquor.

data_table.Investigations: Cervix 3 cm/50% effaced after 8 hours of adequate oxytocin, CTG reassuring, clear liquor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommend caesarean section for failed induction
Rest the oxytocin and restart in 6 hours
Insert a second Foley catheter for further ripening
Administer a further dose of vaginal dinoprostone
Continue oxytocin for another 8 hours before deciding

stem: A 36-year-old woman at 36+2 weeks gestation is found to have a frank breech presentation on routine examination. Ultrasound confirms breech with an estimated fetal weight of 2.9 kg, normal amniotic fluid index, and an anterior placenta. She has had one previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a 3.2 kg baby. She is keen to attempt vaginal birth and asks about external cephalic version. Her blood type is A negative and she has not received her routine 28-week anti-D prophylaxis yet.

data_table.Investigations: USS: frank breech, EFW 2.9 kg, AFI 14, anterior placenta, no fetal anomaly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan for this patient?

options.text: ECV is contraindicated with an anterior placenta
Defer ECV until 38 weeks for best success rate
Schedule elective caesarean section at 39 weeks only
Offer ECV now with anti-D after the procedure
Advise vaginal breech delivery without attempting ECV

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has an estimated blood loss of 1800 mL following vaginal delivery. She has received oxytocin (IM bolus and IV infusion), ergometrine 500 mcg IM (two doses), misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual, and tranexamic acid 1 g IV. Bimanual uterine compression has been performed for 10 minutes. Examination under anaesthesia confirms an empty uterus with no retained products and no genital tract lacerations.

The uterus remains poorly contracted despite all uterotonics. She has received 3 units of packed red cells and 2 units of FFP. Active bleeding continues.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/54 mmHg, HR 132 bpm, temp 36.4
data_table.Investigations: Hb 72 g/L (post-transfusion), Fibrinogen 1.8 g/L, Plt 104 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Repeat bimanual compression for a further 20 minutes
Administer a second dose of tranexamic acid 1 g IV
Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device
Proceed directly to peripartum hysterectomy
Perform uterine artery embolisation immediately

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic MTX vs surgery borderline beta-hCG
stem: A 31-year-old woman presents at 6 weeks gestation with left-sided pelvic pain. She is haemodynamically stable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a 30 mm left adnexal mass with no fetal cardiac activity and no yolk sac. There is no free fluid. Her serum beta-hCG is 4200 IU/L. Repeat beta-hCG 48 hours later is 4500 IU/L (a 7% rise). Her FBC, renal function, and liver function are normal. She has a normal contralateral tube and has completed her family.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 74 bpm
data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG day 1: 4200, day 3: 4500 (7% rise), TVS: 30 mm left adnexal mass, no FCA, no free fluid, Hb 132, Cr 64, ALT 22

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Administer single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM
Administer multi-dose methotrexate protocol
Repeat beta-hCG in 48 hours to assess trajectory
Proceed with laparoscopic salpingectomy
Perform laparoscopic salpingotomy to preserve tube

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents after her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. All three pregnancies were confirmed on ultrasound before pregnancy loss at 8-10 weeks. She has no live children. She has no personal or family history of VTE. Physical examination is normal. Her partner's karyotype is normal. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterine cavity. Her FBC, thyroid function, and fasting glucose are normal.

data_table.Investigations: Pelvic USS: normal uterine cavity, FBC normal, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, partner karyotype normal

lead_in: What is the single most important investigation to request next?

options.text: Parental balanced translocation karyotyping
Thrombophilia screen including Factor V Leiden
Serum progesterone level in the luteal phase
Endometrial biopsy for chronic endometritis
Antiphospholipid antibody panel with repeat at 12 weeks

stem: A 32-year-old woman has been on continuous combined oral contraceptive pill for 18 months for diagnosed endometriosis. Despite this, she has persistent deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, and cyclical rectal bleeding. She has been referred to a gynaecologist. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 35 mm left endometrioma and a 12 mm nodule in the rectovaginal septum extending into the anterior rectal wall. She is not currently trying to conceive but would like to preserve fertility.

data_table.Investigations: TVS: 35 mm left endometrioma, 12 mm rectovaginal septum nodule with rectal wall involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer to a specialist endometriosis centre for MDT assessment
Switch to GnRH agonist therapy with add-back HRT
Proceed directly to laparoscopic excision of endometrioma
Insert a levonorgestrel IUD as second-line hormonal therapy
Request a colonoscopy to assess rectal involvement

subtopic_detail: Letrozole vs clomifene for ovulation induction in PCOS
stem: A 30-year-old woman with PCOS has been trying to conceive for 18 months. She ovulates approximately every 3-4 months. Her BMI is 27. She has achieved a 5% weight loss through lifestyle modification. Her partner's semen analysis is normal. Her day-2 FSH is 5.2 IU/L, AMH is 48 pmol/L, and tubal patency is confirmed on hysterosalpingography. She has no contraindications to either clomifene or letrozole.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 5.2 IU/L, AMH 48 pmol/L, normal HSG, partner SA normal, BMI 27

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line ovulation induction agent?

options.text: Clomifene citrate 50 mg on cycle days 2 through 6
Letrozole 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 2 through 6
Gonadotrophin injections with ultrasound monitoring
Metformin 1500 mg daily as primary fertility agent
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling as primary treatment

stem: A 27-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation has a cervical screening test as part of her routine antenatal care - she was overdue for screening. The result returns HPV 16 positive with negative liquid-based cytology (no abnormal cells detected). She has no history of abnormal cervical screening. She has no symptoms of cervical pathology.

data_table.Investigations: CST: HPV 16 detected, LBC: no abnormal cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test at 12 months from now
Refer for colposcopy assessment during pregnancy now
Defer colposcopy until the 6-week postpartum review
Reassure as cytology is negative and rescreen at 5 years
Perform large loop excision under local anaesthesia now

stem: A 16-year-old presents requesting long-acting contraception. She has a mild intellectual disability and lives in supported accommodation. She has heavy irregular periods that significantly impact her quality of life. Her carers have discussed contraceptive options with her and she understands and consents to depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA). She has no contraindications. Her mother had osteoporosis diagnosed at age 58. She weighs 55 kg.
lead_in: What is the most important counselling point specific to this patient regarding DMPA?

options.text: Bone density may reduce during use but recovers after cessation
DMPA requires liver function monitoring every six months of use
DMPA increases the risk of endometrial cancer with long-term use
DMPA is contraindicated in patients with intellectual disability
DMPA must always be ceased after two years of continuous use

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 8 months of amenorrhoea following cessation of the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has hot flushes, vaginal dryness, and low mood. Her FSH on two occasions 6 weeks apart is 56 and 62 IU/L. Oestradiol is below 100 pmol/L. Anti-Mullerian hormone is undetectable. Karyotype is 46,XX. Autoimmune screen is negative. She is in a relationship and may wish to conceive in the future.

data_table.Investigations: FSH 56 and 62 IU/L (two occasions), oestradiol <100 pmol/L, AMH undetectable, karyotype 46,XX, anti-adrenal and anti-ovarian antibodies negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long-term hormonal management?

options.text: Start tibolone 2.5 mg daily as HRT equivalent
Prescribe alendronate for bone density protection
Use the combined oral contraceptive pill for replacement
Monitor without HRT as she is young and may recover
Commence combined HRT until at least age 50-52

stem: A 24-year-old woman underwent suction evacuation for a complete hydatidiform mole confirmed on histopathology. Her pre-evacuation beta-hCG was 285,000 IU/L. Two weeks post-evacuation, her beta-hCG is 42,000 IU/L and continues to fall. She is clinically well with no vaginal bleeding. Her chest X-ray is normal.

data_table.Investigations: Pre-evacuation beta-hCG 285,000 IU/L, 2-week post-evacuation beta-hCG 42,000 IU/L (falling), CXR normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surveillance plan?

options.text: Discharge from follow-up once hCG is undetectable
Commence prophylactic methotrexate now to prevent GTN
Repeat evacuation to ensure complete removal
Monitor weekly hCG until normal, then monthly for 6 months
Monthly hCG monitoring for 12 months starting now

stem: A 36-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation is diagnosed with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Her initial bile acids are 28 micromol/L and she is commenced on ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 250 mg twice daily. At review 1 week later, her pruritus has partially improved but bile acids have risen to 52 micromol/L. Her ALT is 96 U/L. The CTG is reassuring. She is anxious about fetal wellbeing and asks what monitoring can reduce the risk of stillbirth.

data_table.Investigations: Bile acids 52 micromol/L (was 28), ALT 96, Bilirubin 16, CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling regarding fetal monitoring?

options.text: Daily CTG monitoring will reliably predict and prevent stillbirth
Fetal movement counting is the best surveillance available
No test reliably predicts ICP stillbirth; planned early delivery reduces risk
Weekly umbilical artery Doppler will detect compromise early
Twice-weekly biophysical profile scoring is recommended here

subtopic_detail: Graves disease antithyroid drug choice by trimester
stem: A 29-year-old woman with Graves disease becomes pregnant. She is currently taking carbimazole 10 mg daily with well-controlled thyroid function (TSH 1.2 mIU/L, free T4 16 pmol/L). She is at 6 weeks gestation. She has not been seen by an endocrinologist since her pregnancy was confirmed 1 week ago. She has no symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.

data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.2 mIU/L, Free T4 16 pmol/L, TRAb positive (titre 3.2 IU/L)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her antithyroid medication?

options.text: Continue carbimazole at 10 mg daily throughout the pregnancy
Cease all antithyroid medication for the duration of pregnancy
Add propranolol and continue carbimazole at the current dose
Switch to lithium carbonate as alternative antithyroid agent
Switch to propylthiouracil now, back to carbimazole at 16 wk

stem: A 34-year-old woman at 38 weeks gestation is on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin (1.5 mg/kg daily) for a DVT diagnosed at 28 weeks. Her most recent anti-Xa level was therapeutic. She presents in early labour with regular contractions 4 minutes apart. Her cervix is 4 cm dilated. Her last dose of enoxaparin was 10 hours ago. She is requesting an epidural for pain relief.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 84 bpm
data_table.Investigations: Cervix 4 cm, last enoxaparin dose 10 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding her anticoagulation and anaesthetic options?

options.text: Epidural contraindicated; offer alternative analgesia; withhold LMWH
Administer protamine to reverse enoxaparin before epidural now
Epidural safe to insert as more than 4 hours since last dose
Switch to IV unfractionated heparin and time epidural to aPTT
Insert epidural now with continuous anti-Xa level monitoring

subtopic_detail: TTTS Quintero staging and laser therapy
stem: A 30-year-old woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is referred at 20 weeks gestation after routine ultrasound shows discordant amniotic fluid volumes. The donor twin has a deepest vertical pocket of 1.5 cm with a small or absent bladder. The recipient twin has a deepest vertical pocket of 10 cm with a distended bladder. Both twins have present umbilical artery end-diastolic flow. Neither twin has hydrops. There is no critical Doppler abnormality.

data_table.Investigations: USS: MCDA twins, Donor DVP 1.5 cm with absent bladder, Recipient DVP 10 cm with distended bladder, UA Dopplers normal bilaterally, no hydrops

lead_in: What Quintero stage is this presentation, and what is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stage I - serial surveillance with fortnightly ultrasound
Stage III - urgent referral for fetoscopic laser ablation
Stage II - referral to a fetal medicine centre for laser therapy
Stage IV - immediate delivery via caesarean section
Stage II - perform serial amnioreduction procedures

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia diagnosis and delivery planning
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 20 weeks gestation undergoes her morphology scan. She has a succenturiate placental lobe identified, with the main placental body posterior and the accessory lobe anterior and low. Colour Doppler identifies fetal vessels running across the internal cervical os, connecting the two placental lobes. She has had no vaginal bleeding. This is her second pregnancy after a previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery.

data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan: succenturiate placental lobe, colour Doppler shows fetal vessels traversing internal os

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Repeat TVS at 32 weeks to confirm before finalising a plan
Admit from 30 weeks, give corticosteroids, caesarean at 35-36 weeks
Plan vaginal delivery at term with continuous CTG in labour
Perform amniocentesis at 34 weeks for lung maturity then deliver
Elective caesarean at 39 weeks to maximise fetal maturity

stem: A 37-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation in her fourth pregnancy has a major placenta praevia covering the internal os, with two previous caesarean sections. MRI at 26 weeks reported loss of the normal hypointense myometrial-placental interface with irregular placental lacunae, myometrial thinning to less than 1 mm overlying the lower segment scar, and possible bladder wall invasion. Multidisciplinary team meeting has confirmed suspected placenta percreta. She is currently stable with no bleeding.

data_table.Investigations: MRI: loss of myometrial-placental interface, myometrial thickness <1 mm, irregular lacunae, possible bladder wall involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate planned delivery strategy?

options.text: Attempt manual placental removal at elective caesarean at 37 weeks
Deliver at 39 weeks to maximise maturity with cell salvage ready
Methotrexate therapy to induce placental resorption then deliver
Caesarean hysterectomy at 35-36 weeks at tertiary centre with MDT
Uterine artery embolisation then conservative management in situ

stem:
A 26-year-old nulliparous woman presents to the ED with 2 days of right iliac fossa pain and scant dark vaginal spotting at LMP+7 weeks. Previous PID 3 years ago, treated. No contraception. On arrival: HR 132, BP 88/52, RR 22, SpO2 98%, peripherally cool with delayed capillary refill 4 seconds, pale, conversing but anxious. Abdominal guarding, rebound tenderness across the right iliac fossa, distended abdomen with shifting dullness.

Cervical excitation, right adnexal tenderness with palpable fullness. Urine beta-hCG positive. Bedside FAST shows free fluid in the pelvis and Morrison's pouch. IV access x2 has been obtained; group and hold and crossmatch sent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 bpm, BP 100/60 mmHg, RR 18/min, Temp 37.1 C
data_table.Examination: Lower right abdominal guarding. Cervical excitation positive, right adnexal tenderness and mass.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer immediately to operating theatre for diagnostic laparoscopy with potential laparotomy and activate the massive transfusion protocol
Perform an urgent transvaginal ultrasound to confirm location of pregnancy before further action
Administer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 and admit for monitoring
Commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed pelvic inflammatory disease and reassess in 6 hours
Repeat beta-hCG in 48 hours and discharge home with safety-net advice

stem:
A 29-year-old G1P0 at 41 weeks gestation is undergoing an induction of labour for post-dates. A vaginal dinoprostone (Prostin) pessary was inserted 6 hours ago. The midwife calls you urgently for a review. The patient is distressed, complaining of continuous, severe abdominal pain without relief between contractions. Palpation of the abdomen reveals that she is having 6 contractions every 10 minutes, with increased resting uterine tone.

A continuous cardiotocograph (CTG) is running. The baseline fetal heart rate was 140 bpm an hour ago. For the past 4 minutes, the CTG has demonstrated a single, sudden, and prolonged deceleration down to a nadir of 80 bpm with loss of baseline variability.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 105 bpm, BP 120/75 mmHg, RR 22/min
data_table.Examination: Uterus is hypertonic. Cervix is 3 cm dilated, 1 cm long, membranes intact.
data_table.Investigations: CTG: Prolonged deceleration to 80 bpm for >3 minutes. Contractions: 6 in 10 mins.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate medical intervention?

options.text: Administer an intravenous bolus of magnesium sulfate.
Commence an intravenous oxytocin augmentation infusion.
Perform an artificial rupture of the amniotic membranes.
Perform an immediate emergency category one caesarean section.
Administer a stat dose of subcutaneous terbutaline.

stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 presents to the early pregnancy assessment clinic with mild, vague left-sided pelvic discomfort. She reports 6 weeks of amenorrhoea and a positive home pregnancy test. She denies any vaginal bleeding, shoulder tip pain, or dizziness. On examination, her abdomen is soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness but no rebound or guarding. Speculum examination is unremarkable with a closed cervical os.

Vital signs are within normal limits. A quantitative serum beta-hCG returns at 1500 IU/L. An urgent transvaginal ultrasound is performed, which demonstrates an empty uterus with a homogenous endometrial thickness of 12 mm. Both ovaries appear morphologically normal, there are no visible adnexal masses, and there is no free fluid in the Pouch of Douglas.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 80 bpm, BP 115/75 mmHg, RR 16/min, Temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, mild LIF tenderness. Os closed, no bleeding.
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG: 1500 IU/L. TVUS: Empty uterus, normal adnexa.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer a systemic dose of intramuscular methotrexate.
Arrange an immediate diagnostic and therapeutic laparoscopy.
Perform a surgical dilatation and curettage of the uterus.
Commence oral progesterone supplementation to support pregnancy.
Arrange a repeat serum beta-hCG level in 48 hours.

stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks and 5 days gestation presents with worsening frontal headache and epigastric discomfort for 18 hours. She has chronic hypertension managed with labetalol 200 mg twice daily and gestational diabetes controlled with metformin. Fetal movements are present but reduced compared with baseline. She denies visual loss. Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated. On examination she appears uncomfortable but alert.

Reflexes are brisk with 2 beats of ankle clonus. Fundal height is appropriate for dates. CTG shows baseline 145 bpm with normal variability and two accelerations in 20 minutes. Ultrasound 3 days earlier showed estimated fetal weight on the 18th centile with normal umbilical artery Dopplers. Urine protein:creatinine ratio today is 62 mg/mmol. Blood tests show platelets 112 x10^9/L, ALT 86 U/L, AST 79 U/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, urate 0.42 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 171/112 mmHg repeated after 15 minutes 168/108 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 18/min, Temp 36.8 C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes with clonus, mild RUQ tenderness, no pulmonary oedema

Administer corticosteroids and defer delivery for 48 hours provided CTG remains reassuring

A 29-year-old woman presents with 2 days of light vaginal bleeding and intermittent left iliac fossa pain. She is 7 weeks from her last menstrual period and conceived spontaneously. She has a history of pelvic inflammatory disease 4 years ago and laparoscopic appendicectomy as a teenager. She feels mildly light-headed when standing but has no syncope. Pregnancy test is positive.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows no intrauterine gestational sac, a 19 mm left adnexal heterogeneous mass, and a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum beta-hCG is 2350 IU/L and was 2280 IU/L 48 hours earlier.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/72 mmHg, HR 94 bpm, RR 16/min, Temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Mild left adnexal tenderness, no guarding or rebound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat beta-hCG and ultrasound in 7 days because this is likely an early viable intrauterine pregnancy
Offer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate after confirming suitability for medical management
Proceed directly to emergency laparotomy because free fluid confirms rupture
Arrange dilation and curettage to exclude missed miscarriage before treatment
Commence oral progesterone and repeat beta-hCG after 48 hours

stem: A 37-year-old primigravid woman at 34 weeks' gestation presents with a 2-day history of worsening frontal headache, flashing lights, and right upper quadrant pain. She has had increasing ankle swelling for a week. Her antenatal record shows normal blood pressure until today, and she is taking aspirin 100 mg daily and iron. Begin magnesium sulfate and urgent delivery planning after maternal stabilisation

A 36-year-old multiparous woman develops heavy vaginal bleeding 20 minutes after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks gestation. Labour was induced for gestational hypertension and lasted 18 hours with oxytocin augmentation. She delivered a 4.3 kg infant and required repair of a second-degree perineal tear. The placenta appeared complete on inspection. She has a history of asthma requiring intermittent salbutamol and experienced postpartum haemorrhage after her previous delivery.

On review she feels dizzy and nauseated. The uterus is enlarged and boggy despite ongoing uterine massage. Estimated blood loss is now 1400 mL despite oxytocin infusion and tranexamic acid administration.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/54 mmHg, HR 132 bpm, RR 24/min, Temp 36.5 C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Boggy enlarged uterus, ongoing vaginal bleeding, no retained placental tissue visible
data_table.Investigations: Hb 89 g/L from antenatal baseline 118 g/L, fibrinogen 1.8 g/L
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin infusion running, tranexamic acid already administered, salbutamol PRN

options.text: Administer intramuscular carboprost because uterine atony persists despite oxytocin infusion
Administer intravenous ergometrine while continuing uterine massage and haemorrhage protocol activation
Administer misoprostol while preparing escalation measures for ongoing uterine atony management
Proceed directly to hysterectomy because recurrent postpartum haemorrhage predicts failed medical therapy
Withhold further uterotonics and prioritise fibrinogen replacement because coagulopathy is the primary issue

stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 41 weeks gestation is in labour following induction for post-dates pregnancy. She received dinoprostone overnight followed by oxytocin augmentation for slow progress. Epidural analgesia was inserted 3 hours ago. She is now fully dilated and has been actively pushing for 70 minutes. The fetus is in occipito-posterior position at +1 station. CTG over the preceding 40 minutes shows a baseline rising from 145 to 170 bpm with minimal variability and recurrent late decelerations after most contractions. There have been no accelerations for 35 minutes. Maternal observations show increasing pyrexia despite intravenous fluids. Vaginal examination confirms caput and moulding.

data_table.Examination: Fully dilated, OP position, +1 station, significant caput and moulding
data_table.Investigations: CTG with fetal tachycardia, minimal variability, recurrent late decelerations
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin infusion, epidural infusion, IV fluids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue pushing for another hour because nulliparous women commonly require prolonged second stage labour
Perform rotational instrumental delivery in the birth suite because the cervix is fully dilated
Stop oxytocin, commence intrauterine resuscitation, and proceed to category 1 caesarean section
Perform fetal scalp stimulation and continue labour if a transient acceleration is observed
Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics and reassess the CTG after maternal fever resolves

A 34-year-old G3P2 woman at 35 weeks gestation presents by ambulance with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding that began 45 minutes earlier while at home. She has chronic hypertension treated with nifedipine and continues to smoke 10 cigarettes daily despite counselling. Earlier today she noticed reduced fetal movements. Her previous pregnancies were uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. On arrival she appears distressed and reports constant abdominal pain between contractions.

The uterus feels firm and diffusely tender. Vaginal bleeding is moderate in volume and dark red. CTG demonstrates recurrent prolonged decelerations with minimal variability. A bedside ultrasound shows a live singleton fetus in cephalic presentation with an anterior placenta clear of the cervical os.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 94/60 mmHg, HR 126 bpm, RR 24/min, Temp 36.6 C, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Tender rigid uterus, ongoing dark vaginal bleeding, no signs of labour
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, fibrinogen 1.5 g/L, platelets 142 x10^9/L, pathological CTG

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange formal ultrasound with Doppler assessment because the diagnosis must be confirmed radiologically before delivery
Proceed to urgent caesarean section while initiating maternal resuscitation and blood product support
Commence tocolysis and corticosteroids because the fetus remains preterm at 35 weeks gestation
Perform artificial rupture of membranes and attempt induction because she previously delivered vaginally
Observe with continuous CTG monitoring because vaginal bleeding volume is only moderate

stem:
A 29-year-old woman, para 2, is 20 minutes after a normal vaginal birth at 39 weeks. The placenta delivered spontaneously, but she now has ongoing heavy vaginal bleeding and has soaked through two pads. She had antenatal iron deficiency and a previous postpartum haemorrhage after her first delivery. The current baby weighed 4.2 kg. She received intrapartum oxytocin and had a prolonged second stage.

She has asthma, for which she uses inhaled budesonide-formoterol, and no drug allergies. On examination the uterus feels boggy and enlarged. There are no retained placental fragments visible, and the perineum is intact. Her blood pressure is falling, and she is becoming pale and clammy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 88/54 mmHg, HR 126 bpm, RR 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.5 deg C
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus, ongoing heavy vaginal loss, no perineal tear seen, no retained tissue visible
data_table.Investigations: Hb 86 g/L antenatally; bedside coagulation pending
data_table.Medications: Intrapartum oxytocin given; budesonide-formoterol inhaler; no drug allergies

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg now
Intramuscular carboprost 250 mcg now
Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g now
Intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU now
Immediate hysterectomy without further medical treatment

A 28-year-old primigravida at 31 weeks and 4 days gestation presents with ongoing clear vaginal fluid loss for 18 hours. She has felt intermittent lower abdominal tightening but no regular contractions. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated apart from iron deficiency anaemia. Speculum examination confirms pooling of liquor in the posterior fornix. Initial CTG is reassuring and ultrasound demonstrates cephalic presentation with reduced amniotic fluid volume.

She is admitted for expectant management with corticosteroids and intravenous antibiotics. Thirty-six hours later she develops increasing uterine tenderness and reports feeling feverish. The fetal heart rate baseline rises progressively over the next hour.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.2 C, HR 118 bpm, BP 108/64 mmHg, RR 20/min
data_table.Examination: Uterine tenderness, ongoing liquor leakage, no heavy vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, CRP 112 mg/L, CTG fetal baseline 175 bpm with preserved variability
data_table.Medications: Betamethasone course commenced, IV antibiotics running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue expectant management until corticosteroids are completed because CTG variability remains reassuring
Proceed toward delivery while continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed intrauterine infection
Commence tocolysis because uterine activity may reduce after antibiotic therapy is escalated
Repeat ultrasound and continue observation because fetal tachycardia may reflect maternal dehydration alone
Stop antibiotics because inflammatory markers commonly rise after corticosteroid administration in pregnancy

stem: A 27-year-old woman attends her GP for review of cervical screening results. She had her first cervical screening test at age 25, which was negative for oncogenic HPV. She has no abnormal bleeding, pelvic pain, or postcoital symptoms. She received partial HPV vaccination during adolescence. Her current test result shows oncogenic HPV 16 detected with negative liquid-based cytology. She asks whether she can simply repeat the test in 12 months because the cytology is normal and she feels well. She has no history of immunosuppression or previous cervical procedures.

Refer for colposcopy because oncogenic HPV 16 carries higher cervical neoplasia risk
Repeat HPV testing in 5 years because prior screening at age 25 was normal

stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 38+2 in spontaneous labour has SROM during VE (cervix 6 cm) and the midwife palpates a pulsatile cord at the introitus. CTG shows sustained fetal bradycardia at 70 bpm despite left lateral position. The on-call obstetric registrar and anaesthetist are 5 minutes away, theatre is being prepared and an emergency category-1 caesarean section has been called. The woman is in a single delivery room (no nearby toilets, no easy access to Foley-bag elevation kit). Maternal vital signs are stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 102 bpm, BP 125/80 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Visible umbilical cord at introitus, pulsatile, no presenting part visible, cervix fully assessed at 6 cm, station -2
data_table.Investigations: CTG: sustained fetal bradycardia at 70 bpm for 90 seconds, no recovery with position change
data_table.Medications: Terbutaline 250 mcg SC administered 2 minutes ago

options.text: Place the woman in knee-chest position, elevate the presenting part manually with a vaginal hand, and instil 500-700 mL normal saline into the bladder via Foley catheter to maintain elevation; administer tocolysis (terbutaline 250 mcg SC)
Instruct active maternal pushing to expedite vaginal delivery before theatre arrives
Manually replace the cord into the uterine cavity to restore fetal circulation
Repeat digital VE every 5 minutes to assess for cervical progress before theatre
Wrap the cord in warm saline-soaked gauze outside the vagina and await spontaneous resolution

stem:
A 36-year-old G4P2A1 at 32+1 weeks gestation presents to the birth suite with sudden onset of bright red vaginal bleeding approximately 1 hour ago. She reports no pain and no contractions. The bleeding was initially moderate but has now reduced to spotting. Her obstetric history includes two previous lower-segment caesarean sections (the most recent 2 years ago) and a first-trimester miscarriage managed with suction curettage.

At her 20-week morphology scan, the placenta was noted to be posterior and covering the internal os completely. A follow-up scan at 28 weeks confirmed a major placenta praevia. Her antenatal course has been otherwise uncomplicated. On examination, her abdomen is soft and non-tender with a singleton fetus in cephalic presentation. The fundal height is consistent with dates. Speculum examination reveals a closed cervix with a small amount of dark blood in the posterior fornix.

Fetal cardiotocography shows a baseline of 145 bpm with normal variability, no decelerations, and no uterine activity. Her haemoglobin is 102 g/L (down from 118 g/L at 28 weeks) and haematocrit is 0.31. The estimated blood loss is approximately 400 mL. She is haemodynamically stable with HR 88 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 88 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98%, Temp 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non-tender, fundal height = dates, fetus cephalic, speculum: closed cervix, dark blood posterior fornix
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L (was 118 at 28 wks), Hct 0.31, CTG baseline 145 bpm normal variability no decelerations no contractions

lead_in: Which risk factor in this presentation most strongly raises concern for placenta accreta spectrum disorder over an uncomplicated major placenta praevia?

options.text: Maternal age over 35 years at the time of delivery
The confirmed persistence of a major placenta praevia at 28 weeks gestation
First-trimester miscarriage managed with suction curettage in addition to the two prior caesarean sections
The combination of major placenta praevia with two previous lower-segment caesarean sections
The drop in haemoglobin from 118 g/L at 28 weeks to 102 g/L at presentation with bright red bleeding

A 29-year-old primigravida at 40+0 weeks gestation is in the second stage of labour. She has been pushing for 90 minutes with an epidural in situ. Her pregnancy was complicated by diet-controlled gestational diabetes diagnosed at 28 weeks on the 75 g OGTT (fasting 5.3 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.2 mmol/L, 2-hour 8.6 mmol/L). Fetal surveillance has been normal. The head has delivered spontaneously over an intact perineum.

Following delivery of the head, the chin retracts tightly against the perineum (turtle-neck sign) and restitution does not occur. Gentle downward traction fails to deliver the anterior shoulder. The accoucheur calls for help. The woman has been moved to the end of the bed and her legs are placed in hyperflexion (McRoberts' position). After one further attempt at downward traction, the anterior shoulder remains undelivered.

Suprapubic pressure has been applied by an assistant using a closed fist in a downward and lateral direction with the next contraction. The shoulder has still not delivered. The paediatric team is present and the time since delivery of the head is now 2 minutes and 30 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 110 bpm, BP 135/85 mmHg, fetal HR at last assessment 130 bpm pre-push
data_table.Examination: Turtle-neck sign present, restitution absent, head tightly applied to perineum, McRoberts' position achieved, suprapubic pressure unsuccessful
data_table.Investigations: GDM: 75 g OGTT fasting 5.3, 1h 10.2, 2h 8.6 mmol/L (diagnostic per ADIPS criteria)
data_table.Medications: Epidural in situ (bupivacaine 0.1% + fentanyl 2 mcg/mL at 8 mL/hr)

lead_in: What is the SINGLE BEST next manoeuvre to attempt?

options.text: Apply firmer downward traction on the fetal head combined with continuous suprapubic pressure for a full 60 seconds
Deliver the posterior arm by entering the sacral hollow, locating the humerus, sweeping it across the chest, and delivering the arm
Rotate the fetus by applying pressure to the anterior shoulder through the abdominal wall (Rubin I manoeuvre)
Perform an episiotomy to increase the available space for delivery before attempting further traction
Perform the Gaskin all-fours manoeuvre by rolling the woman onto her hands and knees

stem:
A 24-year-old primigravida at 36+4 weeks gestation is brought to the birth suite by ambulance following a tonic-clonic seizure at home that lasted approximately 2 minutes. She has a known diagnosis of pre-eclampsia with severe features diagnosed 3 days ago, for which she has been receiving oral labetalol 200 mg BD. She had been complaining of a severe frontal headache and epigastric pain since this morning.

On arrival, she is postictal and drowsy with a GCS of 13 (E3 V4 M6). Her blood pressure is 175/115 mmHg on the left arm in the semi-recumbent position, confirmed with a repeat reading 15 minutes later. She has 3+ protein on urine dipstick and hyperreflexia with 4 beats of clonus at the ankle. IV access has been established. She weighs 72 kg.

Her most recent bloods from 2 hours ago show: Hb 108 g/L, platelets 95 x 10^9/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, ALT 125 U/L, urate 0.48 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 175/115 mmHg (confirmed), HR 98 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air, Temp 37.1°C, GCS 13 postictal
data_table.Examination: Postictal, drowsy, hyperreflexia, 4 beats ankle clonus, 3+ proteinuria, epigastric tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L, Platelets 95 x 10^9/L, Creatinine 88 micromol/L, ALT 125 U/L, Urate 0.48 mmol/L (2 hrs ago)
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg PO BD for 3 days (last dose 4 hours ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen for this woman?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour IV for 24 hours after delivery or last seizure
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV loading dose over 5 minutes, then 2 g/hour IV infusion for 24 hours postpartum
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IM loading dose into each buttock (8 g total), then 5 g IM 4-hourly for 24 hours
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV loading dose over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour IV infusion for 24 hours after the last seizure
Magnesium sulfate 6 g IV loading dose over 30 minutes, then 1.5 g/hour IV infusion for 48 hours postpartum
