A 31-year-old G3P2 at 39+1 weeks gestation has just delivered a 4.2 kg infant vaginally following a labour augmented with oxytocin for 14 hours. The placenta delivered spontaneously 10 minutes later. Her estimated blood loss is now 800 mL and ongoing. The uterus is boggy on palpation and the fundus is above the umbilicus. The accoucheur has commenced uterine fundal massage and the midwife is running an IV infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 1 L of normal saline at 250 mL/hour.

The bladder has been emptied with a straight catheter. Despite these measures for 5 minutes, the bleeding continues and the uterus remains atonic. Her current vital signs are HR 112 bpm, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 20. She has no known drug allergies. Her antenatal haemoglobin 2 weeks ago was 115 g/L. She has a history of asthma well-controlled with salbutamol as needed, with no exacerbations in the past year.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 bpm, BP 100/65 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 98%
data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy, fundus above umbilicus, ongoing moderate-heavy vaginal bleeding, placenta appears complete on inspection
data_table.Investigations: Antenatal Hb 115 g/L (2 weeks prior), current estimated blood loss 800 mL and ongoing
data_table.Medications: Oxytocin 40 U in 1 L normal saline at 250 mL/hr IV; salbutamol PRN for asthma

lead_in: Which SINGLE uterotonic agent should be administered next?

options.text: IM syntometrine 1 mL (oxytocin 5 IU + ergometrine 500 mcg) as a single dose
IM carboprost 250 mcg (Haemabate) every 15 minutes up to a maximum of 8 doses
IV tranexamic acid 1 g slowly over 10 minutes as a single dose and IV ergometrine 250 mcg slowly
IV ergometrine 250 mcg slowly over 1-2 minutes, repeated once after 5 minutes if needed
Misoprostol 800 mcg per rectum as a single dose

stem:
A 27-year-old G2P1 at 28+3 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department reporting a sudden gush of clear fluid from her vagina approximately 2 hours ago while sitting at her desk. She has since noted ongoing trickling of fluid. She reports no pain, no contractions, and normal fetal movements. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated to date with a normal morphology scan at 20 weeks.

On examination, her temperature is 37.9°C, HR 92 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, fundal height is 28 cm. On speculum examination, a pool of clear fluid is seen in the posterior fornix with a positive nitrazine test. The cervix is closed and long on visual inspection. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 150 bpm with moderate variability, no decelerations, and irregular tightenings every 10-12 minutes.

Her most recent cervical length at 20 weeks was 42 mm. She received a full course of betamethasone for threatened preterm labour at 26 weeks (which resolved spontaneously).

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.9°C, HR 92 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%
data_table.Examination: Speculum: pooling of clear fluid, positive nitrazine, cervix closed and long; fundal height 28 cm
data_table.Investigations: CTG baseline 150 bpm, moderate variability, no decelerations, tightenings q10-12 min; cervical length 42 mm at 20 wks
data_table.Medications: Betamethasone course completed at 26 weeks (2 doses 24 hrs apart)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit for inpatient monitoring, administer a rescue course of betamethasone (11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart), commence oral azithromycin 1 g stat and ampicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly for 48 hours, then amoxicillin 250 mg PO 8-hourly for 5 days

Admit for immediate induction of labour with intravenous oxytocin, commence empirical IV ampicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily for presumed chorioamnionitis, and plan delivery within 24 hours given the borderline temperature and PPROM at 28+3 weeks

Admit for conservative management with 4-hourly observations (temperature, HR, BP), twice-weekly CTG, weekly bloods (WCC, CRP), administer a rescue course of betamethasone, commence oral erythromycin 250 mg QID for 10 days, and plan delivery at 34+0 weeks if undelivered

Administer a single rescue dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, observe for 4 hours of CTG and maternal vital-sign monitoring, and discharge home with strict return precautions if the temperature normalises and there are no signs of chorioamnionitis or labour, with outpatient review in 48 hours

Admit for inpatient monitoring with 4-hourly observations and twice-weekly CTG, administer a rescue course of betamethasone, commence IV ampicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus oral clarithromycin 500 mg BD for 10 days as latency antibiotics, and plan delivery at 37+0 weeks if undelivered

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 at 39+0 weeks presents in spontaneous labour at 4 cm dilated. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Her GBS status is unknown - the screening swab at 36 weeks was not performed because she was travelling interstate. Her previous pregnancy 4 years ago was uncomplicated, and she delivered vaginally at term. Her first infant did not develop GBS disease.

On direct questioning, she reports no symptoms of a urinary tract infection during this pregnancy and no history of a positive GBS swab. Her temperature is 36.7°C, and observations are normal. The membranes are intact at present. The CTG is reassuring with a baseline of 140 bpm and normal variability. The woman has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7°C, HR 80 bpm, BP 115/72 mmHg, RR 16
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, membranes intact, cephalic presentation, station -1
data_table.Investigations: CTG baseline 140 bpm, normal variability, accelerations present; GBS swab at 36 weeks: NOT DONE
data_table.Medications: Nil regular, no known drug allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis plan?

options.text: No intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is required; treat only if the infant develops clinical signs of sepsis
Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV loading dose, then 600 mg IV 4-hourly until delivery, commencing immediately as she is in labour with unknown GBS status
Take a low vaginal swab for GBS culture and PCR now, and commence benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV loading dose only if the swab returns positive or membranes rupture

Monitor for the development of clinical risk factors - if membranes rupture for ≥18 hours or maternal temperature reaches ≥38.0°C, commence benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV loading dose then 600 mg IV 4-hourly
Cefazolin 2 g IV loading dose then 1 g IV 8-hourly as the preferred antibiotic for unknown GBS status with no risk factors

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida at 29+5 weeks gestation is being managed as an inpatient for early-onset fetal growth restriction. Her pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated with a normal morphology scan at 20 weeks. Serial growth ultrasounds have shown an estimated fetal weight consistently below the 3rd centile since 24 weeks with a falling growth velocity. Umbilical artery Doppler studies today show absent end-diastolic flow.

Previous Dopplers 2 weeks ago showed a raised umbilical artery pulsatility index (>95th centile) but positive end-diastolic flow. Middle cerebral artery Doppler today shows a low pulsatility index consistent with brain-sparing. The ductus venosus Doppler shows a positive a-wave. The amniotic fluid index is 7.5 cm (borderline oligohydramnios). CTG today shows a baseline of 145 bpm with reduced variability (3-5 bpm) and occasional spontaneous accelerations, but no decelerations.

The woman has received a full course of betamethasone (two doses 24 hours apart) completed yesterday. Her blood pressure is 120/78 mmHg, and urinalysis shows no protein.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 120/78 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, RR 16, Temp 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: No protein on urinalysis, fundal height 25 cm (consistent with FGR)
data_table.Investigations: UA Doppler: absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF); MCA PI low (brain-sparing); DV a-wave positive; AFI 7.5 cm; CTG: baseline 145 bpm, reduced variability (3-5 bpm), no decelerations; EFW <3rd centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose for fetal neuroprotection and plan for delivery within 24 hours given the AEDF and reduced CTG variability
Commence IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour maintenance, and plan delivery within 24-48 hours with continuous intrapartum CTG monitoring
Perform immediate caesarean section as the AEDF and reduced CTG variability indicate acute-on-chronic fetal compromise requiring delivery within 2-4 hours
Perform a repeat CTG in 12 hours and only plan delivery if the CTG deteriorates to show recurrent decelerations or the ductus venosus a-wave becomes absent or reversed
Administer a rescue course of betamethasone (two further doses 24 hours apart) and plan for delivery at 32+0 weeks, repeating umbilical artery Dopplers twice weekly

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P1 at 34+2 weeks gestation presents with a sudden small amount of dark red vaginal bleeding that began immediately after she felt a 'popping' sensation and a gush of fluid 30 minutes ago. She reports no pain. Her pregnancy was complicated by a low-lying placenta noted at the 20-week morphology scan, which was reported to have cleared the os by the 32-week follow-up scan.

A velamentous cord insertion was noted on the 32-week scan but vasa praevia was not specifically reported. On arrival, she is haemodynamically stable with HR 88 bpm and BP 120/75 mmHg. Speculum examination shows dark blood in the vagina with ongoing oozing. A bedside cardiotocograph is performed immediately and shows a fetal heart rate baseline of 120 bpm, reduced variability, and a sinusoidal-like pattern with regular shallow oscillations. There are no accelerations and no decelerations. The estimated blood loss is approximately 100 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 88 bpm, BP 120/75 mmHg, RR 18, Temp 36.5°C, SpO2 98%
data_table.Examination: Speculum: dark blood in vagina, ongoing oozing; digital examination deferred; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: CTG: baseline 120 bpm, reduced variability, sinusoidal-like pattern; 32-week scan: low-lying placenta cleared, velamentous cord insertion noted; EBL ~100 mL

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis underlying the CTG pattern?

options.text: Placental abruption causing fetal hypoxia and compensatory fetal heart rate pattern
Placenta praevia with a recurrent low-lying placenta causing marginal sinus bleeding and fetal bradycardia
Vasa praevia with rupture of a fetal vessel traversing the membranes overlying the internal os
Uterine rupture with extrusion of the fetus into the peritoneal cavity and severe fetal distress
Fetal-maternal haemorrhage due to a placental lake rupture during membrane rupture

stem:
A 28-year-old G3P1 at approximately 6+2 weeks gestation by LMP presents to the early pregnancy assessment service with 4 days of mild left iliac fossa pain and spotting. She is haemodynamically stable with HR 78 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 8 mm. The left adnexa demonstrates a 2.4 cm mass with a hyperechoic ring but no visible yolk sac or fetal pole.

There is no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her serum β-hCG is 2100 IU/L, and a repeat 48 hours later is 2850 IU/L (a 36% rise). Her full blood count, renal function, and liver function tests are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, BP 110/68 mmHg, RR 16, Temp 36.4°C
data_table.Examination: Mild left adnexal tenderness, no cervical motion tenderness, no peritoneal signs
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: empty uterus, left adnexal mass 2.4 cm with hyperechoic ring, no yolk sac/fetal pole, no free fluid; β-hCG 2100 → 2850 (48 hr, 36% rise); FBC, UEC, LFTs normal

lead_in: Which of the following findings would make this woman UNSUITABLE for medical management with single-dose methotrexate?

options.text: An adnexal mass measuring 2.4 cm on transvaginal ultrasound
A serum β-hCG of 2850 IU/L with a suboptimal rise of 36% over 48 hours
The presence of a hyperechoic ring around the adnexal mass without a visible yolk sac
A normal platelet count, normal serum creatinine, and normal liver transaminases
The presence of embryonic cardiac activity within the ectopic gestation on ultrasound

stem:
A 32-year-old nulligravid woman presents to the emergency department with progressive abdominal distension, bloating, and reduced urine output over the past 3 days. She underwent oocyte retrieval for IVF 8 days ago after ovarian stimulation with a GnRH antagonist protocol and a trigger injection of hCG. On examination, her abdomen is distended, tense, and diffusely tender without peritonism. A fluid thrill is present.

Her weight today is 68 kg, up from a pre-cycle weight of 62 kg. Her HR is 102 bpm, BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air. Urine output over the past 6 hours has been 120 mL (20 mL/hr). A transvaginal ultrasound shows bilateral enlarged ovaries measuring 10 cm and 11 cm with multiple cysts, and a moderate amount of ascites. Her haemoglobin is 165 g/L, haematocrit 0.49, WCC 16.5 x 10^9/L, serum creatinine 105 micromol/L (pre-cycle 62 micromol/L), ALT 55 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102 bpm, BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended, tense, diffuse tenderness, fluid thrill present; weight gain 6 kg over 8 days
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: ovaries 10 cm and 11 cm, multiple cysts, moderate ascites; Hb 165 g/L, Hct 0.49, WCC 16.5, Creatinine 105 (from 62), ALT 55, Coags normal; urine output 20 mL/hr
data_table.Medications: IVF stimulation cycle with GnRH antagonist protocol; hCG trigger 8 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate NEXT step in management?

options.text: Commence IV fluid resuscitation with a balanced crystalloid at 1-2 mL/kg/hr, insert an indwelling catheter for strict fluid balance, commence prophylactic dose low molecular weight heparin, and admit under the gynaecology team for daily assessment

Perform an ultrasound-guided paracentesis to drain ascites under strict aseptic technique, commence IV fluid resuscitation cautiously, insert an indwelling catheter, and administer prophylactic dose low molecular weight heparin
Administer therapeutic dose low molecular weight heparin, as the haemoconcentration and oliguria indicate severe OHSS with high thrombotic risk requiring full anticoagulation
Discharge home on oral cabergoline 0.5 mg daily for 8 days, with strict instructions for daily weight monitoring, fluid intake of 3 L/day, and return if symptoms worsen
Perform a diagnostic laparoscopy to exclude ovarian torsion, given the bilateral adnexal enlargement and sudden onset of abdominal distension and pain

stem:
A 36-year-old G2P1 at 29+0 weeks gestation was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks on a 75 g OGTT (fasting 5.4 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.5 mmol/L, 2-hour 8.9 mmol/L). Her BMI is 32 kg/m². She has been managed with lifestyle modification (diet and exercise) for 3 weeks. Her fasting BGLs have consistently been 5.0-5.3 mmol/L (target <5.1 mmol/L) and her 2-hour postprandial BGLs are 6.2-6.6 mmol/L (target <6.7 mmol/L).

An ultrasound at 28 weeks showed an estimated fetal weight on the 78th centile with a normal amniotic fluid index. She asks about medication options to improve her fasting glucose. She is concerned about the risk of needing insulin and the need for injections.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, fundal height 30 cm
data_table.Examination: Normal examination; no signs of macrosomia clinically
data_table.Investigations: OGTT: fasting 5.4, 1h 10.5, 2h 8.9 (all diagnostic); fasting BGLs 5.0-5.3 (target <5.1), 2h postprandial 6.2-6.6 (target <6.7); EFW 78th centile, AFI normal
data_table.Medications: Nil pharmacological; lifestyle measures for 3 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing her fasting hyperglycaemia?

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg orally at night, titrate up to 1500 mg daily as tolerated, and continue diet and exercise measures
Commence basal insulin (isophane or insulin detemir) at 0.1 units/kg at night, titrated according to fasting BGL, and cease metformin
Continue lifestyle measures alone for a further 2 weeks, as the fasting BGLs are only marginally above target and postprandial targets are met
Commence glibenclamide (glibenclamide) 2.5 mg orally at night, titrating to a maximum of 20 mg daily
Commence both metformin 500 mg BD and basal insulin 0.2 units/kg at night simultaneously to rapidly achieve glycaemic control

stem:
A 35-year-old G4P3 at 34+5 weeks gestation presents to the birth suite with sudden onset of dark red vaginal bleeding associated with severe continuous lower abdominal pain that began 45 minutes ago. She reports that the pain started abruptly while she was resting and has not subsided. On examination, she appears distressed and in significant pain. Her abdomen is tense and tender with a woody-hard feel on palpation.

The uterus is contracting every 2 minutes with no palpable relaxation between contractions. The fetal heart rate is auscultated at 110 bpm. Vaginal examination is deferred. Speculum examination shows dark blood pooling in the posterior fornix with an estimated blood loss of 250 mL. Her HR is 108 bpm and BP is 150/95 mmHg. An urgent bedside ultrasound shows a posterior placenta clear of the internal os, no retroplacental clot visualised, and a fetus in cephalic presentation with a normal amniotic fluid index. The CTG shows a baseline of 110 bpm with reduced variability, no accelerations, and late decelerations following each contraction.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 108 bpm, BP 150/95 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 97%, Temp 36.5°C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen tense, woody-hard, tender, contracting q2min no relaxation; fetal HR 110 bpm; speculum: dark blood pooling, EBL 250 mL
data_table.Investigations: Bedside USS: posterior placenta clear of os, no retroplacental clot seen, AFI normal; CTG baseline 110 bpm, reduced variability, late decelerations

lead_in: Which finding in this presentation most strongly favours a diagnosis of placental abruption over placenta praevia?

options.text: Dark red vaginal bleeding rather than bright red bleeding, as dark blood indicates concealed haemorrhage characteristic of abruption
A tense, woody-hard uterus with continuous pain and hypertonic contractions that do not relax between tightenings
A history of chronic hypertension and smoking, which are established risk factors for abnormal placentation and low-lying placenta
The CTG showing fetal heart rate baseline of 110 bpm with reduced variability and late decelerations following each contraction
Ultrasound demonstrating a posterior placenta that is clear of the internal os with no retroplacental clot visualised

stem:
A 31-year-old primigravida at 36+6 weeks gestation is admitted to the antenatal ward with new-onset hypertension. She has been well throughout her pregnancy until 3 days ago when she noted mild ankle swelling and a frontal headache. Her blood pressure on arrival is 155/105 mmHg, confirmed on repeat measurement 30 minutes later. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein on dipstick with a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 45 mg/mmol (normal <30).

She reports no visual disturbances, no epigastric pain, and no nausea. On examination, she has mild pitting ankle oedema, normal reflexes with no clonus, and a soft non-tender abdomen. The fetal CTG is reactive with a baseline of 145 bpm, normal variability, and accelerations. Ultrasound shows an appropriately grown fetus on the 55th centile with a normal amniotic fluid index and normal umbilical artery Dopplers.

Her blood results show haemoglobin 118 g/L, platelets 195 x 10^9/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, ALT 28 U/L, and urate 0.36 mmol/L. She has been commenced on oral labetalol 200 mg BD, and her blood pressure has improved to 140/90 mmHg after 24 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 155/105 (confirmed, now 140/90 on labetalol), HR 82 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 98%, Temp 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Mild pitting ankle oedema, normal reflexes, no clonus, soft non-tender abdomen, fundal height = dates
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118, Plt 195, Cr 62, ALT 28, Urate 0.36; PCR 45 mg/mmol; CTG reactive, baseline 145; USS EFW 55th centile, AFI normal, UA Doppler normal
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg PO BD (commenced 24 hrs ago); Betamethasone course completed 12 hrs ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate timing for delivery?

options.text: Induction of labour within the next 24-48 hours, as delivery is recommended for this hypertensive disorder of pregnancy at or beyond 37+0 weeks
Continue oral labetalol and expectant management with twice-weekly review until 39+0 weeks, as her blood pressure is now controlled and she has no severe features
Perform immediate caesarean section, as the proteinuria with a PCR of 45 mg/mmol and hypertension at 36+6 weeks meets severe-features criteria requiring urgent delivery
Discharge home on labetalol 200 mg BD with instructions for daily BP monitoring and twice-weekly CTG and ultrasound, with delivery planned at 40+0 weeks
Wait until 38+0 weeks to allow full corticosteroid effect, then induce labour if the blood pressure remains controlled on oral labetalol without development of severe features

stem:
A 28-year-old primigravida at 40+2 weeks gestation is in active labour with an epidural in situ. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. The membranes ruptured spontaneously 6 hours ago with clear liquor. Oxytocin augmentation was commenced 2 hours ago for slow progress and is currently running at 12 mU/min. She is contracting 4 in 10 minutes. On vaginal examination, the cervix is 7 cm dilated, the presenting part is at station 0, and there is a caput.

A fetal scalp electrode has been placed due to difficulty with external monitoring. The CTG over the past 60 minutes shows a baseline of 165 bpm, variability of 2-3 bpm, and shallow late decelerations of 15 bpm lasting 45 seconds following each contraction. There are no accelerations. The maternal temperature is 37.8°C, HR 98 bpm, BP 115/70 mmHg. The midwife has performed fetal scalp stimulation with no acceleratory response.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal Temp 37.8°C, HR 98 bpm, BP 115/70 mmHg, RR 20
data_table.Examination: Cervix 7 cm, station 0, caput present, clear liquor, FSE in situ
data_table.Investigations: CTG: baseline 165 bpm, variability 2-3 bpm, shallow late decelerations of 15 bpm lasting 45 sec with each contraction, no accelerations, no response to fetal scalp stimulation
data_table.Medications: Epidural in situ; Oxytocin infusion at 12 mU/min

lead_in: How should this CTG be classified, and what is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Classify as suspicious CTG; continue oxytocin, reposition the mother into left lateral, and reassess the CTG in 30 minutes after a 500 mL IV fluid bolus

Classify as pathological CTG; cease the oxytocin infusion immediately, commence maternal oxygen via face mask at 8 L/min, and prepare for expedited delivery if the CTG does not improve within 30 minutes

Classify as pathological CTG; cease the oxytocin infusion, reposition to left lateral, consider terbutaline 250 mcg SC for intrauterine resuscitation, and prepare for immediate delivery if the CTG does not normalise promptly
Classify as suspicious CTG due to maternal pyrexia and epidural; administer paracetamol 1 g IV, continue oxytocin, and reassess CTG in 15 minutes after the temperature normalises
Classify as pathological CTG; perform an immediate category 1 caesarean section without further intrauterine resuscitation measures as the fetus is already compromised

stem:
A 24-year-old primigravida delivered vaginally 10 days ago following induction of labour at 38 weeks for gestational hypertension. The third stage was managed actively with intramuscular oxytocin 10 IU, and the placenta was delivered complete by controlled cord traction. She was discharged home on day 2 post-delivery with no concerns. She now presents to the emergency department with new-onset heavy vaginal bleeding that began 4 hours ago, soaking through 3 maternity pads.

She also reports a 2-day history of dull lower abdominal pain, malaise, and a temperature of 38.2°C measured at home. The lochia has been malodorous for 3 days. On examination, she looks pale and unwell. Her HR is 106 bpm, BP 100/60 mmHg, and temperature is 38.4°C. The uterus is tender, boggy, and palpable 3 cm below the umbilicus. On speculum, there is heavy dark red blood with clots in the vagina, and the os is open with blood and tissue visible. Her haemoglobin is 88 g/L (was 108 g/L antenatally), WCC is 16.2 x 10^9/L, and CRP is 125 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 106 bpm, BP 100/60 mmHg, Temp 38.4°C, RR 18, SpO2 97%
data_table.Examination: Pale, unwell, uterus tender boggy 3 cm below umbilicus, speculum: heavy dark blood with clots, os open, tissue visible
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (from 108 antenatal), WCC 16.2 x 10^9/L, CRP 125 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence IV clindamycin 900 mg 8-hourly and IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily for endometritis, and administer IV oxytocin 40 units infusion for uterine atony
Perform a bimanual examination and attempt digital removal of retained tissue from the uterine cavity under sedation, followed by IV oxytocin and antibiotics

Perform an urgent pelvic ultrasound to assess for retained products of conception, commence IV antibiotics (clindamycin and gentamicin), administer an IV oxytocin infusion, and arrange for suction curettage in theatre if retained products are confirmed
Administer IV tranexamic acid 1 g, IV ergometrine 250 mcg, and oral misoprostol 800 mcg, and observe for 4 hours; if bleeding persists, arrange a pelvic ultrasound
Commence oral doxycycline 100 mg BD and oral metronidazole 400 mg TDS for endometritis, and arrange a pelvic ultrasound as an outpatient within 48 hours if the bleeding settles

stem:
A 38-year-old G2P1 at 30+1 weeks gestation was diagnosed with GDM at 27 weeks on a 75 g OGTT (fasting 5.6 mmol/L, 1-hour 10.8 mmol/L, 2-hour 9.2 mmol/L). She commenced metformin 500 mg BD at diagnosis, titrated to 1 g BD over 2 weeks, and has been on this dose for the past 3 weeks with ongoing dietary modification. Her fasting BGLs have been 5.3-5.8 mmol/L consistently.

Her 2-hour postprandial BGLs have been 6.5-7.2 mmol/L. An ultrasound at 29 weeks showed an estimated fetal weight on the 82nd centile with a normal amniotic fluid index. She weighs 78 kg. Her HbA1c is 5.8% (40 mmol/mol).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, fundal height 32 cm
data_table.Examination: Normal examination
data_table.Investigations: OGTT: fasting 5.6, 1h 10.8, 2h 9.2 (all diagnostic); fasting BGLs 5.3-5.8 (target <5.1); 2h postprandial 6.5-7.2 (target <6.7); EFW 82nd centile; HbA1c 5.8%
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g PO BD (max tolerated dose)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her glycaemic management?

options.text: Continue metformin 1 g BD and add basal insulin (isophane or insulin detemir) at night, starting at 0.1-0.2 units/kg, titrated to achieve fasting BGL below 5.1 mmol/L

Cease metformin and commence basal-bolus insulin regimen with isophane at night and rapid-acting insulin analogue before each meal to target both fasting and postprandial hyperglycaemia simultaneously
Increase metformin to 1.5 g BD (total 3 g daily) and add glibenclamide 2.5 mg at night for an additional 2 weeks before considering insulin
Continue current metformin dose and dietary measures for a further 2 weeks as the fasting BGLs are only marginally above target, then reassess with repeat HbA1c
Commence rapid-acting insulin analogue before breakfast only, as her 2-hour postprandial BGLs are above target while fasting values are approaching acceptable levels

stem:
A 34-year-old primigravida at 37+1 weeks gestation attends her routine antenatal appointment. On abdominal palpation, the fetus is found to be in a breech presentation with the fetal head ballotable at the fundus. A bedside ultrasound confirms a frank breech presentation with the fetal legs extended, a flexed fetal head, normal amniotic fluid index, and a posterior placenta not covering the os.

The estimated fetal weight is on the 55th centile. She is otherwise well with no significant past medical history. She has read about breech vaginal delivery and asks whether this is a safe option for her.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/70 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, fundal height 37 cm
data_table.Examination: Fetus in frank breech on palpation; bedside USS confirms frank breech, flexed head, AFI normal, placenta posterior not covering os, EFW 55th centile
data_table.Investigations: USS: frank breech, flexed head, normal AFI, posterior placenta, EFW 55th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management recommendation?

options.text: Offer external cephalic version, and if unsuccessful or declined, discuss planned caesarean section at 39+0 weeks as the safest mode of delivery for a term breech

Offer external cephalic version, and if unsuccessful, plan a vaginal breech delivery as this primigravida has a frank breech with flexed head and normal fetal weight on the 55th centile, which are favourable factors

Proceed directly to booking an elective caesarean section at 39+0 weeks without offering ECV, as primigravidae have a lower ECV success rate and ECV carries risks of fetal distress and placental abruption
Perform external cephalic version immediately at this visit without tocolysis, as she is 37 weeks, and if successful, discharge home to await spontaneous labour

Advise the woman that breech presentation at 37 weeks has a high chance of spontaneous version before term, and arrange a repeat ultrasound at 39 weeks to reassess presentation before making a delivery plan

stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 33+5 weeks presents with a single episode of painless bright red vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound at 32 weeks showed an anterior placenta completely covering the internal os (major praevia). She is haemodynamically stable, bleeding has settled, CTG reassuring, cervical exam deferred. She has had no previous corticosteroid courses this pregnancy. The plan is admission for monitoring and elective caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks. She is keen on whatever course will best protect her baby's lung function.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 80 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, Temp 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: No active bleeding, soft non-tender uterus, CTG reactive
data_table.Investigations: Known major placenta praevia on previous USS

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid plan?

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart, now
Administer no corticosteroids as she is now beyond 34 weeks
Administer a single dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM
Administer weekly betamethasone 11.4 mg IM until delivery
Administer dexamethasone 6 mg IM, four doses 12-hourly, in place of betamethasone, on the basis of superior neurodevelopmental outcomes

stem: A 30-year-old nullipara at 29+3 weeks presents with new hypertension 170/110 mmHg, headache, and epigastric pain. Urine protein:creatinine ratio 98 mg/mmol. Platelets 130 ×10⁹/L, ALT 110 U/L, creatinine 92 µmol/L. She has received the first dose of betamethasone. CTG is reactive with normal variability. She is commenced on labetalol and magnesium sulfate. After stabilisation, the team discusses timing of delivery.

data_table.Examination: Epigastric tenderness, hyperreflexia, 3 beats clonus
data_table.Investigations: PCR 98, Platelets 130, ALT 110, Cr 92, CTG reactive
data_table.Medications: Labetalol commenced, MgSO₄ infusion, betamethasone first dose given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate timing of delivery?

options.text: Complete the 48-hour steroid course and deliver electively at 48-72 hours, provided maternal and fetal status remain stable
Proceed to delivery within 24 hours, as severe-features hypertensive disease with hepatic involvement mandates delivery regardless of gestational age
Continue expectant management with close monitoring until 34 weeks, as the CTG is reassuring and maternal status is stable on treatment
Administer the second dose of betamethasone at 24 hours and plan delivery for 48 hours after the first dose, with continuous monitoring
Deliver immediately by caesarean, as severe-features hypertension with abnormal LFTs and platelets <150 ×10⁹/L meets haemolysis-elevated-liver-enzymes-low-platelets criteria

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 at 34+1 weeks gestation presents with a 2-week history of intense generalised pruritus, worse on the palms and soles and especially at night, disrupting sleep. She has no rash other than excoriations. Her previous pregnancy 3 years ago ended in an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery. Liver function tests show: ALT 120 U/L, AST 100 U/L, GGT 45 U/L, total bile acids 42 micromol/L.

Viral hepatitis serology, ANA, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies are negative. An ultrasound of the liver and gallbladder is normal. The fetal ultrasound shows normal growth, amniotic fluid index, and umbilical artery Dopplers. The CTG is reactive. She has been commenced on ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg BD, which has partially improved her pruritus after 5 days, but bile acids have risen to 58 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, Temp 36.5°C
data_table.Examination: Excoriations over abdomen and limbs, no jaundice, fundal height 34 cm, non-tender uterus, reactive CTG
data_table.Investigations: ALT 120, AST 100, GGT 45, total bile acids 58 micromol/L (increased from 42); USS: normal fetus, AFI, Dopplers; negative viral/autoimmune screen
data_table.Medications: Ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg BD for 5 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan regarding timing of delivery?

options.text: Continue ursodeoxycholic acid, monitor bile acids weekly, and plan delivery at 37+0 weeks if bile acids remain above 40 micromol/L
Plan delivery at 39+0 weeks after a further ultrasound for growth and amniotic fluid, as the fetus is currently well and bile acids are only moderately elevated
Recommend induction of labour at 37+0 weeks gestation, with continuous intrapartum CTG monitoring, and administer intramuscular vitamin K 10 mg to the mother prior to delivery
Deliver by elective caesarean section at 37+0 weeks, as vaginal delivery with raised bile acids carries an increased risk of fetal distress
Add oral dexamethasone 4 mg BD to further reduce bile acids and delay delivery until 38+0 weeks if bile acids fall below 40 µmol/L

stem: A 28-year-old primigravida delivers a vigorous infant weighing 3.6 kg vaginally after an uncomplicated spontaneous labour. The placenta delivered spontaneously 5 minutes later with gentle cord traction by the attending midwife. Immediately following placental delivery, the woman experiences sudden severe lower abdominal pain, a vasovagal episode with bradycardia (HR 40 bpm), and estimated blood loss of 600 mL. On inspection, a firm, dark red mass is seen protruding from the vagina, approximately 10 cm in diameter, with the placenta still partially attached. The uterine fundus is not palpable abdominally. Her blood pressure drops to 80/50 mmHg, and she appears pale and diaphoretic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 40 bpm, BP 80/50 mmHg, RR 20, SpO₂ 96%
data_table.Examination: Firm dark red mass protruding from vagina, placenta partially attached, fundus not palpable abdominally, EBL 600 mL
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable in acute emergency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step to manage the uterine inversion?

options.text: Attempt immediate manual replacement of the uterus using the Johnson manoeuvre (pushing the fundus upwards through the cervix with the palm, applying pressure at the last-delivered part first)
Administer intramuscular terbutaline 250 mcg to relax the uterus before attempting replacement, then transfer to theatre for manual replacement under general anaesthesia
Remove the placenta from the inverted uterus first to reduce bulk and facilitate replacement, then push the fundus upwards with a fist
Perform the O'Sullivan hydrostatic reduction by infusing warm saline into the vagina via a silastic vacuum cup to create a seal, pushing the uterus back into position
Transfer immediately to operating theatre for a laparotomy and Huntington procedure (using Allis forceps to pull the round ligaments and uterus back through the inversion ring)

stem:
A 35-year-old G2P1 at 39+4 weeks is in active labour with spontaneous rupture of membranes 2 hours ago, meconium-stained liquor, and a prolonged second stage. She suddenly becomes agitated, complains of difficulty breathing, and then collapses. The maternal heart rate is 140 bpm with a faint pulse, blood pressure 60/30 mmHg, SpO₂ 78% on room air. She becomes cyanotic and unresponsive.

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is started immediately. The fetal heart rate drops to 60 bpm. An emergency caesarean is performed in the labour ward. Intraoperatively, she develops severe coagulopathy with diffuse oozing from all surgical sites, and laboratory tests show: haemoglobin 70 g/L, platelets 20 ×10⁹/L, fibrinogen <0.5 g/L, APTT >100 sec, PT >60 sec, and elevated D-dimers.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140 bpm, BP 60/30 mmHg, SpO₂ 78% RA, collapse during labour
data_table.Examination: Cyanotic, unresponsive, severe coagulopathy intraoperatively, diffuse oozing, fetal bradycardia 60 bpm
data_table.Investigations: Hb 70, Plt 20, fibrinogen <0.5, APTT >100, PT >60, elevated D-dimers

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Pulmonary thromboembolism secondary to deep vein thrombosis
Amniotic fluid embolism causing cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, and disseminated intravascular coagulation
Septic shock due to chorioamnionitis from meconium-stained liquor, causing hypotension and DIC
Anaphylactic reaction to an administered medication causing hypotension and distributive shock, with secondary coagulopathy
Placental abruption with massive concealed haemorrhage leading to hypovolaemic shock and coagulopathy

stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 underwent suction curettage for a suspected molar pregnancy at 10 weeks gestation after an ultrasound showed a 'snowstorm' appearance and no fetal pole. Histopathology confirms a complete hydatidiform mole. She is keen to conceive again as soon as possible. Her hCG level 2 weeks post-evacuation is 2500 IU/L, down from 120,000 IU/L pre-operatively. She has no vaginal bleeding, and pelvic ultrasound shows an empty uterus with normal adnexa.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 115/70 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: No vaginal bleeding, uterus well involuted, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: hCG 2500 IU/L (was 120,000); USS: empty uterus, normal adnexa; histology: complete mole

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding future pregnancy?

options.text: She may attempt pregnancy once hCG becomes undetectable, with no increased risk in subsequent pregnancies and no surveillance needed
Avoid pregnancy for at least 6 months after hCG normalises, use reliable contraception, with monthly hCG surveillance throughout that period
She should undergo a hysterectomy because complete moles have a 15-20% risk of progression to choriocarcinoma and future pregnancy is contraindicated
She requires a single dose of intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m² immediately to prevent progression to persistent trophoblastic disease at any stage
She should undergo CT chest and abdomen to stage the disease before pregnancy, as complete moles frequently metastasise to the lungs

stem:
A 30-year-old primigravida at 12+3 weeks gestation presents to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of acute onset severe right iliac fossa pain, associated with nausea and vomiting. The pain began suddenly while she was walking and has been constant since. She has no vaginal bleeding. On examination, she is in significant pain, HR 100 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg.

The abdomen is tender in the right lower quadrant with voluntary guarding but no peritonism. A bedside transvaginal ultrasound shows a viable intrauterine pregnancy consistent with dates, a normal left ovary, and an enlarged right ovary measuring 7 cm with multiple peripheral follicles and absent internal blood flow on colour Doppler. The right ovarian vein is not well visualised. The appendix is not visualised. Her inflammatory markers are normal, and urine dipstick is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 18, Temp 36.5°C
data_table.Examination: Tender RIF, voluntary guarding, no peritonism, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus appropriate size
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: viable IUP, normal left ovary, right ovary 7 cm with peripheral follicles, absent internal Doppler flow; WCC 10.2, CRP 4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with ovarian detorsion and ovarian cystectomy if a benign cyst is identified, with ovarian conservation
Oophorectomy via laparotomy, as the absent Doppler flow indicates irreversible ischaemia and the ovary cannot be salvaged
Conservative management with analgesia, antiemetics, and observation for 24 hours, as the pain may resolve spontaneously
CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to confirm the diagnosis before proceeding to surgery
Aspiration of the ovarian cyst under ultrasound guidance to reduce size and relieve the torsion without surgery

stem: A 28-year-old primigravida at 22+5 weeks presents with painful regular contractions and cervical dilation 3 cm with bulging membranes. Fetal ultrasound: singleton, cephalic, AFI normal, estimated fetal weight 540 g (50th centile). She has been counselled with the neonatology team. After detailed discussion of likely outcomes at periviable gestation, the family has indicated they wish for active resuscitation if the infant is liveborn.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm, bulging membranes
data_table.Investigations: USS: singleton, cephalic, AFI normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan regarding antenatal corticosteroids?

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart, since active resuscitation is planned
Withhold ACS as gestation is below 23 weeks where benefit is uncertain
Administer a single dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM only
Administer dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 6 hours for four doses
Defer the decision until membranes rupture and only give if delivery is within 24 hours

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents after her third consecutive miscarriage at 9 weeks. She had one previous live birth at term 4 years ago. She has no significant medical history.

data_table.Examination: Normal general and pelvic exam
data_table.Investigations: Products of conception: normal female karyotype

lead_in: What is the most appropriate set of investigations?

options.text: Anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies, plus pelvic ultrasound for anomalies
Antiphospholipid antibodies, parental karyotypes, inherited thrombophilia screen, and outpatient diagnostic hysteroscopy
Full blood count, thyroid function tests, fasting glucose, and 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test
Serum anti-Müllerian hormone, early follicular FSH, oestradiol level, and ovarian antral follicle count
MTHFR mutation testing, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, and fasting homocysteine level

stem:
A 16-year-old girl reports 8 months of severe crampy lower abdominal pain with each period, missing school for 1-2 days each cycle. Her cycles are regular at 28 days with menarche at 13. She has tried regular paracetamol 1 g qid with minimal benefit. There is no pain outside of menses, no dyspareunia (she is not sexually active), no abnormal bleeding, no urinary or bowel symptoms and no fever.

Examination is normal. Pregnancy test negative. She is otherwise well, has no contraindication to NSAIDs and no medication allergies. Her mother is concerned and asks whether laparoscopy is required to exclude endometriosis before further treatment.

data_table.Examination: Normal abdominal and external genital exam
data_table.Investigations: None

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence regular naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 3-5 days starting 1-2 days before menses, with review at 3 months
Refer for diagnostic laparoscopy now to exclude endometriosis
Continue paracetamol 1 g four times daily and add codeine 30 mg qid as needed
Commence GnRH agonist (goserelin) to induce amenorrhoea
Reassure and recommend transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation as first-line

stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks gestation reports severe pain over the pubic symphysis that radiates to the inner thighs, worse with walking, climbing stairs, and turning in bed. Examination reveals tenderness over the symphysis pubis and positive FABER test.

data_table.Examination: Tender symphysis pubis, positive FABER, no neurological deficits
data_table.Investigations: USS: fetus well, cephalic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Refer to a women's health physiotherapist for pelvic girdle exercises, support belt fitting, and analgesia
Induction of labour at 37 weeks gestation to minimise further musculoskeletal damage and ongoing maternal discomfort
Strict bed rest for the remainder of the pregnancy with bedside toileting and meals provided
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection into the symphysis pubis joint under image guidance in interventional radiology
Prescribe regular oral opioid analgesia such as immediate-release oxycodone for severe ongoing pelvic pain

A 34-year-old G1P0 at 28 weeks with known fundal fibroid (8 cm at 20-week scan) presents with 36 hours of severe localised pain over the uterine fundus, mild nausea, and a low-grade temperature of 37.6. There is no vaginal bleeding, no leaking of fluid, no contractions and no urinary symptoms. Examination: tender over the fundal fibroid, no peritonism, normal bowel sounds, uterus otherwise soft.

CTG reactive, fetus active. Ultrasound: 9 cm fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture and central cystic change, no free fluid, normal placental position, normal Dopplers. White cell count mildly elevated 14, CRP 35, urinalysis nil. Beta-hCG appropriate for gestation.

data_table.Examination: Severe tenderness over the uterine fundus, no peritonism, bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: USS: 9 cm fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture, no free fluid, fetus well

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for analgesia (paracetamol +/- short-course oral or IV opioids), hydration, monitoring of fetal wellbeing and serial CTG, with avoidance of NSAIDs at this gestation
Commence indometacin 50 mg orally tds for 7 days
Proceed to elective myomectomy at this gestation
Diagnose placental abruption and proceed to immediate caesarean section
Commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed septic fibroid

stem: A 30-year-old G3P0 at 14+0 weeks attends a recurrent-pregnancy-loss clinic. She has had two previous second-trimester losses at 20 and 22 weeks, both with painless cervical dilation and rapid delivery of a liveborn infant who died shortly after delivery. No infection, no bleeding, no abruption identified at either loss. There are no other risk factors for preterm birth (no smoking, no LLETZ, no Mullerian anomaly, no DES exposure). Current TVUS cervical length 38 mm with closed internal os. She is otherwise well and asks specifically about the option of a prophylactic suture.

data_table.Examination: Normal pelvic exam, closed cervix
data_table.Investigations: TVS: cervical length 38 mm, closed os

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer a history-indicated cervical cerclage at 12-14 weeks now
Serial TVUS cervical length every 2 weeks, with ultrasound-indicated cerclage only if length falls below 25 mm before 24 weeks
Commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg daily from 16 weeks without cerclage
Bed rest at home from 16 weeks with avoidance of intercourse and exercise
Await spontaneous cervical change and place emergency rescue cerclage only if dilation occurs

stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 36+2 weeks presents with reduced fetal movements for 12 hours. Bedside ultrasound confirms intrauterine fetal demise. She is haemodynamically stable, no bleeding, no contractions. The senior registrar has confirmed and broken the news, with bereavement midwifery support called. She is keen to take the baby home and is asking whether she could await spontaneous labour rather than be induced now.

data_table.Examination: No fetal heart auscultated, uterus size consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: USS: no cardiac activity, fetal demise confirmed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate counselling and management plan?

options.text: Counsel that delay beyond about 48 hours after fetal death raises DIC risk; offer induction of labour as the preferred option while supporting her preferences
Proceed to category 1 caesarean section as soon as theatre is available despite the absence of a maternal indication for any operative delivery here
Discharge home and await spontaneous labour at term despite the rising coagulopathy risk over 48 hours after fetal death in utero today
Administer betamethasone now and induce labour in 48 hours despite the fetal demise removing any benefit of antenatal corticosteroid administration
Repeat ultrasound and CTG in 24 hours to reconfirm the diagnosis before discussing options with her and her partner about the next steps today

stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 at 38+0 weeks presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and minimal vaginal bleeding. Examination: tense, tender, woody-hard uterus, fundal height larger than expected. HR 128, BP 88/54, RR 24, SpO2 97%, peripherally cool. CTG: fetal bradycardia 70 bpm with absent variability. She has chronic hypertension on labetalol and was a smoker until early pregnancy. Bedside ultrasound: posterior placenta, no praevia, retroplacental haematoma visible. Bloods sent: Hb 78 g/L, platelets 92, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L.

data_table.Examination: Tense, tender, woody-hard uterus, minimal PV loss
data_table.Investigations: CTG: bradycardia 90 bpm, reduced variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol and proceed immediately to category 1 caesarean section
Commence tocolysis with nifedipine and observe with serial CTG
Insert two large-bore IV cannulae, give 2 L crystalloid bolus and reassess in 30 minutes
Attempt artificial rupture of membranes to expedite vaginal delivery
Transfer to tertiary centre for higher-level obstetric input

stem: A 28-year-old nullipara at 41 weeks is in labour with oxytocin augmentation. The CTG shows a baseline of 150 bpm with normal variability but repetitive late decelerations after each contraction. Contractions are 5 in 10 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 100, BP 110/70
data_table.Examination: Cervix 6 cm, contractions 5:10
data_table.Investigations: CTG: baseline 150, normal variability, late decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease the oxytocin infusion, reposition the mother to left lateral, and consider acute tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg SC
Continue oxytocin at the same rate and prepare for immediate vaginal delivery
Perform an immediate caesarean section without further assessment
Apply a fetal scalp electrode and take a fetal scalp blood sample
Administer a maternal oxygen mask at 8 L/min and increase the oxytocin to achieve better contractions

stem: A 28-year-old primipara, 6 weeks postpartum, reports persistent low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep when the baby sleeps, and feelings of guilt. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) score is 14. She is breastfeeding. She has no suicidal ideation.

data_table.Examination: Normal physical examination
data_table.Investigations: EPDS score 14, TSH normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for psychological therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and consider sertraline 50 mg daily, with risk-benefit discussion in breastfeeding
Reassurance that the 'baby blues' are normal and will resolve without any intervention or follow-up within a few weeks
Immediate admission to a mother-baby psychiatric unit due to perceived risk of harm to the baby in the home setting
Commence fluoxetine 20 mg daily and advise her to stop breastfeeding due to neonatal serotonergic risk concerns
Advise increased exercise and structured social engagement only, with reassessment in routine clinic in four weeks' time

stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 8+2 weeks gestation presents with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal cramps. Speculum examination shows the cervical os is open with a small amount of tissue at the os and minimal bleeding now. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, endometrial thickness 8 mm, no retained sac, no adnexal mass and no free fluid. Beta-hCG today is 1200 IU/L (was 8500 IU/L two days ago).

She is haemodynamically stable with Hb 122 g/L, blood group A Rh-positive and no allergies. She has had no prior surgery, takes no regular medications and is keen to be at home with her partner. She asks what you would recommend as a first option.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 85 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, Temp 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Open os, tissue in canal; minimal bleeding now
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: empty uterus, endometrial thickness 8 mm; no retained sac

lead_in: What would you first recommend as her management?

options.text: Outpatient expectant management with bleeding precautions and review with repeat beta-hCG in one to two weeks
Proceed directly to suction curettage in theatre today
Administer single-dose methotrexate as the pregnancy may be ectopic
Admit for IV oxytocin infusion to expedite expulsion of retained products
Discharge home with no follow-up; the falling beta-hCG indicates resolution

A 34-year-old G2P1 at 30+2 weeks gestation with known chronic hypertension presents with worsening epigastric pain, nausea, and headache. Her blood pressure is 160/105 mmHg despite oral labetalol 200 mg three times daily. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein. Laboratory results reveal: haemoglobin 105 g/L, platelets 55 ×10⁹/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 280 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 240 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 650 U/L, haptoglobin <0.3 g/L, serum creatinine 115 µmol/L, urate 0.52 mmol/L.

Peripheral blood film shows schistocytes. CTG shows a baseline of 150 bpm with reduced variability and occasional late decelerations. She has received the first dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg IM 6 hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 160/105, HR 98 bpm, RR 20, SpO₂ 96%, Temp 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Epigastric tenderness, hyperreflexia, 3 beats clonus, uterine fundus soft
data_table.Investigations: Plt 55, AST 280, ALT 240, LDH 650, haptoglobin <0.3, Cr 115; CTG: reduced variability, late decelerations; Betamethasone dose 1 given 6h ago
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg TDS PO, IV hydralazine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan regarding delivery?

options.text: Administer the second dose of betamethasone at 24 hours and aim for delivery at 48 hours from the first dose, provided maternal and fetal conditions remain stable
Proceed to delivery within 24 hours, preferably after administering the second dose of betamethasone at 12 hours from the first if maternal and fetal status permit, but do not delay beyond 24 hours
Give the second dose of betamethasone now (6 hours after first) and deliver immediately after the infusion, as expedited delivery is required regardless of steroid status
Commence magnesium sulfate infusion for fetal neuroprotection and expectantly manage for 48 hours to complete the steroid course, as long as platelets remain above 50 ×10⁹/L
Perform immediate caesarean delivery under general anaesthesia without waiting for the second betamethasone dose

stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks gestation with severe pre-eclampsia is being managed with intravenous magnesium sulfate (4 g loading dose, then 1 g/hour) and oral labetalol 200 mg BD. Four hours after commencing the magnesium infusion, she has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes. The seizure self-terminates. On examination, she is postictal with a GCS of 10. Blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, patellar reflexes present but reduced. The magnesium level 1 hour ago was 1.8 mmol/L (therapeutic range 1.7-3.5 mmol/L). Urine output has been 30 mL/hr.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 150/100, HR 90 bpm, RR 16, SpO₂ 95%, GCS 10, patellar reflexes reduced
data_table.Examination: Postictal, no focal neurological signs, fundus soft
data_table.Investigations: Mg²⁺ 1.8 mmol/L, urine output 30 mL/hr, CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer an additional 2 g intravenous bolus of magnesium sulfate over 5-10 minutes and continue the maintenance infusion at 1 g/hour
Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion immediately, administer intravenous calcium gluconate 1 g for magnesium toxicity, and commence intravenous phenytoin loading dose
Give intravenous midazolam 5 mg to terminate the seizure and arrange an urgent non-contrast CT head to exclude intracranial haemorrhage
Prepare for immediate caesarean delivery, as recurrent seizures despite magnesium indicate impending fetal demise
Administer intravenous labetalol 20 mg to urgently lower blood pressure to below 140/90 mmHg, as hypertension is the trigger for seizure recurrence

stem:
A 31-year-old primigravida at 30+6 weeks with early-onset fetal growth restriction (estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile) has been managed as an inpatient for the past week. Today's umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF), middle cerebral artery Doppler shows a low pulsatility index (brain-sparing), and ductus venosus Doppler shows a positive a-wave. Amniotic fluid index is 6.5 cm.

CTG demonstrates a baseline of 145 bpm, reduced variability (4 bpm), and occasional spontaneous accelerations, but no decelerations. She received a full course of betamethasone (two doses 24 hours apart) 8 days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 78 bpm
data_table.Examination: No proteinuria, fundal height 26 cm
data_table.Investigations: UA Doppler: AEDF; MCA: low PI; DV: positive a-wave; AFI 6.5 cm; CTG: reduced variability, no decelerations; Betamethasone completed 8 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate timing for delivery?

options.text: Administer a rescue course of betamethasone and deliver within 24 hours, given AEDF and reduced CTG variability
Deliver within 24-48 hours, giving a rescue course of betamethasone as the prior course was 8 days ago, and commence magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
Immediate caesarean delivery within 2 hours, as AEDF with reduced variability indicates acute fetal decompensation
Continue expectant management with daily CTG and repeat Dopplers in 72 hours, as a positive DV a-wave is reassuring
Deliver at 34 weeks once the rescue steroid course is effective, as AEDF alone is not an indication for preterm delivery

A 34-year-old G2P1 at 39+2 weeks gestation is in spontaneous labour with a prolonged second stage and meconium-stained liquor. The membranes ruptured 5 hours ago. She suddenly becomes agitated, complains of difficulty breathing, and then collapses with loss of consciousness. The cardiac monitor shows pulseless electrical activity. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is commenced immediately, and an emergency caesarean section is performed in the labour ward 6 minutes after the arrest.

A live infant is delivered with Apgars of 3, 5, and 7. Following delivery, the mother has return of spontaneous circulation but is noted to have diffuse oozing from the surgical wound, venipuncture sites, and the uterus is atonic with heavy bleeding. Laboratory investigations drawn 20 minutes after arrest show: haemoglobin 62 g/L, platelets 18 ×10⁹/L, fibrinogen 0.4 g/L, activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) >120 seconds, prothrombin time (PT) >60 seconds, D-dimer >100,000 ng/mL.

A massive transfusion protocol has been activated and the patient is receiving packed red blood cells and fresh frozen plasma. She has received 4 units of FFP and 6 units of RBCs, but continues to bleed profusely. Her repeat fibrinogen level is 0.6 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, BP 80/45 mmHg on vasopressors, SpO₂ 94% on ventilator
data_table.Examination: Diffuse oozing surgical wound and venipuncture sites, atonic uterus, ongoing massive haemorrhage
data_table.Investigations: Hb 62, Plt 18, fibrinogen 0.4 (repeat 0.6), APTT >120, PT >60, D-dimer >100,000
data_table.Medications: MTP activated, 6 units RBCs, 4 units FFP given

lead_in: What is the most critical blood product to administer next?

options.text: Cryoprecipitate 10 units (or fibrinogen concentrate 4 g) to raise the fibrinogen level above 2.0 g/L
Pooled platelets 1 adult dose to correct the severe thrombocytopenia
More fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg to replace all clotting factors simultaneously
Prothrombinex-HT 25 IU/kg to reverse the elevated INR and APTT
Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g bolus followed by infusion, as hyperfibrinolysis is the dominant pathology

stem:
A 36-year-old G5P3 with two previous lower-segment caesarean sections and one first-trimester curettage has a known anterior major placenta praevia. Antenatal ultrasound and MRI suggest placenta accreta without frank percreta. She has expressed a strong desire for future fertility. At 36+0 weeks, she experiences a self-limited bleed and an elective caesarean is performed at 37+0 weeks. The surgical team includes a gynaecological oncologist.

At delivery, a high transverse uterine incision is made above the placental edge. After delivery of the infant, the placenta does not separate spontaneously. Gentle controlled cord traction is unsuccessful, and the myometrium over the lower segment is noted to be thin and vascular with the placenta invading the uterine wall. Attempts at manual removal cause torrential haemorrhage of approximately 1.5 L in 3 minutes. The uterus is otherwise well-contracted, and the upper segment is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120 bpm, BP 95/60 mmHg, SpO₂ 98%
data_table.Examination: Uterine lower segment invasion, torrential haemorrhage on attempted removal, normal upper segment
data_table.Investigations: Antenatal imaging: accreta without percreta; estimated blood loss 1.5 L in 3 min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical approach?

options.text: Leave the placenta in situ, close the uterus, and consider postoperative methotrexate or uterine artery embolisation, with delayed hysterectomy if needed
Proceed immediately to total abdominal hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ, as this is the safest management for accreta
Perform a uterine compression suture (B-Lynch) and uterine artery ligation to control bleeding, then close
Attempt to remove the placenta piecemeal with sharp dissection and oversew the bleeding sites
Perform a caesarean hysterectomy but preserve the ovaries and refer for surrogacy

stem: A 29-year-old primigravida with early-onset fetal growth restriction (estimated fetal weight <3rd centile) is being monitored as an inpatient at 29+3 weeks. Serial ultrasound today shows new reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) in the umbilical artery. Previous Dopplers 3 days ago showed absent end-diastolic flow. Ductus venosus Doppler shows a positive a-wave. Amniotic fluid index is 5.2 cm (oligohydramnios). CTG shows a baseline of 140 bpm, reduced variability (3-5 bpm), and no accelerations, but no decelerations. She received a full course of betamethasone 10 days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 135/85, HR 76 bpm
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 25 cm, soft uterus
data_table.Investigations: UA: REDF; DV: positive a-wave; AFI 5.2 cm; CTG: reduced variability, no accelerations, no decelerations; Steroids completed 10 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate timing of delivery?

options.text: Deliver within 24 hours, administering a rescue course of betamethasone as the prior course was over 7 days ago, and commence magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
Deliver within 24 hours, as REDF with oligohydramnios and reduced CTG variability indicates acute fetal decompensation requiring delivery after a single dose of betamethasone if feasible
Immediate caesarean delivery within 2 hours, as REDF with reduced variability is a preterminal fetal heart rate pattern that cannot await even a partial steroid course
Administer a rescue course of betamethasone over 48 hours and deliver at 48 hours if the CTG remains unchanged
Continue expectant management with daily Dopplers and CTG three times daily, as a positive DV a-wave suggests the fetus is still compensating
