A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a 3-month history of abdominal bloating and early satiety. She has lost 5 kg unintentionally over the past 3 months. Her mother died of ovarian cancer at age 62. On examination, there is a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals a right adnexal mass measuring 7 cm with irregular solid components, septations, and moderate ascites.

Both ovaries are visualised; the left is atrophic. The serum CA-125 level is 320 U/mL. The ultrasound gives a morphology score (U) of 3 (multilocular cyst with solid areas, ascites, and bilateral involvement). She is postmenopausal (M score = 3).

data_table.Examination: RUQ mass, shifting dullness
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: 7 cm complex mass, solid components, septations, ascites; CA-125 320 U/mL; RMI = U x M x CA-125 = 3 x 3 x 320 = 2880

lead_in: What is the calculated RMI and the most appropriate next step?

options.text: RMI = 2880; refer to a gynaecological oncologist for consideration of surgical staging
RMI = 960; repeat CA-125 in 3 months and reassess
RMI = 2880; schedule a simple oophorectomy by a general gynaecologist
RMI = 1440; refer for a CT scan, and if negative, discharge to GP
RMI = 2880; this is a low risk; manage conservatively with repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks

stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida with diet-controlled GDM and an EFW of 4.5 kg has just had the fetal head deliver with retraction and turtle-neck sign. McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure (30 seconds), attempted delivery of the posterior arm (twice), and internal rotation manoeuvres (Rubin II and Woods' screw) have all failed. Time from delivery of the head: 4 minutes. CTG showed normal trace before delivery.

The woman has an epidural in situ. The midwife asks the senior registrar if firm fundal pressure should now be tried while preparing for the next manoeuvre.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 115 bpm, BP 140/90 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Turtle-neck sign, failed McRoberts, suprapubic pressure, posterior arm delivery, internal rotations; fetal bradycardia 50 bpm
data_table.Investigations: GDM, macrosomia

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Roll the woman onto hands and knees (Gaskin all-fours manoeuvre) and reattempt delivery of the posterior arm
Apply firm fundal pressure to dislodge the impacted shoulder
Perform symphysiotomy to enlarge the pelvic outlet
Perform Zavanelli cephalic replacement and proceed to caesarean section
Repeat McRoberts and suprapubic pressure for another 60 seconds

stem: A 29-year-old primigravida at 36+3 weeks gestation collapses in the emergency department waiting room. She was brought in by her partner after complaining of sudden severe chest pain and dyspnoea at home. On arrival, she is unresponsive and pulseless. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is started immediately with manual left uterine displacement. The cardiac monitor shows ventricular fibrillation. Defibrillation is attempted with 200 J biphasic, but there is no return of spontaneous circulation after two shocks. CPR continues for 4 minutes. The fetal heart rate was last documented as 130 bpm 15 minutes earlier.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal: unresponsive, pulseless, VF on monitor, CPR in progress; Fetal: last heart rate 130 bpm 15 min ago
data_table.Examination: No pulse, cardiac arrest, uterine fundus at term
data_table.Investigations: Rhythm: VF, unsuccessful defibrillation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding delivery of the fetus?

options.text: Perform emergency perimortem caesarean section immediately at the bedside, within 4-5 minutes of the cardiac arrest, to improve maternal resuscitation and fetal survival
Transfer the patient immediately to the operating theatre for a caesarean section, continuing CPR during transport, as a sterile environment is essential
Administer intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the refractory ventricular fibrillation and defer delivery until maternal circulation is restored
Continue CPR with left uterine displacement for a further 10 minutes before considering delivery, as the fetal heart rate was normal 15 minutes ago
Administer a tocolytic agent (terbutaline 250 mcg SC) to relax the uterus and improve CPR effectiveness

stem: A 31-year-old woman with primary obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome (three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages; persistent lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG and anti-beta2GPI IgG on testing 12 weeks apart, no history of thromboembolic event) is now 6 weeks pregnant. She has been on warfarin 5 mg daily for the past 9 months as 'prevention' prescribed by another clinician. She has had no thrombosis. She has no other medical conditions and no allergies.

data_table.Examination: Normal
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant positive, aCL IgG >40, anti-β2 GPI IgG >40; viable IUP 6 weeks

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate medication regimen for this pregnancy?

options.text: Continue warfarin 5 mg daily throughout pregnancy as she is already established on it
Stop warfarin immediately and commence low-dose aspirin 100 mg daily plus prophylactic-dose enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily, continuing through pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum
Continue warfarin until 12 weeks then switch to LMWH
Continue warfarin until 6 weeks then aspirin alone for the rest of the pregnancy
Stop warfarin and commence intravenous immunoglobulin monthly as primary therapy

stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 32+1 weeks presents in preterm labour with regular painful contractions and cervical dilatation of 4 cm. Her GBS status is unknown (swab not yet performed at 36 weeks). She has no known allergies. Membranes are intact.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm, intact membranes, preterm labour
data_table.Investigations: GBS status unknown, CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic plan?

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g loading dose, then 600 mg 4-hourly until delivery
No antibiotics are required, as membranes are intact and the risk of GBS transmission is low
Take a low vaginal swab for GBS culture and PCR, and commence antibiotics only if the swab returns positive
Commence intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading then 1 g 8-hourly as it covers both GBS and Gram-negative organisms
Give intramuscular benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units as a single dose and continue monitoring

stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks with PROM 28 hours ago develops T 39.2, HR 124, RR 28, BP 88/52 (MAP 64), confused with GCS 14. Tender uterus, purulent vaginal discharge, fetal HR 175 bpm with reduced variability. Lactate 4.6, WCC 19. IV access obtained, bloods sent, blood cultures taken. The on-call team has called for theatre.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.2°C, HR 120, RR 28, BP 90/55, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Confused, tender uterus, purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.5, procalcitonin 22, blood cultures pending

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole) and a 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid bolus within the next hour, while preparing for emergency delivery
Transfer to ICU for central venous access before commencing antibiotics
Proceed immediately to caesarean section as the primary intervention before fluids or antibiotics
Administer IV paracetamol 1 g and reassess vital signs in 30 minutes before further intervention
Order CT abdomen and pelvis to identify the source before starting antibiotics

stem: A 39-year-old G4P3 with three prior caesarean sections and a known anterior major placenta praevia (with suspected accreta on MRI) presents at 33+4 weeks with massive vaginal bleeding. She is taken directly to theatre for an emergency caesarean. The bladder is adherent to the lower segment, and the placental bed is invading the myometrium. After delivery of the infant, torrential haemorrhage ensues from the placental bed despite leaving the placenta in situ. The estimated blood loss reaches 3 L within 10 minutes, and the patient becomes hypotensive.

data_table.Examination: Torrential haemorrhage from lower segment, bladder adherent
data_table.Investigations: Antenatal MRI: accreta; intraoperative: massive bleeding, placenta left in situ

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Total abdominal hysterectomy with placenta left in situ, with internal iliac artery ligation or pelvic packing if bleeding persists
Attempt piecemeal manual removal of the adherent placenta in theatre to gain control of the bleeding
Close the uterus with placenta in situ and transfer for emergency uterine artery embolisation in interventional radiology
Apply a B-Lynch compression suture and intrauterine balloon tamponade with gauze packing if needed
Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and recombinant factor VIIa as definitive medical management here

stem: A 38-year-old G4P3 with two prior caesarean sections and a known anterior major placenta praevia with suspected percreta on MRI delivers a live infant by classical caesarean section at 35 weeks. The placenta is left in situ as it invades the bladder serosa. The estimated blood loss is 1.2 L, controlled with compression and rapid blood product transfusion. She remains haemodynamically stable. She expresses a strong wish to preserve her uterus.

data_table.Examination: Uterus intact, placenta in situ, minimal ongoing bleeding
data_table.Investigations: MRI: percreta; intraoperative: placenta invading bladder

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adjuvant therapy?

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m² as a single dose, with uterine artery embolisation arranged within 24 hours
Proceed urgently to immediate emergency hysterectomy under general anaesthesia in the operating theatre now
Administer oral mifepristone 200 mg daily for 7 days to induce placental necrosis and resorption
Observe without any adjuvant therapy and monitor with serial transvaginal ultrasound and beta-hCG measurements
Commence a continuous intravenous oxytocin infusion at standard postpartum dose for 24 hours total

stem: A 30-year-old G3P0 at 21+5 weeks presents with pelvic pressure and a bulging sensation. Speculum: cervix dilated 3 cm with exposed amniotic membranes visible at the os. No fever, no uterine tenderness; WCC 10.2, CRP 8, vaginal swab GBS negative, fetal fibronectin not applicable, no pooling of liquor. Ultrasound: viable fetus, cervical length 0 mm with funnelling, normal AFI, no fetal anomalies. Neonatology has counselled the woman and she wants every appropriate intervention to prolong the pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm, bulging membranes, no infection signs
data_table.Investigations: Cervical length 0 mm, funneling, fetal fibronectin negative, no infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combination of management steps?

options.text: Offer emergency McDonald cerclage, short-course indometacin tocolysis (48 hours) given gestation under 32 weeks, antibiotic prophylaxis, and antenatal corticosteroids when delivery becomes likely
Cerclage is contraindicated with bulging membranes; give only bed rest and corticosteroids
Place cerclage and give corticosteroids but avoid indometacin entirely due to ductal closure risk
Induce labour now as 21+5 is non-viable and ongoing pregnancy is futile
Place an abdominal cervicoisthmic cerclage today and commence IV magnesium sulfate

stem: A 37-year-old G5P4 with four prior lower-segment caesarean sections has anterior major placenta praevia. Ultrasound and MRI at 30 weeks confirm placenta accreta (loss of retroplacental clear zone, lacunae, hypervascularity at uterovesical interface), without percreta or bladder invasion. Fetal growth and Dopplers are normal. She has completed a course of betamethasone. She has been counselled about haemorrhage and hysterectomy and accepts a planned caesarean hysterectomy. The MDT is finalising timing and team composition.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 120/80, HR 78, fundal height 30 cm
data_table.Examination: Non-tender uterus
data_table.Investigations: USS + MRI: placenta accreta, no percreta, no bladder involvement; EFW 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34-35+6 weeks at a tertiary centre by a multidisciplinary team (obstetrician, gynae-oncology, interventional radiology, anaesthesia, haematology, neonatology), with cell salvage and MTP on standby and a vertical/midline abdominal incision
Elective caesarean at 39 weeks under a single general obstetrician at her local hospital
Plan vaginal delivery with active third-stage management and theatre on standby
Plan delivery at 32 weeks to maximise prevention of any spontaneous labour
Admit at 34 weeks for inpatient monitoring and deliver only when spontaneous labour or distress occurs

stem: A 30-year-old woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 21+2 weeks gestation is referred for a routine ultrasound. Ultrasound shows twin A with polyhydramnios (deepest vertical pocket 10 cm) and a distended bladder. Twin B has oligohydramnios (deepest vertical pocket 1.5 cm), the bladder is not visualised, and there is absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery. Both fetuses are structurally normal, and the placenta is anterior.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal BP 115/70, HR 82
data_table.Examination: Cervix 28 mm, closed
data_table.Investigations: USS: twin A DVP 10 cm, bladder full; twin B DVP 1.5 cm, bladder not seen, UA AEDF

lead_in: What is the most appropriate Quintero stage and recommended management?

options.text: Quintero stage III; refer urgently for fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses at a tertiary fetal medicine centre
Quintero stage I; serial amnioreduction to reduce the polyhydramnios and close ultrasound surveillance every 2 weeks
Quintero stage II; laser photocoagulation is recommended but may be deferred for 1 week to allow steroid administration for fetal lung maturity
Quintero stage IV; delivery of both fetuses at 22 weeks by classical caesarean section to prevent fetal death
Quintero stage I; observe without intervention as stage I TTTS has a high rate of spontaneous resolution

stem:
A 22-year-old G1P0 at 8 weeks gestation presents to the antenatal clinic for her first visit. She has a history of Eisenmenger syndrome secondary to a large unrepaired ventricular septal defect, with a resting oxygen saturation of 88% on room air and a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 95 mmHg on her most recent echocardiogram 6 months ago. She is NYHA functional class II, managing her daily activities but becoming dyspnoeic on moderate exertion.

She is on sildenafil 20 mg three times daily and bosentan 125 mg twice daily. She is unaware she was pregnant and has not received preconception counselling. On examination, she has central cyanosis, clubbing, and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. She is strongly against termination and wishes to continue the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 100/70, HR 90, SpO₂ 88% RA, RR 20
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, clubbing, loud P₂, uterus 8-week size
data_table.Investigations: PASP 95 mmHg on echo 6 months ago; VSD unrepaired
data_table.Medications: Sildenafil 20 mg TDS, bosentan 125 mg BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial counselling regarding maternal risk?

options.text: The maternal mortality risk is approximately 30-50%, and pregnancy is strongly contraindicated; compassionate counselling about termination should be offered, but if she continues, a multidisciplinary team in a tertiary pulmonary hypertension centre must manage her
With careful management in a shared-care model between the GP and a general obstetrician, the risk of maternal death is only 1-2%, and she can be reassured
She should be admitted immediately for therapeutic termination of pregnancy under general anaesthesia, as the risk of continuing pregnancy is too high to allow her to decline
Continue bosentan throughout pregnancy as the benefits of pulmonary vasodilation outweigh the teratogenic risks
Refer for cardiac surgery to close the VSD during the second trimester to improve haemodynamics and reduce mortality

stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 at 17 weeks gestation undergoes a routine cervical screening test, which reveals high-risk human papillomavirus type 16 and a reflex liquid-based cytology showing high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. Colposcopy with directed biopsy shows a 2.5 cm exophytic lesion confined to the cervix. Histopathology confirms squamous cell carcinoma with 4 mm depth of invasion and 6 mm horizontal spread, consistent with FIGO stage IB1. Pelvic MRI shows no parametrial invasion, no lymphadenopathy, and a normal upper genital tract.

data_table.Examination: 2.5 cm exophytic cervical lesion, no parametrial involvement on MRI
data_table.Investigations: Histology: SCC, depth 4 mm, horizontal 6 mm, FIGO IB1; MRI: no parametrial spread, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Perform a laparoscopic pelvic lymphadenectomy to stage the nodes; if negative, continue the pregnancy to term and deliver by caesarean section with radical hysterectomy at the same time
Perform an immediate radical hysterectomy with the fetus in situ, as any delay in treatment compromises maternal survival
Administer neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy during the second and third trimesters and delay surgery until after delivery
Perform a large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) to remove the tumour completely, and continue the pregnancy with close colposcopic surveillance
Deliver the fetus by hysterotomy at 18 weeks to allow immediate radical hysterectomy, as any delay beyond 20 weeks is unsafe

subtopic_detail: PPROM at 32 weeks - corticosteroid timing and antibiotics
stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 presents at 32+2 weeks gestation with a history of a sudden gush of clear fluid 3 hours ago. She denies contractions, vaginal bleeding, or fever. Her previous pregnancy was an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery. A sterile speculum examination reveals pooling of clear fluid in the posterior vaginal fornix. An AmniSure test is positive. Her GBS status from routine screening is not yet available.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, T 36.9 C, RR 16
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, non-tender, cephalic presentation, no contractions palpable, cervix not digitally examined
data_table.Investigations: CTG: baseline 140 bpm, moderate variability, accelerations present, no decelerations. WCC 10.2 x10^9/L, CRP 4 mg/L, urine MCS sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM and commence erythromycin for 10 days
Plan immediate delivery by caesarean section given preterm rupture status
Commence IV ampicillin and plan induction of labour within 24 hours
Administer dexamethasone and plan elective delivery at 34 weeks gestation
Observe without corticosteroids as fetal lungs are likely mature enough

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis progressing to abscess - management
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents 4 weeks postpartum with a 5-day history of worsening pain and swelling in her right breast. She was commenced on oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily by her GP 3 days ago for mastitis but has not improved. She is continuing to breastfeed from both breasts. She has no drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 bpm, BP 115/72 mmHg, T 38.8 C, RR 18
data_table.Examination: Right breast erythematous and swollen in upper outer quadrant, fluctuant 4 cm mass palpable, tender, overlying skin tense but not necrotic, left breast normal, no axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Breast ultrasound: 3.5 cm well-defined hypoechoic collection with internal debris in the upper outer quadrant consistent with an abscess, no other collections identified. WCC 15.8 x10^9/L, CRP 89 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch to IV antibiotics and review clinical response at 48 hours
Perform ultrasound-guided needle aspiration and continue oral antibiotics
Arrange formal surgical incision and drainage under general anaesthesia
Cease breastfeeding from both breasts and commence cabergoline
Increase flucloxacillin dose to 1 g four times daily and add metronidazole

subtopic_detail: Pelvic organ prolapse - management selection based on stage and symptoms
stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a 12-month history of worsening vaginal heaviness and a sensation of something protruding from the vagina. She reports urinary frequency, difficulty emptying her bladder, and needing to digitally reduce the prolapse to void. She is not sexually active and has no stress incontinence. She completed supervised pelvic floor muscle training for 6 months with a physiotherapist with minimal improvement. Her BMI is 28 kg/m2.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg
data_table.Examination: POP-Q examination: stage II anterior vaginal wall prolapse extending to the hymen on Valsalva, mild posterior wall laxity, no uterine descent, atrophic vaginal mucosa, post-void residual volume 120 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: no haematuria, no infection. Renal function: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Proceed to anterior colporrhaphy as definitive surgical correction
Prescribe duloxetine 40 mg daily for her urinary voiding symptoms
Trial vaginal pessary fitting combined with topical vaginal oestrogen
Recommend structured weight loss program and repeat pelvic floor training
Commence systemic hormone replacement therapy for prolapse support

stem: A 26-year-old G1P1 is reviewed on day 3 following an emergency caesarean section for failure to progress in the first stage of labour. She had prolonged rupture of membranes for 22 hours prior to delivery and multiple vaginal examinations during labour. She has developed worsening lower abdominal pain, fever, and malodorous vaginal discharge over the past 12 hours. She is breastfeeding and has no drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 105 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg, T 38.6 C, RR 20
data_table.Examination: Abdomen tender in the suprapubic region, uterine fundus palpable at the umbilicus and markedly tender on bimanual examination, offensive lochia, caesarean wound clean with no erythema or discharge
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 15.4 x10^9/L, CRP 145 mg/L, Hb 105 g/L, blood cultures taken, high vaginal swab sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily with outpatient review
IV cefazolin 2 g 8-hourly as single-agent intravenous therapy
IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 8-hourly as broad-spectrum cover
IV ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole as triple combination
Oral metronidazole 400 mg 8-hourly with oral erythromycin 500 mg daily

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to a fertility clinic with an 18-month history of inability to conceive. She has a diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome based on oligo-ovulation with cycles every 60-90 days, clinical hyperandrogenism with hirsutism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. She has completed 3 months of structured lifestyle modification with dietary counselling and exercise, achieving 5% weight loss but remaining anovulatory. Her partner has a normal semen analysis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 76 bpm
data_table.Examination: BMI 32 kg/m2, Ferriman-Gallwey score 12, no acanthosis nigricans, no thyromegaly, normal pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Day 2 FSH 5.2 IU/L, LH 14.8 IU/L, oestradiol 180 pmol/L, testosterone 2.8 nmol/L, SHBG 22 nmol/L, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, prolactin 280 mIU/L, fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L, HbA1c 38 mmol/mol, AMH 48 pmol/L. Hysterosalpingogram: bilateral tubal patency confirmed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in fertility management?

options.text: Commence clomifene citrate 50 mg daily for days 2 to 6 of cycle
Proceed directly to in vitro fertilisation given the prolonged duration
Add metformin 500 mg three times daily as sole ovulation induction agent
Commence low-dose gonadotrophin injections with ultrasound monitoring
Commence letrozole 2.5 mg daily for days 2 to 6 as ovulation induction

subtopic_detail: Pre-eclampsia with severe features: delivery timing
stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset of severe headache and visual disturbance. She has no prior history of hypertension. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated until now. She has epigastric pain on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 175/112 mmHg (confirmed on two readings 15 minutes apart), HR 92 bpm, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 180 mg/mmol (elevated), platelet count 92 x10^9/L, ALT 185 U/L, AST 210 U/L, creatinine 95 micromol/L, LDH 620 U/L, Hb 118 g/L, blood film: fragmented red cells
data_table.Fetal assessment: CTG: reassuring baseline 140 bpm, normal variability, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence oral labetalol and expectant management until 37 weeks
Stabilise with IV labetalol and magnesium sulfate then defer delivery
IV labetalol, magnesium sulfate, betamethasone, and deliver within 48 hours
Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia without delay
Commence plasma exchange for suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

stem: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, presents at 30 weeks gestation with a gush of clear fluid per vagina 3 hours ago. Her speculum examination confirms pooling of clear amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix. She is not contracting. Group B Streptococcus status is unknown. Her previous pregnancy was an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 80 bpm, temperature 36.8 C, RR 16/min
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 120 g/L, WCC 10.2 x10^9/L, CRP 5 mg/L. Vaginal swab taken for GBS. CTG: reassuring
data_table.Fetal assessment: Ultrasound: cephalic presentation, AFI 5 cm (reduced), EFW 1450 g on 30th percentile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Immediate induction of labour with IV oxytocin to prevent infection
Expectant management with regular observation and no medications
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection and immediate caesarean section
Betamethasone IM, prophylactic erythromycin, and expectant management
Amnioinfusion to restore amniotic fluid volume and prevent infection

stem: A 34-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2 (two previous caesarean sections), is found to have an anterior placenta praevia completely covering the internal cervical os on her 20-week morphology ultrasound. She has had no vaginal bleeding. She is now 32 weeks gestation and a repeat ultrasound confirms the placenta still completely covers the os with suspected placenta accreta spectrum on greyscale and colour Doppler imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 115/70 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, Hb 116 g/L
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound 32 weeks: anterior placenta praevia major (completely covering os), loss of clear zone between placenta and myometrium, bridging vessels on Doppler, bladder wall irregularity. Fetal growth on 40th percentile, normal liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Plan elective caesarean at 36 to 37 weeks with a multidisciplinary team
Arrange MRI pelvis for definitive PAS diagnosis and defer delivery plan
Admit now for inpatient observation until delivery at 39 weeks
Attempt vaginal delivery under close senior obstetric supervision
Prophylactic uterine artery embolisation at 34 weeks to reduce bleeding

stem: A 30-year-old woman attends her GP for a routine cervical screening test. She has no symptoms and no history of abnormal cervical screening. She is not pregnant. Her HPV vaccination status is 3 doses of Gardasil at age 13. Her result returns as HPV 16 detected with possible high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (pHSIL) on liquid-based cytology.

data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test: HPV 16 positive, LBC: possible high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (pHSIL)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test in 12 months to confirm persistence
Refer to a gynaecologist for large loop excision of the transformation zone
Prescribe topical imiquimod cream for HPV clearance before reassessment
Reassure the patient as HPV vaccination provides adequate protection
Refer for colposcopy with directed biopsy within 8 weeks

stem: A 28-year-old nulliparous woman presents with a 3-year history of progressive dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and non-menstrual pelvic pain. She has been using regular NSAIDs with diminishing effect. She does not wish to conceive in the next 2 to 3 years. A recent laparoscopy confirmed endometriosis (rASRM stage II) with peritoneal implants and a 3 cm left ovarian endometrioma. The endometrioma was drained and the peritoneal deposits were ablated.

data_table.Investigations: Laparoscopy 6 weeks ago: rASRM stage II, peritoneal implants ablated, left ovarian endometrioma drained. CA-125 45 U/mL (mildly elevated). Transvaginal ultrasound post-op: 1.5 cm residual left ovarian endometrioma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long-term medical management?

options.text: Commence GnRH agonist (leuprorelin) depot for 12 months
Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system for symptom control
Commence continuous combined oral contraceptive pill without breaks
Prescribe danazol 200 mg twice daily for symptom suppression
Continue NSAIDs alone and plan repeat laparoscopy in 12 months

stem: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, presents 3 weeks postpartum with progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and bilateral ankle swelling over the past 10 days. Her pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. She has no prior cardiac history. She had a normal postpartum echocardiogram as part of a research study at delivery. Her initial presentation was attributed to normal postpartum fluid redistribution by her GP 1 week ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 100/68 mmHg, HR 110 bpm, RR 28/min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 37.0 C
data_table.Examination: JVP elevated to 6 cm above sternal angle, bibasal crackles to mid-zones, displaced apex beat (6th intercostal space, anterior axillary line), bilateral pitting ankle oedema, S3 gallop on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: BNP 1850 pg/mL (markedly elevated), ECG: sinus tachycardia, non-specific ST-T changes, low voltage. CXR: cardiomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions, upper lobe pulmonary venous diversion

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate urgent investigation?

options.text: Peripartum cardiomyopathy - urgent transthoracic echocardiography
Post-partum pulmonary embolism - urgent CT pulmonary angiography
Postpartum thyroiditis with cardiac complication - thyroid function tests
Normal postpartum fluid redistribution - reassurance and follow-up
Post-partum pre-eclampsia - IV magnesium sulfate and labetalol

stem: A 30-year-old primigravida has just delivered a 4.2 kg baby via normal vaginal delivery after a prolonged second stage. The midwife attempted controlled cord traction during the third stage. Immediately following this the woman develops sudden severe lower abdominal pain, profound hypotension, and heavy vaginal bleeding. The midwife reports she can no longer palpate the uterine fundus abdominally. On vaginal examination, a smooth round mass is palpable in the vagina with the placenta still attached.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 70/40 mmHg, HR 130 bpm, SpO2 95% on room air, pallor
data_table.Examination: No uterine fundus palpable abdominally, smooth round mass visible at introitus with placenta attached, estimated blood loss 1200 mL and continuing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer IV ergometrine 250 mcg to contract the uterus and stop bleeding
Manually remove the placenta then attempt uterine replacement with tocolysis
Call for general anaesthesia and take to theatre for abdominal approach
Commence aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and delay replacement
Immediate manual replacement via the Johnson manoeuvre with IV fluids

subtopic_detail: Obstetric cholestasis - bile acid threshold and delivery timing
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 35 weeks gestation presents with a 2-week history of intense generalised pruritus that is worse at night, concentrated on the palms and soles. She has no rash apart from excoriations. Her pregnancy has been otherwise uncomplicated. She has no history of liver disease. Her sister had a similar presentation in her third trimester.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 82, Temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Serum bile acids: 55 micromol/L (normal < 10 micromol/L). ALT 85 U/L (mildly elevated). Bilirubin 18 micromol/L (normal). Hepatitis B and C serology: negative. Liver ultrasound: normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid and delivery at 37 weeks gestation
Topical emollients and antihistamines until spontaneous labour
Colestyramine and weekly bile acid monitoring until term
Ursodeoxycholic acid and delivery at 36 weeks gestation
Dexamethasone for fetal lung maturity and delivery at 34 weeks

stem: A 24-year-old woman, G2P1 (previous mid-trimester loss at 20 weeks), presents at 18 weeks gestation with a sensation of vaginal pressure. She has no contractions, no bleeding, and no history of ruptured membranes. A speculum examination shows no pooling of liquor and the cervix appears visually shortened. She is afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 78, Temp 36.5 C
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: cervical length 12 mm with funnelling to the external os. Membranes visible at the external os but not bulging beyond it. No uterine contractions on tocography. Fetal heart rate 150 bpm with normal anatomy scan. CRP 4 mg/L (normal). White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Vaginal progesterone pessary alone with serial cervical lengths
Bed rest and tocolysis with repeat assessment in 1 week
Oral antibiotics and expectant management until viability
Induction of labour as pregnancy is not viable at 18 weeks
Emergency rescue cerclage after excluding ruptured membranes

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 33 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset severe constant abdominal pain. She has no vaginal bleeding. She has a history of chronic hypertension on labetalol. Her uterus is tense and tender on palpation, described as 'woody hard'. The fetal heart rate tracing shows recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 150/95 mmHg, HR 115, RR 22, SpO2 98%, Temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tense, tender, and firm ('woody'). Fundal height 35 cm (above dates). No visible vaginal bleeding on speculum. Cervix closed.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 95 g/L (was 118 g/L at booking), platelets 110 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 1.8 g/L (low), INR 1.3, APTT 38 s. Kleihauer test: positive.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Emergency caesarean section with concurrent resuscitation
Tocolysis with nifedipine and antenatal corticosteroids
Amniotomy and oxytocin augmentation for vaginal delivery
Abdominal ultrasound to confirm retroplacental clot first
IV magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection and observe for 4 hours

stem: You are the registrar attending a vaginal delivery. A 32-year-old woman, G2P1, has had a normal first stage and is now in the second stage. The fetal head delivers but immediately retracts against the perineum (turtle sign). Gentle downward traction on the head does not deliver the anterior shoulder. An assistant has already called for help.

data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered, chin tight against perineum (turtle sign). Anterior shoulder impacted behind the symphysis pubis. Mother in lithotomy position.

lead_in: After calling for help and performing an episiotomy, what is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Fundal pressure to push the anterior shoulder past the pubis
McRoberts position with directed suprapubic pressure applied
Delivery of the posterior arm by sweeping across the chest
Rubin II rotational manoeuvre to disimpact the anterior shoulder
Move to all-fours position immediately (Gaskin manoeuvre)

subtopic_detail: Breech at term - ECV eligibility and management
stem: A 37-year-old woman, G3P2, is found to have a frank breech presentation at her 36-week antenatal visit. Her two previous deliveries were uncomplicated vaginal births at term. She has a normal amniotic fluid index, anterior placenta in the upper segment, and no uterine anomalies on prior ultrasound. She would prefer a vaginal birth if possible.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 115/70 mmHg, HR 76
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: frank breech, estimated fetal weight 2800 g, AFI 14 cm, anterior upper segment placenta, no fetal anomalies. CTG: reactive.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Elective caesarean section at 39 weeks for breech presentation
Planned vaginal breech delivery at an experienced unit
External cephalic version at 37 weeks with tocolysis
Moxibustion and postural exercises until 38 weeks then review
Observation until 39 weeks as spontaneous version may occur

subtopic_detail: Third and fourth degree perineal tear - recognition and repair
stem: You are the registrar assessing a primiparous woman who has just had a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 4.1 kg baby after a prolonged second stage. An episiotomy was not performed. On perineal examination under good lighting, you identify a tear involving the vaginal mucosa, perineal skin, perineal muscles, and you can see the fibres of the external anal sphincter. The internal anal sphincter appears intact on examination, and the anal mucosa is undamaged.

data_table.Examination: Perineal tear involving vaginal mucosa, perineal skin, perineal body muscles, and the external anal sphincter capsule with visible torn fibres. Internal anal sphincter visually intact. Anal mucosa intact. No active arterial bleeding.

lead_in: What is the correct classification and most appropriate management?

options.text: Second degree tear - repair in the delivery room by midwife
3a tear - repair with continuous suture technique in the room
3b tear - formal repair by a doctor in theatre with PDS sutures
3a or 3b tear - sphincter repair in theatre with antibiotics
Fourth degree tear - repair under general anaesthesia urgently

subtopic_detail: Vulvar lichen sclerosus - management and malignancy surveillance
stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a 2-year history of vulvar pruritus and soreness. She has tried over-the-counter antifungal cream without improvement. On examination there are white atrophic plaques involving the labia minora, clitoral hood, and perianal skin in a 'figure-of-eight' distribution. There is partial fusion of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris. No areas of hyperkeratosis or ulceration are seen.

data_table.Examination: White porcelain-like atrophic plaques in figure-of-eight distribution involving labia minora, clitoral hood, and perianal skin. Partial labial fusion. Clitoral burying. No hyperkeratotic, erosive, or ulcerated areas. No lymphadenopathy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical oestrogen cream applied nightly for 12 weeks
Topical antifungal and hydrocortisone combination cream
Vulvar biopsy and surgical excision of all affected skin
Superpotent topical corticosteroid and long-term follow-up
Potent topical corticosteroid with annual vulvar review

subtopic_detail: Menopause - MHT eligibility with cardiovascular considerations
stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with debilitating vasomotor symptoms (8-10 hot flushes daily, severe night sweats disrupting sleep) for the past 18 months since her last menstrual period. She has tried lifestyle modifications and phytoestrogens without benefit. Her BMI is 26 kg/m2. She has no personal history of breast cancer or thromboembolic disease. She is a non-smoker with no hypertension or diabetes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg, HR 72
data_table.Investigations: Mammogram (screening): BI-RADS 1 (normal). Cervical screening: negative HPV at age 50. Fasting lipids: total cholesterol 5.4 mmol/L, LDL 3.2 mmol/L, HDL 1.5 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her vasomotor symptoms?

options.text: Combined continuous MHT with oral oestradiol and progesterone
Oral oestradiol alone without progesterone at low dose
Gabapentin 300 mg nightly as a non-hormonal first-line agent
Tibolone daily as it avoids the need for added progesterone
Venlafaxine extended-release as primary vasomotor treatment

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset severe left iliac fossa pain and vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test is positive. She has a history of a previous right salpingectomy for ectopic pregnancy. On examination she is pale with generalised abdominal tenderness and guarding, particularly in the left lower quadrant.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 85/55 mmHg, HR 128, RR 22, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.4 C
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic. Abdomen: generalised tenderness with guarding, worst in the left iliac fossa. Cervical excitation tenderness on bimanual. Left adnexal mass palpable.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L, beta-hCG 8500 IU/L. FAST ultrasound: free fluid in the Pouch of Douglas and Morrison's pouch.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: IM methotrexate with serial beta-hCG monitoring
Emergency laparotomy with left salpingectomy
Laparoscopic left salpingotomy to preserve fertility
Fluid resuscitation and repeat beta-hCG in 48 hours
Interventional radiology uterine artery embolisation

subtopic_detail: Gestational trophoblastic disease - post-molar hCG surveillance
stem: A 25-year-old woman had an uneventful suction evacuation for a complete hydatidiform mole confirmed on histopathology 8 weeks ago. Her initial post-evacuation beta-hCG was 85,000 IU/L. Weekly beta-hCG levels have been declining steadily: 42,000, 18,000, 7,500, 3,200, 1,400, 650, 320, 280. The last two levels at weeks 7 and 8 show a plateau (320 to 280 IU/L over 3 weekly readings).

data_table.Investigations: Serial beta-hCG: Week 1: 42,000 IU/L, Week 2: 18,000, Week 3: 7,500, Week 4: 3,200, Week 5: 1,400, Week 6: 650, Week 7: 320, Week 8: 280 IU/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue weekly beta-hCG monitoring for another 4 weeks
Repeat suction evacuation of the uterus under ultrasound guidance
Oral combined contraceptive pill to suppress gonadotrophins
Hysterectomy for definitive treatment of persistent mole
Referral to GTD centre for FIGO staging and chemotherapy

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation collapses in the hospital corridor. She is found to be pulseless and apnoeic. The cardiac arrest team begins CPR. The uterine fundus is palpable above the umbilicus. After 4 minutes of high-quality CPR with adrenaline administered, there is no return of spontaneous circulation.

data_table.Vital signs: Cardiac arrest. No pulse. No spontaneous breathing. Uterine fundus palpable 4 cm above the umbilicus (consistent with approximately 34 weeks).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue CPR for a further 10 minutes before considering surgery
Left lateral tilt and continue CPR until ROSC is achieved
Transfer to theatre for caesarean section under sterile conditions
Perimortem caesarean section performed at the point of arrest
Bedside ultrasound to confirm fetal viability before proceeding

subtopic_detail: Ovarian cyst in pregnancy - management by trimester
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation is found to have a 7 cm simple unilocular ovarian cyst on her dating scan. She is asymptomatic with no pain, nausea, or fever. A repeat ultrasound at 14 weeks confirms the cyst is persistent, simple (anechoic, thin-walled, no solid components, no internal septations), measuring 7.2 cm on the left ovary. CA-125 is 45 U/mL.

data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound 8 weeks: 6.8 cm simple left ovarian cyst. Ultrasound 14 weeks: 7.2 cm simple left ovarian cyst, unchanged morphology. No ascites. CA-125: 45 U/mL (note: CA-125 is physiologically elevated in pregnancy, especially first trimester).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent laparotomy for ovarian cyst removal this week
Observation with repeat ultrasound at 18-20 weeks
Laparoscopic cystectomy between 14 and 18 weeks gestation
CT pelvis to better characterise the cyst before deciding
Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the cyst contents

subtopic_detail: Fibroids in pregnancy - red degeneration management
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 22 weeks gestation presents with acute onset right-sided abdominal pain, nausea, and low-grade fever. She has a known 8 cm intramural uterine fibroid documented on her dating scan. The pain is localised to the right flank and is constant. She has no vaginal bleeding or contractions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 98, BP 120/75 mmHg, Temp 37.8 C, RR 18
data_table.Examination: Localised tenderness over the right lateral aspect of the uterus corresponding to the known fibroid location. The fibroid is exquisitely tender on palpation. No peritoneal signs. Cervix closed and long on digital examination.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 42 mg/L. Urinalysis: no leucocytes, no nitrites. Ultrasound: 8.5 cm intramural fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture suggesting internal haemorrhage. Fetus viable, normal amniotic fluid.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Analgesia, hydration, and supportive care with monitoring
Urgent myomectomy to remove the degenerating fibroid
IV antibiotics for suspected infected fibroid or abscess
Uterine artery embolisation to infarct the fibroid
Delivery by caesarean section to relieve the complication

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents to the early pregnancy assessment unit at 7 weeks gestation with mild left iliac fossa pain and light vaginal bleeding. She is haemodynamically stable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 22 mm left adnexal mass with a yolk sac but no cardiac activity, and an empty uterus. There is a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She has no significant past medical history, normal renal and hepatic function, and no history of methotrexate allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 118/72 mmHg, Temp 36.8
data_table.Investigations: beta-hCG 4,200 IU/L; FBC: Hb 128 g/L, WCC 7.8, platelets 245; LFTs and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta-hCG monitoring
Administer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2
Repeat the beta-hCG in 48 hours to assess the trajectory
Proceed with laparoscopic salpingostomy or salpingectomy
Administer anti-D immunoglobulin and reassess in one week

stem: A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome is reviewed in the gynaecology clinic. She takes warfarin for a previous deep vein thrombosis and hydroxychloroquine for her SLE. She had a miscarriage at 14 weeks gestation six months ago and does not wish to become pregnant for at least three years. Her periods are regular and she is normotensive. She asks about the most effective reversible contraception that is safe for her.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, BMI 24
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.4 (target 2.0-3.0); recent FBC, UEC, LFTs all normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive recommendation?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing low-dose oestrogen
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection every 12 weeks
Levonorgestrel intrauterine device for long-acting protection
Etonogestrel subdermal implant inserted in the non-dominant arm
Copper intrauterine device for non-hormonal long-acting effect

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset right iliac fossa pain that woke her from sleep 4 hours ago. She reports two episodes of vomiting. Her last menstrual period was 12 days ago and she has a known 6 cm right ovarian dermoid cyst found incidentally on ultrasound 3 months ago. She has no vaginal bleeding or discharge. On examination she has right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding but no rebound. Bowel sounds are present.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 122/78 mmHg, Temp 37.1, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta-hCG: negative; FBC: WCC 12.4 x10^9/L; CRP 18 mg/L; urinalysis: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast urgently
Administer analgesia and commence a trial of oral antibiotics
Observe with serial abdominal examinations over six hours
Request urgent pelvic ultrasound with Doppler flow assessment
Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without imaging

stem: A 28-year-old woman in her second pregnancy is reviewed at 20 weeks gestation. Her first pregnancy ended in a spontaneous second-trimester loss at 18 weeks with painless cervical dilatation. Her current pregnancy has been uncomplicated so far. A transvaginal ultrasound at her morphology scan shows a cervical length of 18 mm with funnelling of the internal os. She has no contractions, no vaginal bleeding, and the membranes are intact. The fetus has normal anatomy on ultrasound.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 112/68 mmHg, HR 78, Temp 36.7
data_table.Investigations: Cervical length 18 mm with funnelling; fetal anatomy normal; amniotic fluid index normal; group B streptococcus status unknown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly as monotherapy
Bed rest and weekly cervical length surveillance by ultrasound
Commence tocolytic therapy with nifedipine to prevent contractions
Insert a cervical cerclage and commence vaginal progesterone
Insert an emergency rescue cerclage after excluding infection

stem: A 34-year-old multiparous woman at 39 weeks gestation is in active labour with artificial rupture of membranes performed 20 minutes ago. She suddenly becomes agitated and dyspnoeic, then loses consciousness. Within minutes she develops tonic-clonic seizure activity. After initial resuscitation and seizure termination with midazolam, she is intubated. An emergency caesarean section is performed. Post-delivery, she develops profuse uterine bleeding that does not respond to uterotonics. Blood is noted to be non-clotting from IV sites and surgical wound.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 135, BP 72/40 mmHg, SpO2 88% on FiO2 1.0, Temp 36.2
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.08, lactate 8.4 mmol/L; FBC: Hb 68 g/L, platelets 32 x10^9/L; coags: PT 28 sec, APTT 62 sec, fibrinogen 0.4 g/L; D-dimer >20,000 ng/mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol and give cryoprecipitate
Administer IV heparin infusion to treat the underlying DIC
Commence IV magnesium sulfate for presumed eclamptic seizures
Perform perimortem hysterectomy to control uterine haemorrhage
Administer IV tranexamic acid 1 g and repeat uterotonics only

stem: A 35-year-old woman in her fourth pregnancy is found to have an anterior low-lying placenta at her 20-week morphology scan. She has had two previous caesarean sections and one vaginal delivery. She is asymptomatic with no vaginal bleeding. The sonographer notes lacunae within the placental substance and loss of the normal retroplacental clear zone on ultrasound. The woman asks about the implications of these findings.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 76
data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan: anterior low-lying placenta covering internal os, multiple placental lacunae, loss of retroplacental clear zone, bladder wall irregularity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure that the placenta will likely migrate and rescan at 32 weeks
Refer to a tertiary centre for MRI and multidisciplinary planning
Schedule elective caesarean section at 39 weeks at the local hospital
Commence low-dose aspirin to prevent placental insufficiency
Arrange serial ultrasounds every 2 weeks to monitor invasion depth

stem: A 29-year-old primigravida is referred at 28 weeks gestation after her fundal height measures 3 cm below expected. She has no significant medical history and is a non-smoker. Transvaginal ultrasound confirms a structurally normal fetus. Serology screening for infection is negative and karyotype is normal.

data_table.Ultrasound findings: Estimated fetal weight: Below 3rd centile for gestation; Abdominal circumference: Below 3rd centile for gestation; Umbilical artery Doppler: Absent end-diastolic flow; Middle cerebral artery Doppler: Reduced pulsatility index (brain-sparing); Ductus venosus Doppler: Normal a-wave; Amniotic fluid index: 6 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer antenatal corticosteroids and plan delivery within 48 hours following multidisciplinary discussion at a tertiary centre
Continue twice-weekly Doppler surveillance and cardiotocography with plan for delivery only if ductus venosus a-wave becomes reversed
Reassure the patient that this likely represents a constitutionally small fetus and repeat growth ultrasound in two weeks with standard antenatal care
Start low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily and low-molecular-weight heparin for presumed uteroplacental thrombosis and review in one week
Admit for continuous cardiotocography monitoring and plan to continue the pregnancy until at least 34 weeks to optimise neonatal outcomes

stem: A 33-year-old multigravida is seen at 35 weeks gestation for a routine growth scan. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. She has no hypertension, proteinuria, or symptoms. The fetus is cephalic and structurally normal. A previous growth scan at 30 weeks showed the estimated fetal weight on the 25th centile. The current scan results are provided.

data_table.Ultrasound findings: Estimated fetal weight: 12th centile (decreased from 25th centile at 30 weeks); Abdominal circumference: 10th centile; Growth velocity (AC): Reduced - crossing centiles downward; Umbilical artery Doppler PI: Normal; Middle cerebral artery Doppler PI: Reduced (below 5th centile); Cerebroplacental ratio (CPR): Below 5th centile; Amniotic fluid: Normal deepest vertical pocket

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure that all parameters are acceptable as the umbilical artery Doppler is normal and the EFW remains above the 10th centile, and continue standard antenatal care
Diagnose late-onset fetal growth restriction based on reduced growth velocity and abnormal CPR, increase surveillance, and plan delivery at 37 weeks gestation
Administer antenatal corticosteroids and deliver immediately by caesarean section given the evidence of fetal brain-sparing on middle cerebral artery Doppler
Repeat the growth ultrasound in three weeks at 38 weeks gestation and plan routine delivery at 39 weeks if growth velocity normalises on the next scan
Start low-dose aspirin 150 mg daily to improve placental perfusion and plan delivery at 39 weeks gestation if no further decline in growth velocity is observed

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 33 weeks gestation presents with a 2-week history of progressive generalised pruritus that is worst on the palms and soles and disrupts her sleep. She has no rash, jaundice, or abdominal pain. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg and urinalysis is normal. Investigation results are provided.

data_table.Blood results: Serum bile acids: 52 micromol/L (reference: <6 micromol/L); ALT: 78 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); AST: 65 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); Bilirubin: 18 micromol/L (reference: <20 micromol/L); Platelets: 245 x10^9/L (reference: 150-400 x10^9/L); INR: 1.0 (reference: 0.9-1.1)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence prednisolone 25 mg daily and plan delivery at 39 weeks gestation with weekly bile acid monitoring to assess treatment response
Start colestyramine 4 g twice daily as first-line bile acid binding therapy and plan delivery at 39 weeks gestation with fortnightly bile acid monitoring
Commence ursodeoxycholic acid 250 mg twice daily with dose titration, weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring, and plan delivery at 37 weeks gestation
Start ursodeoxycholic acid 250 mg twice daily with dose titration, weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring, and plan delivery at 38 weeks gestation
Start rifampicin 150 mg twice daily as first-line therapy for severe pruritus, weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring, and plan delivery at 37 weeks gestation

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation with a twin pregnancy presents with severe pruritus on her palms, soles, and trunk. She was commenced on ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily one week ago after initial bile acids were reported at 65 micromol/L. She has no epigastric pain, visual disturbance, or headache. Her blood pressure is 122/74 mmHg. Repeat investigation results are provided.

data_table.Blood results: Serum bile acids: 112 micromol/L (reference: <6 micromol/L); ALT: 128 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); AST: 105 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); Bilirubin: 32 micromol/L (reference: <20 micromol/L); Platelets: 210 x10^9/L (reference: 150-400 x10^9/L); INR: 1.3 (reference: 0.9-1.1); LDH: 180 U/L (reference: 120-250 U/L); Blood film: No schistocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase ursodeoxycholic acid to 500 mg three times daily, add colestyramine 4 g twice daily, and plan delivery at 37 weeks with twice-weekly bile acid and liver function monitoring
Administer vitamin K 10 mg orally, increase ursodeoxycholic acid to maximum dose, and continue monitoring with plan for delivery at 36 weeks based on serial bile acid levels
Stop ursodeoxycholic acid as it has been ineffective, commence dexamethasone 12 mg daily for 3 days to reduce bile acids, and deliver at 37 weeks gestation after completing the course
Administer vitamin K 10 mg orally to correct the coagulopathy, continue ursodeoxycholic acid at maximum tolerated dose, and plan delivery within the next 48 hours after fetal assessment

Admit for continuous cardiotocography of both twins, commence intravenous vitamin K 10 mg, and await bile acid levels to trend down on the current dose of ursodeoxycholic acid before deciding on delivery timing

stem:
A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with a sensation of vaginal heaviness and a bulge that she can feel at the vaginal introitus, worsening by the end of the day. She reports difficulty evacuating her bowels and occasionally needs to digitally support the posterior vaginal wall to defecate. She is otherwise well, has a BMI of 28 kg/m2, and had three vaginal deliveries.

She is not sexually active. On examination, there is a Stage II cystocele and rectocele with the leading edge reaching the hymen. She has not tried any treatment for this condition.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for vaginal hysterectomy with anterior and posterior colporrhaphy as she has a symptomatic multi-compartment prolapse requiring definitive surgical correction
Commence topical vaginal oestrogen and refer for sacrocolpopexy with mesh as this provides the most durable repair for multi-compartment prolapse in postmenopausal women
Advise weight loss to a BMI below 25 kg/m2 and commence oral hormone replacement therapy to improve pelvic tissue support, with review in six months to assess symptom improvement
Commence topical vaginal oestrogen and prescribe a bulk-forming laxative for bowel symptoms, with review in three months and surgical referral only if symptoms persist unchanged
Commence topical vaginal oestrogen, refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training, and offer a trial of a vaginal pessary with review in three to six months to assess symptom response

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents 6 months after the vaginal delivery of her third child. She reports involuntary urine leakage when she coughs, sneezes, or lifts her toddler. She denies urgency, frequency, nocturia, or pain. She does not leak during sleep. She has no urinary tract infection symptoms and a midstream urine culture was negative. She has a BMI of 26 kg/m2 and is otherwise well.

On examination, there is mild anterior vaginal wall descent but no prolapse beyond the hymen. A cough stress test in standing is positive with a small volume leak.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist for a minimum of three months with a structured exercise program and regular review
Commence oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for 3 months to reduce detrusor overactivity contributing to her urinary incontinence and review symptom response at follow-up
Refer for urodynamic studies to confirm the diagnosis of stress urinary incontinence before commencing any treatment, as clinical assessment alone is insufficient in multiparous women
Refer for mid-urethral sling surgery as a definitive treatment given she has completed her family and has demonstrated stress incontinence on clinical examination with a positive cough test
Recommend general fitness exercise including Pilates and yoga for core strengthening, reduce caffeine intake, and review in six months to assess whether symptoms have resolved spontaneously

stem:
A 35-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a 12-month history of progressively heavy menstrual bleeding. Her periods occur regularly every 28 days and last 8 to 9 days. She soaks through a super pad every 2 hours on her heaviest days and has passed clots. She reports fatigue and exertional dyspnoea. She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.

She is not taking any hormonal contraception or anticoagulants. Her cervical screening is up to date and normal. Clinical examination reveals a slightly bulky uterus with no adnexal mass.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial set of investigations?

options.text: Hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy, coagulation studies including von Willebrand screen, and thyroid function tests to identify structural and haematological causes simultaneously
Full blood count, serum ferritin, and pelvic ultrasound to assess for anaemia and structural pathology as the initial step in the systematic evaluation of heavy menstrual bleeding
Serum beta-hCG, thyroid function tests, and prolactin level to exclude hormonal and endocrine causes of heavy menstrual bleeding before any imaging is performed on this patient
Pelvic MRI to characterise any fibroids and adenomyosis, von Willebrand factor assay, and endometrial biopsy to exclude endometrial pathology as the comprehensive first-line investigation
Full blood count, serum ferritin, coagulation studies with von Willebrand screen, thyroid function tests, and saline infusion sonohysterography as a comprehensive baseline workup

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents for review of her heavy menstrual bleeding. She was initially treated with tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses and mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily, which has provided only partial relief after 3 months. Her periods still last 8 days with heavy flow. She does not desire future fertility. Pelvic ultrasound showed a normal-sized uterus with a single intramural fibroid measuring 2 cm in diameter not distorting the endometrial cavity. Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L and ferritin is 12 microg/L. She has no contraindications to hormonal therapy.

data_table.Previous treatment: Tranexamic acid: 1 g TDS during menses - 3 months - partial response; Mefenamic acid: 500 mg TDS during menses - 3 months - partial response

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer for total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy as she has completed her family and medical treatment has failed to control her symptoms
Add the combined oral contraceptive pill to her current regimen of tranexamic acid and mefenamic acid to achieve additional menstrual suppression for the next six months
Refer for uterine artery embolisation to treat the intramural fibroid, as the fibroid is the likely cause of her heavy menstrual bleeding and medical management has been insufficient
Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the intramural fibroid combined with endometrial ablation as a combined surgical approach to definitively manage both the fibroid and the heavy bleeding
Insert a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (52 mg) and commence oral iron supplementation, with review at three to six months to assess treatment response and haemoglobin improvement

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department 5 days after oocyte retrieval during an IVF cycle. She underwent controlled ovarian hyperstimulation with gonadotrophins and received an hCG trigger. Twenty-two oocytes were retrieved. She reports progressive abdominal distension, nausea, reduced oral intake, and has passed only small volumes of dark urine over the past 12 hours. Her observations and investigation results are provided.

data_table.Observations: Heart rate: 105 bpm; Blood pressure: 98/62 mmHg; Respiratory rate: 22 breaths/min; Oxygen saturation: 96% on room air; Temperature: 37.2 C
data_table.Blood results: Haemoglobin: 162 g/L (reference: 115-160 g/L); Haematocrit: 0.48 (reference: 0.33-0.44); White cell count: 18.2 x10^9/L (reference: 4.0-11.0 x10^9/L); Platelets: 380 x10^9/L (reference: 150-400 x10^9/L); Sodium: 131 mmol/L (reference: 135-145 mmol/L); Potassium: 5.4 mmol/L (reference: 3.5-5.0 mmol/L); Creatinine: 125 micromol/L (reference: 45-90 micromol/L); Albumin: 22 g/L (reference: 35-50 g/L)
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound: Bilaterally enlarged ovaries (right 10 cm, left 9 cm) with multiple large follicles and moderate free fluid in the pelvis and paracolic gutters

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence intravenous furosemide 40 mg to manage the fluid overload causing abdominal distension, restrict intravenous fluids, and commence prophylactic subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily
Admit for observation, commence oral fluid intake encouragement with a target of 2 litres daily, withhold anticoagulation as there is no confirmed thrombosis, and plan outpatient review in 48 hours

Admit and commence intravenous crystalloid resuscitation targeting a urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hour, commence prophylactic subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily, and consider intravenous albumin infusion

Admit and perform immediate therapeutic paracentesis to drain the ascitic fluid causing abdominal distension and oliguria, commence intravenous colloid, and withhold anticoagulation until after the procedure

Commence intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, administer cabergoline 0.5 mg daily to reduce VEGF-mediated capillary permeability, commence prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily, and restrict oral fluid intake

stem:
A 32-year-old woman in her third pregnancy presents at 20 weeks gestation for a routine morphology ultrasound. Her obstetric history includes two previous mid-trimester losses: the first at 18 weeks and the second at 21 weeks, both characterised by painless cervical dilatation without antecedent bleeding or infection. In the current pregnancy she has had no vaginal bleeding, contractions, or discharge.

She was not offered cervical length surveillance earlier in this pregnancy. The morphology scan shows a structurally normal fetus. A transvaginal cervical length measurement is performed.

data_table.Ultrasound findings: Cervical length (transvaginal): 15 mm; Funnelling: Present - V-shaped internal os funnelling; Fetal presentation: Cephalic; Membranes: Intact, no prolapse into cervical canal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly as the primary intervention and perform serial cervical length measurements every two weeks with cerclage only if the cervix shortens below 10 mm
Insert an Arabin cervical pessary as a non-surgical alternative to cerclage, commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly, and perform cervical length surveillance every two weeks until 28 weeks

Admit for bed rest and tocolysis with nifedipine 20 mg sustained-release twice daily, commence antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation, and plan expectant management until viability at 24 weeks
Perform a McDonald cerclage within the next 24 to 48 hours after confirming no evidence of infection or labour, and commence vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly as adjunctive therapy
Refer for transabdominal cerclage placement as this provides superior outcomes to transvaginal cerclage when the cervix has already shortened to 15 mm with funnelling at 20 weeks gestation

stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks gestation presents with a 24-hour history of epigastric pain, nausea, and malaise. She has had an uncomplicated pregnancy to date. On examination her blood pressure is 152/96 mmHg. She has right upper quadrant tenderness but no peripheral oedema. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein. Her investigation results are provided.

data_table.Blood results: Haemoglobin: 98 g/L (reference: 115-160 g/L); Platelets: 68 x10^9/L (reference: 150-400 x10^9/L); Blood film: Schistocytes and fragmented red cells; LDH: 820 U/L (reference: 120-250 U/L); AST: 310 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); ALT: 285 U/L (reference: <35 U/L); Bilirubin: 42 micromol/L (reference: <20 micromol/L); Creatinine: 95 micromol/L (reference: 45-90 micromol/L); INR: 1.1 (reference: 0.9-1.1); Fibrinogen: 3.8 g/L (reference: 2.0-4.0 g/L); Urate: 0.45 mmol/L (reference: 0.15-0.35 mmol/L)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral labetalol 200 mg twice daily, administer antenatal corticosteroids, and plan delivery at 37 weeks gestation if the platelet count stabilises above 100 x10^9/L
Stabilise with intravenous antihypertensive therapy, commence magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, administer antenatal corticosteroids, and plan delivery within 24 to 48 hours
Commence plasma exchange for presumed thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura given the microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, and defer delivery until the platelet count improves
Commence N-acetylcysteine for hepatoprotection given the markedly elevated transaminases, restrict intravenous fluids to prevent pulmonary oedema, and plan delivery at 36 weeks gestation
Diagnose acute fatty liver of pregnancy based on the liver dysfunction and haemolysis, commence intravenous dextrose infusion to prevent hypoglycaemia, and plan immediate caesarean delivery

stem: A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation collapses in the emergency department waiting room. She is found to be in cardiac arrest with an initial rhythm of pulseless electrical activity. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is commenced immediately following advanced life support protocols. Manual left uterine displacement is applied. Intravenous access is established and adrenaline 1 mg is administered. After 4 minutes of high-quality CPR, the patient remains in cardiac arrest with no return of spontaneous circulation. The fetal heart was documented as present on a brief bedside ultrasound performed during a rhythm check.

data_table.Clinical details: Gestation: 32 weeks (confirmed by antenatal records); Uterine fundal height: At the umbilicus, consistent with gestation; Time since arrest: 4 minutes; CPR quality: High quality with manual uterine displacement; Rhythm: PEA throughout; Reversible causes addressed: IV access, adrenaline given, no obvious cause identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue CPR with manual left uterine displacement for a further 6 minutes to complete a standard 10-minute resuscitation cycle before considering any surgical intervention for the arrest

Place the patient in a full left lateral position for CPR to relieve aortocaval compression, as this is more effective than manual uterine displacement, and continue resuscitation for a further 10 minutes

Transfer the patient urgently to the operating theatre for perimortem caesarean section under optimal surgical conditions, continuing CPR during transfer to ensure the best possible surgical environment

Consult the on-call obstetrician to attend and perform the perimortem caesarean section while continuing CPR, as the procedure requires an experienced obstetrician to minimise maternal surgical complications

Commence perimortem caesarean section immediately at the current location while continuing CPR, aiming for delivery within 1 minute of skin incision, performed by the most experienced clinician available
